chunks.text: None routinely required — Diagnosis is clinical; investigations are reserved for atypical course, prolonged symptoms, or red-flag features suggesting pneumonia.
Chest X-ray (only if pneumonia cannot be excluded clinically) — To rule out consolidation if exam findings are equivocal or symptoms persist beyond expected course.
Acute Bronchitis (infective) — Respiratory
veryLikely: Respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, influenza, RSV, coronavirus); likely: Bordetella pertussis (if prolonged cough >2 weeks, paroxysmal, or known exposure)
Abdominal ultrasound or CT — Characterizes the abscess (typically single, right lobe, in amoebic disease) and guides the decision on aspiration.
Amoebic serology (IgG) — Highly sensitive for invasive amoebiasis and useful when aspiration is not performed or is inconclusive.
Stool microscopy for E. histolytica (trophozoites/cysts) — Supportive if positive, but a substantial proportion of liver abscess patients have negative stool studies at the time of presentation.

Diagnostic aspiration (if no improvement in 5-7 days, large/left-lobe abscess, or diagnostic uncertainty) — Classic 'anchovy paste' aspirate supports amoebic etiology; also allows bacterial culture to exclude/identify a pyogenic or mixed process.
Amoebic Liver Abscess (infective) — Hepatobiliary / Tropical Fever
veryLikely: Entamoeba histolytica; possible: Concurrent or preceding intestinal amoebiasis (only a minority have concurrent diarrhea at presentation)

[guideline] empiric → Metronidazole / Followed by a luminal agent (Paromomycin or Diloxanide furoate) Highly effective tissue amoebicide for invasive disease including liver abscess, with response typically seen within days; first-line for amoebic liver abscess based on strong clinical/imaging suspicion.
[guideline] alternative → Tinidazole (alternative tissue amoebicide)
Chest X-ray — Aspiration classically affects dependent lung segments (posterior upper lobes if aspirated supine, basal segments of lower lobes if upright) — helpful in confirming the diagnosis.
Swallowing assessment (if recurrent or ongoing risk) — Identifies the underlying mechanism (dysphagia, reduced consciousness) to prevent recurrence.
CBC, CRP — Supports severity assessment and baseline for response monitoring.
Aspiration Pneumonia (infective) — Respiratory

veryLikely: Oral anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Fusobacterium), Streptococcus pneumoniae; likely: Staphylococcus aureus, Enterobacteriaceae (if hospital-associated aspiration); possible: Klebsiella pneumoniae (classically associated with aspiration in alcoholics)

[guideline] empiric → Amoxicillin-clavulanate Provides reliable coverage of oral anaerobes alongside typical community pathogens, addressing the polymicrobial nature of aspiration pneumonia in a single well-tolerated agent.
[guideline] alternative → Clindamycin (penicillin allergy)
[guideline] alternative → Piperacillin-tazobactam (hospital-associated or severe)
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI brain — Confirms the diagnosis, localizes the abscess, and is essential for surgical planning; MRI is more sensitive, particularly for early/cerebritis-stage lesions.
Stereotactic aspiration or surgical drainage with culture — Provides definitive microbiological diagnosis and is often therapeutic, particularly for abscesses >2.5cm.
Blood cultures — May identify the organism in hematogenous spread, supporting de-escalation.
Echocardiography (if hematogenous spread suspected) — Screens for infective endocarditis as the source, which would change the overall management plan significantly.
HIV testing (if risk factors or atypical presentation) — Relevant given the broader differential (e.g., toxoplasmosis) in immunocompromised hosts.
Brain Abscess (infective) — Central Nervous System

veryLikely: Streptococcus species (including anaerobic/microaerophilic strains), Anaerobes (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium); likely: Staphylococcus aureus (especially post-neurosurgery or hematogenous spread), Enterobacteriaceae (especially with otogenic or sinus source); possible: Nocardia, Toxoplasma, or fungal causes in immunocompromised patients (broader workup needed)
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole / Add Vancomycin if S. aureus risk (post-neurosurgery, hematogenous spread, endocarditis) This combination covers the major contiguous-spread pathogens (streptococci, anaerobes, and many Enterobacteriaceae) and provides good CNS penetration, appropriate pending culture/aspirate results.
[guideline] alternative → Meropenem (broader gram-negative coverage, e.g. otogenic source with Pseudomonas risk)
Sputum culture (every exacerbation) — Tracks colonization status over time and directly informs both current and future empiric choices.
Chest X-ray (if new symptoms or to exclude complications) — Excludes pneumonia or other acute complications superimposed on chronic bronchiectatic changes.
Pulse oximetry — Assesses for hypoxia, particularly relevant in patients with significant structural lung disease.
Bronchiectasis Exacerbation (infective) — Respiratory

veryLikely: Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (especially in advanced/long-standing disease); likely: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis; possible: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (in chronic, treatment-refractory cases — separate workup)

[guideline] empiric → Per prior sputum culture if available; empirically Amoxicillin-clavulanate if no Pseudomonas history / Ciprofloxacin (if prior Pseudomonas colonization) Bronchiectasis exacerbations are typically treated with longer courses than simple bronchitis given the structural lung disease; prior culture history should directly guide empiric choice given high rates of chronic colonization.
[guideline] alternative → Piperacillin-tazobactam (severe exacerbation with Pseudomonas history)
Chest X-ray — Confirms presence and pattern of consolidation; supports diagnosis and baseline for response assessment.
CBC — Leukocytosis with neutrophilia supports a bacterial process and provides a baseline.
CRP — Elevated CRP supports bacterial etiology and can track response.
Pulse oximetry — Screens for hypoxia which would reclassify severity and site of care.
Community Acquired Pneumonia (non-severe) (infective) — Respiratory
veryLikely: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae; likely: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae; possible: Legionella pneumophila, Respiratory viruses (influenza, RSV)

[guideline] empiric → Amoxicillin / Azithromycin (if atypical features or comorbidity) Amoxicillin is first-line for outpatient CAP without comorbidity — it reliably covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, the dominant pathogen, with a narrow spectrum that limits collateral damage.
[guideline] alternative → Doxycycline
[guideline] alternative → Levofloxacin

Urine culture (from newly placed catheter if replacing, or freshly collected sample) — Essential given the high resistance burden and biofilm-related polymicrobial colonization in this population — guides definitive therapy.
Blood cultures (if systemically unwell) — CA-UTI can be a source of bacteremia/urosepsis; positive cultures confirm systemic involvement.
Renal function tests — Baseline assessment, particularly relevant if upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis) is suspected.
Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (infective) — Genitourinary

veryLikely: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis; likely: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterococcus species, Candida species (colonization common, true infection less so); possible: Polymicrobial flora, especially with long-term catheterization

[guideline] empiric → Per prior urine culture if available; empirically Ceftriaxone if unknown Empiric choice should ideally be guided by prior catheter-associated culture history given the high rate of resistant organisms in this population; ceftriaxone is a reasonable default pending current culture results.
[guideline] alternative → Piperacillin-tazobactam (if Pseudomonas risk or prior resistant organism)
Erysipelas (S. pyogenes superficial dermal/lymphatic infection with sharply demarcated, raised, indurated borders and abrupt fiery-red swelling) (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Necrotizing fasciitis / deeper necrotizing soft-tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Purulent cellulitis associated with a focal staphylococcal lesion such as a furuncle, carbuncle, or abscess (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Herpes zoster (dermatomal vesicular eruption may be mistaken for cellulitis early) (Harrison 22e p.93)
Gram stain and culture of drainage, open wound, or identifiable portal of entry when present, for definitive etiology (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy of involved skin in selected cases, recognizing low (~20%) culture yield (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Stasis dermatitis, which when acutely inflamed with crusting and exudate is easily confused with cellulitis; symmetric bilateral leg involvement favors stasis dermatitis (Harrison 22e p.428, p.436)
Eczema (Harrison 22e p.93)
Lymphedema (Harrison 22e p.93)
Contact dermatitis (Harrison 22e p.428)

Bacteria reach the dermis and subcutaneous soft tissue after disruption of the epidermal barrier by cracks, abrasions, cuts, burns, insect bites, surgical incisions, IV catheters, trauma, tinea/fungal infection, or pressure and venous-stasis ulcers. Organisms already colonizing the skin (notably S. aureus and group A streptococci) most readily exploit such breaks, though many exogenous bacteria can be introduced. Streptococcal disease characteristically spreads diffusely via lymphatics, producing lymphangitis, whereas staphylococcal disease spreads from a central focus such as an abscess or infected foreign body. Much of the expanding erythema reflects the action of bacterial extracellular toxins and host-derived inflammatory mediators rather than high bacterial burden. Progression to deeper structures with loss of vascular integrity (purple bullae, ecchymosis, cutaneous anesthesia) signals possible necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095, p.1007).

Non-purulent cellulitis (no associated abscess, focal purulence, or drainage) is a rapidly spreading, diffuse process typically due to S. pyogenes, often accompanied by lymphangitis and fever; purulent cellulitis arising from a focal lesion (furuncle, carbuncle, abscess, surgical wound) is more likely staphylococcal (Harrison 22e p.1095).

Even with needle aspiration of the advancing edge or punch biopsy of involved tissue, cultures are positive in only about 20% of cases, suggesting low bacterial numbers and that much of the spreading erythema is driven by extracellular toxins and host inflammatory mediators (Harrison 22e p.1095).

When a draining wound or visible portal of entry is present, Gram stain and culture of that material can give a definitive microbiologic diagnosis, unlike cultures of intact cellulitic skin (Harrison 22e p.1095).

A careful exposure/epidemiologic history is diagnostically valuable because many less common causative organisms occupy characteristic ecological niches (e.g., cat/dog bite, freshwater laceration, fish/swine handling, aquarium water) (Harrison 22e p.1095).
Bilateral, symmetric lower-leg involvement favors a mimic such as stasis dermatitis, whereas true cellulitis is usually unilateral (Harrison 22e p.428).
Routine cultures of intact cellulitic skin are frequently negative (positive in only ~20% even with aspiration or biopsy), so negative cultures do NOT exclude cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1095).

When patients labeled 'cellulitis' are reviewed by dermatology, roughly one-third have an alternative diagnosis (e.g., eczema, lymphedema), so an overcall risks unnecessary hospitalization and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.93).
Bilateral symmetric lower-extremity erythema is more likely stasis dermatitis than cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.428).
Early necrotizing fasciitis may present with pain or unexplained fever as the only manifestation; do NOT rely on overt cutaneous inflammation to exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1095).
Purple/hemorrhagic bullae, ecchymosis, or cutaneous anesthesia suggesting loss of vascular integrity and possible necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Pain or tenderness disproportionate to visible skin findings, or unexplained fever with deep soft-tissue pain even without overt skin inflammation (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Brawny edema, dark-red induration, skin friability with bluish/maroon/black discoloration, or systemic toxicity/shock indicating deep necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095)

Harrison distinguishes non-purulent cellulitis (diffuse, spreading, typically streptococcal, often with lymphangitis and fever) from purulent cellulitis (associated with a focal lesion such as furuncle, carbuncle, abscess, or surgical wound, typically staphylococcal, the FDA-preferred term for these). Loss of vascular integrity (purple bullae, ecchymosis, cutaneous anesthesia, systemic toxicity) marks progression toward necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095).
None routinely required for typical mild-moderate cellulitis — Diagnosis is clinical; cultures of intact cellulitic skin have low yield.
Blood cultures (if systemically unwell or immunocompromised) — Identifies bacteremic spread in more severe presentations.
Wound/abscess culture (if purulent drainage present) — Identifies organism and susceptibility, particularly important given variable MRSA prevalence.
CBC, CRP — Supports severity assessment and provides a baseline to track response.
Cellulitis (infective) — Skin & Soft Tissue

veryLikely: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus); likely: Staphylococcus aureus (more likely if purulent drainage or abscess present); possible: MRSA (if risk factors: prior MRSA, IV drug use, recent hospitalization)

[guideline] empiric → Cefazolin (IV) or Cephalexin (oral, mild) First-generation cephalosporins reliably cover streptococci and methicillin-susceptible S. aureus, the dominant pathogens in non-purulent cellulitis.
[guideline] alternative → Clindamycin
[guideline] alternative → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or Doxycycline (if MRSA risk/purulent)
Dengue (co-circulating Aedes-borne flavivirus; may coinfect) (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060)
Zika virus infection (Aedes-borne; can also cause joint manifestations) (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060)
Other arthritogenic alphaviruses with clinically similar presentations: Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus, Sindbis virus, o'nyong-nyong virus, Mayaro virus (Harrison 22e p.1712)

CHIKV is an arthropod-borne alphavirus (family Togaviridae) spread by Aedes mosquitoes. It produces an acute febrile illness with prominent joint involvement; rheumatic manifestations span arthralgia with or without inflammatory signs (periarticular redness, swelling, immobility). Adults experience more severe and articular-predominant disease than children. Chronic musculoskeletal sequelae are thought to relate to host factors, with increased risk in patients who have preexisting osteoarthritis, severe acute disease, or the HLA-B27 subtype, and may be associated with cryoglobulins (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is an arthritogenic alphavirus transmitted by Aedes (yellow-fever and Asian tiger) mosquitoes; after a 2-10 day incubation it causes abrupt high fever, sometimes with a saddleback pattern, plus severe arthralgia (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Migratory polyarthritis predominantly involves the small joints of the hands, wrists, ankles, and feet, though larger joints may also be affected; periarticular swelling and immobility are common, while frank effusions are less frequent (Harrison 22e p.1712).

A rash appears at onset or several days in, often coinciding with defervescence around day 2-3, is most intense over trunk and limbs, and may desquamate; children more often develop a bullous rather than maculopapular/petechial rash (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Although petechiae and epistaxis are occasionally seen, CHIKV should not be classified as a cause of viral hemorrhagic fever; older reports of 'chikungunya hemorrhagic fever' largely reflected concurrent dengue coinfection (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1706).

A recovery period of weeks is common, and a substantial proportion of middle-aged to older patients go on to develop chronic, sometimes disabling arthritis or arthralgia syndromes typically involving the same joints (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Pregnant women are not at increased risk of severe disease, but there is a high risk of maternal-fetal transmission, especially intrapartum, which has occasionally led to fetal death (Harrison 22e p.1712).

A live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine was approved in the United States in 2023 for adults at increased exposure risk and is contraindicated in immunocompromised persons; about 12% of recipients developed chikungunya-like symptoms in trials (Harrison 22e p.1060).
Do not label CHIKV as a viral hemorrhagic fever despite occasional petechiae/epistaxis; apparent 'hemorrhagic' cases historically reflected concurrent dengue infection (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1706).
Do not assume severe disease in pregnancy; the principal pregnancy concern is intrapartum vertical transmission rather than maternal severity (Harrison 22e p.1712).
Do not consider the live-attenuated vaccine safe in immunocompromised persons, in whom it is contraindicated (Harrison 22e p.1060).

Life-threatening illness is rare; most patients recover, though recovery may take weeks. A significant fraction of middle-aged to older patients develop chronic, potentially disabling arthritis/arthralgia. Deaths have been reported, typically in the setting of large outbreaks. Children generally have milder disease and are less frequently hospitalized (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060).
Cardiorespiratory, neurologic, renal, or ocular complications in severe acute disease (uncommon but reported, typically in hospitalized patients) (Harrison 22e p.1712)
Pregnancy near delivery, given high risk of intrapartum maternal-fetal transmission and reported fetal death (Harrison 22e p.1712)
Chikungunya IgM serology / RT-PCR (early illness) — Confirms the diagnosis; RT-PCR is most sensitive in the first few days, IgM becomes detectable slightly later.
Dengue NS1/serology (concurrent testing) — Co-circulation with dengue is common and clinical distinction is imperfect — concurrent testing avoids missing dengue, which has different monitoring needs.
CBC — Typically shows lymphopenia rather than the thrombocytopenia more characteristic of dengue, supporting clinical distinction.
Chikungunya (infective) — Tropical Fever
veryLikely: Chikungunya virus
Blood cultures — Frequently positive in cholangitis and identifies organism/susceptibility for de-escalation.
Liver function tests — Cholestatic pattern (elevated bilirubin, ALP, GGT) supports the diagnosis and tracks resolution after drainage.
Abdominal ultrasound — First-line imaging to identify biliary dilation and the level of obstruction.
MRCP or CT abdomen (if ultrasound inconclusive) — Better characterizes the cause and location of obstruction (stone, stricture, malignancy) to guide definitive drainage strategy.
Bile culture (at time of ERCP/drainage) — Identifies the causative organism directly from the infected source for the most targeted de-escalation.
Acute Cholangitis (infective) — Hepatobiliary

veryLikely: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae; likely: Enterococcus species, Enterobacter species; possible: Anaerobes (Bacteroides species) — particularly with prior biliary instrumentation or surgery
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Piperacillin-tazobactam Provides reliable coverage of gram-negative enteric organisms and anaerobes, the dominant pathogens in cholangitis, and is appropriate first-line per Tokyo Guidelines for moderate-severe disease.
[guideline] alternative → Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole
[guideline] alternative → Meropenem (if prior biliary instrumentation, MDR risk, or severe/grade III disease)
Abdominal ultrasound — First-line imaging — gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid support the diagnosis.
Liver function tests — Typically mildly elevated; significant jaundice should prompt consideration of choledocholithiasis or cholangitis instead.
CBC — Leukocytosis supports the diagnosis and tracks response.
Blood cultures (if systemically unwell) — May identify bacteremia and guide de-escalation.
Acute Cholecystitis (infective) — Hepatobiliary
veryLikely: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae; likely: Enterococcus species, Anaerobes (Bacteroides) — more relevant in severe/gangrenous cholecystitis

[guideline] empiric → Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole Covers the typical gram-negative and anaerobic biliary pathogens; definitive treatment is cholecystectomy, with antibiotics primarily bridging to surgery or covering milder cases managed non-operatively.
[guideline] alternative → Piperacillin-tazobactam (more severe disease)

Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis, AFB smear, CBNAAT/Xpert, and culture — CSF in TB meningitis classically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, and high protein; CBNAAT provides faster confirmation and rifampicin resistance status than culture.
MRI brain with contrast — Identifies basal meningeal enhancement, tuberculomas, infarcts, and hydrocephalus — all characteristic complications requiring specific management.
Chest X-ray — Concurrent or prior pulmonary TB is common and supports the diagnosis.
HIV testing — TB meningitis is disproportionately seen in HIV co-infection, which changes overall management and prognosis.
CNS Tuberculosis (TB Meningitis) (infective) — Central Nervous System / Tuberculosis
veryLikely: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol (HRZE) + Corticosteroids Same four-drug backbone as pulmonary TB but with a longer continuation phase given the severity of CNS involvement; adjunctive corticosteroids are specifically indicated in TB meningitis (unlike most TB) as they reduce mortality and neurological sequelae.
[guideline] alternative → Modified regimens per drug-susceptibility/resistance testing
Urine culture and sensitivity — Essential in complicated UTI given higher rates of resistant organisms — guides definitive therapy.
Renal function tests — Assesses baseline renal function, particularly relevant if structural abnormality or obstruction is suspected.
Renal ultrasound (if recurrent or treatment failure) — Evaluates for obstruction, stones, or structural abnormality contributing to complicated infection.
Complicated Urinary Tract Infection (infective) — Genitourinary

veryLikely: Escherichia coli (often with resistant phenotypes); likely: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus species; possible: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (catheter-associated, prior instrumentation)

[guideline] empiric → Ciprofloxacin (if local resistance acceptable) or based on prior culture Provides reliable broad coverage of typical complicated UTI pathogens; duration extended relative to uncomplicated cystitis given higher relapse risk.
drugRefs: ciprofloxacin or based on prior culture

chunks.text: [guideline] alternative → Ceftriaxone (if oral therapy not tolerated or resistance suspected)
Pulse oximetry / ABG — Assesses for hypoxia or hypercapnic respiratory failure, which determines need for ventilatory support and site of care.
Chest X-ray — Excludes pneumonia, pneumothorax, or other alternative/complicating diagnoses presenting similarly.
Sputum culture (if frequent exacerbator or treatment failure) — Identifies resistant or atypical organisms (e.g., Pseudomonas) in patients with recurrent exacerbations.
Acute COPD Exacerbation (infective) — Respiratory

veryLikely: Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis; likely: Respiratory viruses (a substantial proportion of exacerbations are viral, not bacterial); possible: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (in severe COPD with frequent exacerbations, prior isolation, or recent hospitalization)

[guideline] empiric → Amoxicillin-clavulanate Covers the three classic bacterial triggers (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis) when antibiotics are indicated by Anthonisen criteria, particularly sputum purulence.
[guideline] alternative → Doxycycline
[guideline] alternative → Levofloxacin (severe exacerbation, frequent exacerbator, or Pseudomonas risk)
Urinalysis — Confirms pyuria and supports the diagnosis before starting therapy.
Urine culture (only if treatment failure, recurrence, or atypical features) — Not routinely needed in straightforward uncomplicated cystitis, but useful if symptoms persist or recur.
Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis (infective) — Genitourinary
veryLikely: Escherichia coli; likely: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus saprophyticus; possible: Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus species

[guideline] empiric → Nitrofurantoin First-line for uncomplicated cystitis — narrow urinary-tract-specific spectrum, low resistance rates, and minimal collateral ecological damage compared to broader agents.
[guideline] alternative → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
[guideline] alternative → Fosfomycin

Stool C. difficile toxin EIA and/or PCR (per local two-step algorithm) — Confirms the diagnosis; testing only symptomatic patients (not all diarrhea, and never asymptomatic patients) avoids overdiagnosis of colonization.
Abdominal X-ray or CT (if severe/fulminant presentation suspected) — Screens for toxic megacolon or ileus, which would change management to include surgical involvement.
CBC, renal function, albumin — Supports severity classification (e.g., leukocytosis >15,000, rising creatinine define severe disease per IDSA criteria) which guides treatment intensity.
Clostridioides difficile Infection (infective) — Gastrointestinal
veryLikely: Clostridioides difficile (toxigenic strains)

[guideline] empiric → Oral Vancomycin Oral (not IV) vancomycin is first-line for C. difficile infection — it acts locally in the gut lumen and is not systemically absorbed, which is precisely why it works here despite IV vancomycin having no role in typical gut infections.
[guideline] alternative → Fidaxomicin (preferred where available/affordable)
[guideline] alternative → Metronidazole (only if vancomycin/fidaxomicin unavailable, non-severe disease)
Zika virus disease (often misdiagnosed as dengue; low-grade fever, itchy maculopapular rash, arthralgia/myalgia, nonpurulent conjunctivitis)
Influenza
Other arboviral fevers presenting as fever-and-myalgia syndrome
Chikungunya
Zika virus infection
Yellow fever
Leptospirosis
Other viral hemorrhagic fevers
Antigen-detection ELISA or RT-PCR (nucleic acid amplification) during the acute phase, useful within roughly the first 5 days of illness (p.1714, 1721)
Combination point-of-care testing pairing NS1 antigen with IgM antibody assay, increasingly used clinically (p.1721)
Paired (acute and convalescent) serology during recovery (p.1714)
Serum AST (often modestly elevated without true hepatic synthetic dysfunction) (p.1714)
Tourniquet test as a bedside marker of microvascular fragility (p.1714)

Dengue is caused by the four flavivirus (orthoflavivirus) serotypes DENV-1 to DENV-4, transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti (and the secondary vector Aedes albopictus), which bite during the day. After infection of one serotype, the cross-protection against a different (heterotypic) serotype is only transient and wanes within weeks to a few weeks of convalescence; subsequent heterotypic infection can produce classic dengue or, less often, severe dengue. The progression to severe disease centers on immune-mediated enhancement, in which enhancing, non-neutralizing antibodies are implicated, whereas neutralizing antibodies are associated with lower viremia on reinfection. The hallmark of severe dengue is a vascular-leak syndrome producing increased capillary permeability, intravascular volume depletion, hypoalbuminemia, and serosal (pleural, ascitic) effusions; recent evidence assigns the DENV NS1 protein a key role in this vascular leak. Host/viral risk modifiers include age (susceptibility to severe dengue drops markedly after 12 years), the specific sequence and timing of serotype infections (e.g., DENV-1 then DENV-2 tends to be more severe), and viral-variant heterogeneity (p.1711, 1721).

Symptomatic dengue evolves through three phases: febrile, critical (plasma leakage), and recovery; most patients never enter the critical phase, but the possibility must be actively considered in every case (p.1714).

The critical/plasma-leakage phase characteristically begins around the time fever subsides (defervescence, roughly days 3-5), so worsening at this transition - not at peak fever - signals deterioration (p.1721).
A 'saddle-back' fever pattern (recurrence of fever after defervescence and a brief remission) can occur in a subset of patients (p.1714).
Most primary DENV infections are subclinical, and only about 25% of the ~400 million annual infections cause clinical illness (p.1711).
Incubation is approximately 4-7 days (p.1714).
A positive tourniquet test (>=10 new petechiae per square inch on the upper arm after BP-cuff inflation for 5 min) reflects microvascular damage and is more often linked to severe dengue (p.1714).
Near defervescence a maculopapular rash typically starts on the trunk and spreads to the extremities and face; a separate transient macular rash may appear at illness onset (p.1714).
During recovery a patchy erythematous pruritic rash that desquamates may develop as extravascular fluid and effusions are reabsorbed (p.1722).
Early IgG appearing about 4 days after onset and rising rapidly suggests a secondary (rather than primary) infection, where IgG otherwise appears later and at much lower titers (p.1721).
Anchoring on the febrile phase and missing the critical phase, which paradoxically begins as fever declines rather than at its peak (p.1721).
Serologic cross-reactivity with antigenically similar orthoflaviviruses (yellow fever, Zika, Japanese encephalitis virus) - including after vaccination - can confound serologic diagnosis (p.1721).
Relying on antigen/nucleic-acid tests outside their acute-phase window: after about day 5 diagnosis must shift to serology (p.1721).
Failing to distinguish secondary from primary infection: early, rapidly rising IgG points to secondary infection and higher severe-disease risk (p.1721).

Most patients with uncomplicated dengue recover from the acute illness within 7-10 days, though convalescence may be prolonged and post-acute fatigue and depression are recognized sequelae. Among the millions of annual DENV infections, about 500,000 progress to severe dengue, with an overall case-fatality rate near 2.5%; with early recognition and good supportive care most patients with severe dengue respond well, and CFR at experienced tropical centers can be as low as ~1% (p.1714, 1721-1722).
Onset of restlessness or lethargy together with thrombocytopenia (<100,000/uL) and hemoconcentration 2-5 days into illness, typically at defervescence (p.1721)
Signs of plasma leakage: rising hematocrit/hemoconcentration, hypoalbuminemia, and serosal effusions (pleural effusion, ascites) (p.1721)
Circulatory compromise with narrowed pulse pressure, hepatomegaly, and cyanosis progressing to shock (p.1721)
Severe or spontaneous bleeding in the absence of a predisposing lesion (p.1721)
Severe organ dysfunction: altered mental status or seizures (CNS), arrhythmias (cardiac), acute kidney injury (renal), hepatic injury (p.1721)
Respiratory distress from plasma leakage (p.1721)

Harrison endorses the WHO pragmatic categories that replaced the older 'dengue fever / dengue hemorrhagic fever / dengue shock syndrome' terminology: dengue without warning signs, dengue with warning signs (which directs inpatient management), and severe dengue. Severe dengue is defined as confirmed or presumptive dengue plus at least one of: (1) plasma leakage severe enough to cause shock or respiratory distress, (2) severe bleeding, or (3) severe organ dysfunction. Every patient with presumptive dengue of any severity should be assessed up front for warning signs and for the criteria of severe dengue, with the provisional diagnosis of severe dengue made clinically (p.1704, 1721).
NS1 antigen (early, days 1-5 of fever) — Detects dengue viral antigen early in illness before antibody response develops.
Dengue IgM/IgG serology (later in illness) — Confirms diagnosis when NS1 is negative or testing occurs later in the course; IgG pattern can also suggest primary vs. secondary infection.
CBC with platelet count (serial) — Tracks thrombocytopenia and hematocrit trends, central to monitoring for plasma leakage and bleeding risk.
Hematocrit (serial) — A rising hematocrit with falling platelets signals plasma leakage and impending severe dengue — the single most important trend to follow.
Liver function tests — Transaminitis is common in dengue and severe elevation can indicate more severe disease.
Dengue Fever (infective) — Tropical Fever
veryLikely: Dengue virus (DENV-1 to DENV-4)

Blood cultures (peripheral and through each catheter lumen if not removed) — Differential time-to-positivity (catheter culture positive significantly earlier than peripheral) supports a catheter-related source.
Catheter tip culture (if removed) — Confirms the device as the source when growth matches blood culture results.
Echocardiography (if S. aureus bacteremia, prosthetic valve, or persistent bacteremia) — Screens for endocarditis, a serious complication of device-related bacteremia, particularly with S. aureus.

Diabetic foot infection arises from the interaction of peripheral sensory, motor, and autonomic neuropathy with abnormal foot biomechanics, peripheral arterial disease, and impaired wound healing. Sensory neuropathy removes protective pain sensation, allowing unrecognized repetitive or major trauma; impaired proprioception causes abnormal weight-bearing and callus/ulcer formation. Motor and sensory neuropathy produce structural deformities (hammer/claw toe, prominent metatarsal heads, Charcot joint). Autonomic neuropathy causes anhidrosis with dry, fissured skin. Peripheral arterial disease and poor healing then allow minor skin breaks to enlarge and become infected. Foot osteomyelitis is almost always acquired by the exogenous (contiguous) route, progressing from skin/soft-tissue infection into bone, and can also follow deep wound infection after foot surgery (p.1111, 3271).

A wound that probes to bone (rock-hard, gritty base without intervening soft tissue) strongly predicts underlying osteomyelitis; the probe-to-bone test has a positive predictive value of ~90% in high-pretest-probability populations (p.1112).

In a hospitalized diabetic patient with a chronic deep foot ulcer, the pretest probability of osteomyelitis is high (~65%), so a positive probe-to-bone test can often establish the diagnosis clinically without imaging (p.91, 1112).
A negative probe-to-bone test lowers the likelihood of osteomyelitis (likelihood ratio ~0.2) (p.92).

An infected ulcer is a clinical diagnosis; superficial swab cultures recover multiple organisms of uncertain significance and correlate poorly with bone biopsy (only ~24% concordance in one study) (p.1111-1112, 3271-3272).
Culture-pathogen concordance between deep samples and bone is best for S. aureus (40-50%) and poorest for coagulase-negative staphylococci, anaerobes, and gram-negative bacilli (p.1112).
About 34% of people with diabetes develop a foot ulcer in their lifetime; among those with an ulcer, ~5% per year progress to foot osteomyelitis (p.1111).
Gas gangrene-like findings may occur in a diabetic foot wound even in the absence of clostridial infection (p.3272).
Do NOT rely on superficial swab cultures to guide therapy — they grow contaminants/colonizers and correlate poorly with bone culture (p.1112, 3272).
Plain x-rays have limited sensitivity (30-90%) for diabetic foot osteomyelitis and are mainly useful for follow-up of confirmed cases, not for early diagnosis (p.1112).
A negative probe-to-bone test does not fully exclude osteomyelitis, especially when pretest probability is low — pursue MRI (p.1112).
Antiseptic agents should be avoided and topical antibiotics are of limited value in wound care (p.3272).

Diabetes is the leading cause of nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation. Diabetic foot osteomyelitis increases amputation risk; a foot ulcer (or subsequent ulceration) carries a 14-24% risk of eventual amputation. Adequate management of early-stage infection lowers the amputation rate, and wound debridement combined with antibiotics makes amputation unnecessary in roughly two-thirds of patients (p.1111-1112, 3271).
Wound that probes to bone (high likelihood of osteomyelitis) (p.1112, 3272)
Chronic ulcer failing to respond to therapy (prompt plain radiographs to assess for osteomyelitis) (p.3272)
Underlying peripheral arterial insufficiency / ischemic limb (contributes to non-healing and amputation risk) (p.3272)
Charcot foot deformity complicated by chronic osteomyelitis (p.1111)

Harrison references the IWGDF/IDSA 2023 guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of diabetes-related foot infections but does not reproduce the detailed IDSA/IWGDF grading scale in this text. Infections are described broadly as mild/non-limb-threatening versus more severe (p.1112, 3272).
Deep tissue/bone culture (avoid superficial swab alone) — Superficial swabs poorly correlate with the true infecting organism; deep culture better guides targeted therapy.
Plain X-ray of the foot — Screens for osteomyelitis and gas in soft tissue.
MRI (if osteomyelitis suspected and X-ray inconclusive) — More sensitive for early osteomyelitis than plain films.
HbA1c and glycemic control assessment — Poor glycemic control impairs healing and infection clearance; relevant to overall management.
Vascular assessment (ABI/Doppler) — Peripheral arterial disease impairs healing and antibiotic delivery to tissue — relevant to overall treatment plan and need for revascularization.

[guideline] alternative → Clindamycin + Ciprofloxacin (penicillin allergy)
[guideline] alternative → Vancomycin (if MRSA risk) added to above regimens

Dilated fundoscopic eye examination for choroidal tubercles (pathognomonic, up to ~30% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy for improved bacteriologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1390)

Liver function tests including alkaline phosphatase (elevated with hepatic involvement) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Tuberculin skin test (may be falsely negative in up to half of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Xpert MTB/RIF as the initial test when TB meningitis is suspected; positive results prompt immediate treatment (Harrison 22e p.1393)

Miliary/disseminated TB results from hematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis when an acquired immune response fails to contain infection. Bacilli carried to regional lymph nodes reach the central venous return and the systemic circulation, seeding multiple organs with innumerable small (1-2 mm) yellowish granulomas resembling millet seeds. Occult hematogenous dissemination commonly follows primary infection; in the very young and the immunocompromised (including people living with HIV), insufficient immunity allows progression to fatal miliary disease or tuberculous meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1386, 1390).

Presentation is notoriously nonspecific and protean, varying with the organs predominantly seeded; constitutional features (fever, night sweats, anorexia, weakness, weight loss) dominate in most patients (Harrison 22e p.1390).

Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopic eye examination are pathognomonic of miliary TB and are present in up to roughly 30% of cases, so dilated fundoscopy is a high-yield bedside step (Harrison 22e p.1390).
A high index of suspicion is essential; the diagnosis is easily missed and untreated miliary TB is lethal, whereas early treatment is curative (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Sputum-smear microscopy is negative in most cases, so a negative smear does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1390).
The tuberculin skin test may be negative in up to half of patients, with reactivity sometimes returning during chemotherapy; a negative TST therefore cannot rule out disease (Harrison 22e p.1390).
In adults miliary TB may arise from either recent infection or reactivation of old disseminated foci, whereas in children it more often follows primary infection (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Granulomas are often found on liver or bone-marrow biopsy, and bronchoalveolar lavage with transbronchial biopsy improves bacteriologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Relying on sputum-smear microscopy or the tuberculin skin test to exclude the diagnosis, since both are frequently negative in miliary TB (Harrison 22e p.1390).

Expecting a typical chest radiograph: early in the course, and especially among people living with HIV, the CXR may show no abnormality; findings may instead be large or interstitial infiltrates or pleural effusion rather than the classic miliary reticulonodular pattern (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Overlooking cryptic miliary TB in elderly patients with only mild intermittent fever and anemia (Harrison 22e p.1390).

Unrecognized miliary TB is lethal, but with proper early treatment it is amenable to cure. Cryptic miliary TB (seen in the elderly) runs a chronic course with mild intermittent fever and anemia, ultimately progressing to meningeal involvement before death. The nonreactive (acute septicemic) form is rapidly fatal with multiple necrotic, nongranulomatous lesions at postmortem. Glucocorticoid therapy has not proved beneficial in miliary TB (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Meningismus, present in fewer than 10% of cases, signals possible concurrent tuberculous meningitis and warrants urgent CNS evaluation (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Pancytopenia with an acute septicemic course suggests nonreactive miliary TB, a rare and rapidly fatal form from massive dissemination (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation has been reported and indicates severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Chest X-ray / CT chest — Classic miliary pattern (diffuse small nodules) supports the diagnosis, though it may be subtle or absent early.

Blood culture for mycobacteria (if available) and AFB smear of any accessible fluid/tissue — May provide microbiological confirmation; mycobacterial blood culture has reasonable yield in disseminated disease, particularly in HIV co-infection.

Liver or bone marrow biopsy (if hepatosplenomegaly/cytopenias and other tests inconclusive) — Can provide histological confirmation (caseating granulomas, AFB on staining) when other less invasive tests are unrevealing.
HIV testing — Essential given the strong association between disseminated TB and immunosuppression, with direct treatment implications.
Lumbar puncture (if any neurological signs) — Screens for concurrent CNS involvement, which would extend treatment duration.

Streptococcus pyogenes infecting the epidermis is translocated laterally to deeper structures via lymphatics, producing the characteristic rapid superficial spread of erysipelas. Subsequent engorgement or obstruction of lymphatics causes flaccid edema of the epidermis. The infection is confined to the superficial dermis and superficial lymphatics (in contrast to cellulitis, which involves deeper subcutaneous tissue), and extension to deeper soft tissues is rare (Harrison 22e p.1051-1052, p.1210).
Abrupt onset of fiery-red swelling of the face or extremities, with well-defined indurated margins (notably along the nasolabial fold), rapid progression, and intense pain (Harrison 22e p.1052).

The sharply demarcated, raised border distinguishes erysipelas from cellulitis and reflects involvement limited to the superficial (upper) dermis and superficial lymphatics rather than the deeper subcutaneous tissue (Harrison 22e p.1051, p.1210).
A peau d'orange (orange-peel) texture of the skin is characteristic and is thought to reflect involvement of superficial lymphatics (Harrison 22e p.1210).
Lesion typically develops over a few hours and is accompanied by fever and chills; flaccid superficial blebs/bullae may appear on the second or third day (Harrison 22e p.1052, p.1210).
Classic distribution is the malar area of the face (often extending over the bridge of the nose to the contralateral malar region) or the lower extremities (Harrison 22e p.1210).
Infants and elderly adults are most commonly affected, and the severity of systemic toxicity varies (Harrison 22e p.1052).
Desquamation of the involved skin occurs roughly 5-10 days into the illness (Harrison 22e p.1052).
Classic cases with typical features are almost always due to beta-hemolytic streptococci, usually group A and occasionally group C or G (Harrison 22e p.1210).

Atypical erysipelas may involve an unusual anatomic site, appear less intensely red, fade into surrounding skin, or cause only mild systemic illness, in which case a specific clinical diagnosis cannot reliably be made and broader empirical coverage (including S. aureus) is prudent (Harrison 22e p.1210-1211).
Extension to deeper soft tissues is rare in true erysipelas; if present, reconsider the diagnosis and exclude a deeper or necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1052).

In most parts of the world, acute rheumatic fever is NOT a sequela of streptococcal skin infection (unlike pharyngitis), though post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis may follow either skin or throat infection (Harrison 22e p.1210).

Generally responds well to therapy; with appropriate treatment, fever, pain, and the intense red color diminish, although swelling may continue to progress initially. Recurrence at the same site (sometimes years later) is not uncommon, particularly where normal lymphatic drainage has been disrupted (Harrison 22e p.1052, p.1210-1211).

Edema with purple bullae, ecchymosis, and cutaneous anesthesia suggests loss of vascular integrity and necessitates exploration of deeper structures for necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1051).
Unexplained fever with disproportionate pain and tenderness in soft tissue, even without acute cutaneous inflammation, should raise suspicion for a deeper necrotizing process (Harrison 22e p.1051).
None routinely required — Diagnosis is clinical based on the characteristic appearance; cultures of intact skin have low yield.
Blood cultures (if systemically unwell) — May identify bacteremic spread in more severe presentations.

chunks.text: Most cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents suppress bone marrow function, and polymorphonuclear neutrophils, with their very short circulating half-life of roughly 6-8 hours, are the cell line most rapidly and severely depleted. As the neutrophil count falls, the host loses the first-line cellular defense that normally contains commensal flora at mucosal surfaces; below an ANC of 500/uL control of endogenous mouth and gut organisms is impaired, and below 200/uL the local inflammatory response is essentially absent, so signs of infection are blunted. The combination of profound neutropenia and chemotherapy-induced mucosal barrier injury allows translocation and rapid dissemination of bacteria from the patient's own gut and oral flora. Neutropenia is most commonly iatrogenic, arising from cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapy. (Harrison 22e p.499-500, p.617)

Leptospires enter through cuts, abraded skin, or mucous membranes (especially conjunctival and oral). The highly motile organisms proliferate, cross tissue barriers, and disseminate hematogenously to all organs (leptospiremic phase), evading innate immune mechanisms such as complement-mediated killing and phagocytosis; an exaggerated proinflammatory response correlates with mortality. With the immune phase, antibodies appear and leptospires clear from blood but persist in liver, lung, kidney, heart, and brain. Renal pathology shows acute tubular damage and interstitial nephritis, progressing to interstitial edema and acute tubular necrosis, with dysregulated nephron transporters causing impaired sodium absorption, potassium wasting, and polyuria. Liver histology shows focal (not widespread) hepatocellular necrosis, inflammation, bile canaliculus plugging, and hepatocyte apoptosis, with disruption of intercellular junctions and bile leakage. Petechiae and hemorrhages occur across many organs. Hemorrhage is associated with thrombocytopenia (likely platelet consumption); a consumptive coagulopathy with elevated coagulation-activation markers, reduced anticoagulant markers, and dysregulated fibrinolysis may progress to overt DIC. Endothelial cell activation (raised soluble E-selectin and von Willebrand factor) correlates with severity, and leptospires/leptospiral proteins disrupt endothelial barrier function, increasing permeability. The LPS has unusually low endotoxic potency, yet serovar-specific anti-LPS antibodies are central to protective humoral immunity (p.1441-1442).

Classically biphasic: an acute leptospiremic phase (fever lasting ~3-10 days, organism culturable/PCR-detectable in blood) followed by an immune phase in which symptoms may resolve as antibodies appear and leptospires can be recovered from urine; the two phases are not always distinct, mild cases may lack the second phase, and severe disease can be monophasic and fulminant (p.1442).
Idea that specific serogroups cause distinct clinical syndromes has been refuted, although some serovars tend to cause more severe disease (p.1442).
Serology lacks sensitivity in the early acute phase (up to day 5) and cannot guide a timely treatment decision; PCR (notably real-time PCR) can confirm diagnosis during the first 5 days (p.1443).
MAT antibodies generally do not reach detectable levels until the second week of illness, and the antibody response may be blunted by early antibiotics (p.1443).
Incubation is usually 1-2 weeks but ranges from 2 to 30 days (p.1442).
Conjunctival suffusion (redness without exudate) is a characteristic but non-pathognomonic sign; muscle pain is intense, especially in the calves, back, and abdomen (p.1442).
Headache is intense and frontal or retro-orbital, sometimes with photophobia, resembling dengue (p.1442).
Weil's syndrome denotes the severe triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage (p.1442-1443).

Severe pulmonary hemorrhage (with or without jaundice) is increasingly recognized as an important and widespread presentation; hemoptysis may not become apparent until the patient is intubated (p.1439, 1442).
Jaundice occurs in only ~5-10% of patients, can be deep with an orange skin cast, and is usually NOT associated with fulminant hepatic necrosis (p.1442).

Aseptic meningitis is more common in children than adults; altered mental status in severe disease may reflect leptospiral meningitis, which can occur in anicteric patients lacking other hallmarks (p.1442-1443).
Autoimmune-associated uveitis is a recognized, potentially chronic late sequela (p.1443).
Absence of a travel or freshwater-exposure history does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1443).
Absence of renal involvement does not rule out leptospirosis (p.1443).
Relying on serology in the first ~5 days risks a false-negative; antibodies are often undetectable until the second week and early antibiotics blunt the response (p.1443).
Cross-reactions are frequent in MAT, so the infecting serovar/serogroup cannot be definitively identified without isolating the organism (p.1443).
Leptospiral meningitis may present without jaundice or other classic severe-disease hallmarks, making it easy to miss (p.1443).
Jaundice can be profound yet usually does not signify fulminant hepatic necrosis, so hepatic transaminase rises are only moderate (p.1442-1443).
The transient rash may be misdiagnosed as scrub typhus or a viral exanthem (p.1442).
Dual infection (e.g., with dengue, rickettsiae, or hantavirus) can occur, so a positive alternative test does not exclude leptospirosis (p.1443).

Most patients recover, with renal and hepatic function typically returning to normal in survivors (hemodialysis can be lifesaving). Overall mean case-fatality is near 10% for severe cases; severe leptospirosis carries a case-fatality of 1-50%. Mortality is highest in the elderly and those with pulmonary hemorrhage or Weil's syndrome. Untreated leptospiral meningitis has reported mortality of ~13% versus ~2% with antibiotics. Pregnancy is associated with high fetal mortality. Post-leptospirosis sequelae include prolonged fatigue, myalgia, malaise, headache, depression-like symptoms persisting for years, and chronic autoimmune uveitis (p.1443-1444).

Harrison distinguishes mild leptospirosis (sudden-onset flu-like febrile illness with headache, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion; usually self-limiting over 7-10 days, low mortality) from severe leptospirosis, which is often rapidly progressive with multiorgan involvement. Severe disease classically presents as Weil's syndrome (triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage) and/or severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome, with a case-fatality of 1-50% (p.1442-1443).

Infection begins when a female Anopheles inoculates sporozoites, which reach the liver and undergo preerythrocytic schizogony, each sporozoite yielding 10,000 to >30,000 merozoites. Released merozoites invade red cells, becoming trophozoites that multiply roughly 6- to 20-fold each asexual cycle (every 48 h for P. falciparum/P. vivax/P. ovale, 72 h for P. malariae, 24 h for P. knowlesi); symptoms begin around densities of ~50 parasites/uL. In P. vivax and P. ovale a fraction of liver forms persist as dormant hypnozoites for weeks to a year or more, causing the relapses characteristic of these species (P. falciparum, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi do not relapse). Disease results from red-cell invasion and destruction plus the host inflammatory response: schizont rupture releases material that activates monocytes/macrophages and proinflammatory cytokines, producing fever. The central pathology of severe falciparum malaria is cytoadherence: ~12-15 h after invasion 'knobs' on the infected red cell extrude the variant adhesin PfEMP1, which binds endothelial receptors (ICAM-1 and endothelial protein C receptor in brain, VAR2CSA/chondroitin sulfate A in placenta, CD36 elsewhere). Cytoadherence, rosetting (adherence to uninfected red cells), and agglutination sequester mature parasites in vital organs, especially the brain, obstructing microcirculatory flow and metabolism while escaping splenic clearance. Uninfected red cells also become less deformable in severe disease. P. falciparum invades cells of all ages and can reach very high densities (P. knowlesi can also, owing to its 24-h cycle), whereas other species spare most red cells and rarely exceed ~2% parasitemia. The spleen augments clearance and 'pits' damaged ring forms; severe lactic acidosis arises from anaerobic glycolysis in sequestered beds, parasite lactate production, gut-derived acids, and failed hepatic/renal clearance, and hypoglycemia from impaired gluconeogenesis with increased glucose consumption. (Harrison 22e pp.1760-1765)

Malaria is not a clinical diagnosis: any patient in or from an endemic area with fever needs thick and thin blood smears (or a rapid test if reliable microscopy is unavailable) to confirm infection and identify the species (Harrison 22e p.1766).
Specific retinal changes (patchy retinal opacification/whitening, vessel decolorization, pale-centered hemorrhages) on funduscopy support a diagnosis of cerebral malaria (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765).

In severe malaria the usual adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (sweating, tachycardia, gooseflesh) are absent and its neurologic effects cannot be distinguished from the disease itself, so glucose must be checked actively (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Quinine can provoke hypoglycemia by stimulating pancreatic insulin secretion, compounding the hypoglycemia of severe malaria (Harrison 22e p.1764).

Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema may appear even after several days of effective antimalarial therapy and is readily precipitated by over-vigorous IV fluids; mortality exceeds 80% (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Acidotic ('respiratory distress') breathing in a child with severe anemia is usually due to metabolic acidosis, not 'anemic heart failure' as previously mislabeled (Harrison 22e pp.1765-1766).

Approximately 6% of children and <1% of adults with severe malaria have concomitant bacteremia (higher with >20% parasitemia in adults), and nontyphoidal Salmonella bacteremia is specifically associated with P. falciparum (Harrison 22e p.1765).

In high-transmission areas low-density parasitemia is a common incidental finding, so severe malaria is easily overdiagnosed and must be distinguished from sepsis with coincidental parasitemia (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1767).
Sudden delayed hemolysis can follow artesunate treatment of hyperparasitemia in nonimmune patients, from synchronous loss of once-parasitized 'pitted' red cells (Harrison 22e p.1765).

Early symptoms are nonspecific (malaise, headache, fatigue, abdominal discomfort, myalgia, then fever) and resemble a minor viral illness, so a high index of suspicion is essential (Harrison 22e p.1763).

The classic regular febrile paroxysms (chills, rigors, fever spikes at fixed intervals) are now unusual and, when present at presentation, suggest P. vivax or P. ovale (often a relapse); prompt effective treatment prevents the synchronized fever pattern from developing (Harrison 22e p.1763).
Mild thrombocytopenia is usual in malaria; a normal platelet count should call the diagnosis into question (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1768).
In falciparum malaria, peripheral parasitemia underestimates true parasite burden because mature parasites sequester in deep vascular beds and only younger ring forms circulate (Harrison 22e p.1762).

A PfHRP2-based rapid test can stay positive for weeks after treatment, which helps diagnose severe malaria in a patient who has already taken antimalarials and cleared peripheral parasites but is a drawback in high-transmission settings (Harrison 22e p.1767).

Persistent gametocytemia after a full treatment course does not indicate drug resistance or a need to re-treat, because mature P. falciparum gametocytes are unaffected by most antimalarials (Harrison 22e p.1767).
Any obtundation, delirium, abnormal behavior, or generalized seizure in falciparum malaria must be taken seriously as a possible herald of cerebral malaria (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1764).
Cerebral malaria is a diffuse symmetric encephalopathy without true meningism; focal neurologic signs are unusual and signs of meningeal irritation are absent (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Treating malaria as a clinical diagnosis; confirmation by smear or rapid test is required (Harrison 22e p.1766).
Mistaking acidotic breathing in a severely anemic child for 'anemic congestive cardiac failure' (Harrison 22e pp.1765-1766).
Accepting a normal platelet count without question, as mild thrombocytopenia is the rule in malaria (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1768).
Relying on peripheral parasitemia to gauge true burden in falciparum malaria, since mature parasites are sequestered (Harrison 22e p.1762).
Overdiagnosing severe malaria in high-transmission areas where low-density parasitemia is a common incidental finding, missing concurrent sepsis (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1767).
Over-vigorous IV fluid administration, which can precipitate noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Missing hypoglycemia because its usual autonomic signs are absent in severe disease and its neurologic effects mimic malaria itself (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Re-treating on the basis of persistent gametocytemia, which does not signify drug resistance after a full course (Harrison 22e p.1767).
False-negative RDTs from PfHRP2/3 gene-deleted parasites (notably in the Horn of Africa); RDTs also cannot quantify parasitemia (Harrison 22e p.1767).
Using serology to diagnose acute illness; serology has no role in acute diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1768).

Promptly and appropriately treated uncomplicated falciparum malaria has a mortality of <0.1%, but risk rises steeply once vital-organ dysfunction occurs or parasitemia exceeds 2%. Cerebral malaria carries roughly 20% mortality in adults and 15% in children even with treatment; about 10% of surviving children (especially with hypoglycemia, severe anemia, repeated seizures, or deep coma) have residual neurologic deficits, most of which improve or resolve within 6 months, though persistent language and cognitive deficits, increased epilepsy risk, and reduced life expectancy occur in some. Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema in adults has >80% mortality. Plasma bicarbonate and lactate are the best biochemical prognosticators. Among complications, poor prognosis is indicated by >20% mature pigment-containing parasites or >5% of neutrophils containing pigment, and by hyperparasitemia. In severe acute renal failure that survives, urine flow returns in a median of 4 days and creatinine normalizes in a mean of 17 days; early dialysis improves survival. (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1765, 1767)

Severe falciparum malaria (WHO-based criteria, Harrison 22e Table 231-2, p.1764) is defined by one or more of: unarousable coma/cerebral malaria (no localizing response, coma >30 min after a generalized convulsion, Glasgow Coma Score <11 or Blantyre <3 in young children); acidemia/acidosis (arterial pH <7.25, base deficit >8 meq/L, or plasma bicarbonate <15 mmol/L; venous lactate >=5 mmol/L; deep labored 'respiratory distress' breathing); severe normochromic normocytic anemia (hematocrit <15% or Hb <50 g/L with parasite density >10,000/uL); renal failure (creatinine >265 umol/L / >3 mg/dL); noncardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS (or O2 sat <92% on room air with respiratory rate >30/min); hypoglycemia (glucose <2.2 mmol/L / <40 mg/dL); hypotension/shock (systolic BP <70 mmHg in children 1-5 y or <80 mmHg in adults with impaired perfusion); significant bleeding/DIC; convulsions (>2 generalized seizures in 24 h); hemoglobinuria (macroscopic black/brown/red urine, not due to oxidant drugs or G6PD deficiency); extreme weakness/prostration; hyperparasitemia (>5% in nonimmune, >10% in any patient); and jaundice (bilirubin >50 umol/L / >3 mg/dL) with parasitemia >100,000/uL or other vital-organ dysfunction. Note: criteria thresholds for renal failure are for adults; lower values define severe disease in children. (Harrison 22e p.1764)
