Quantification of parasitemia (RDTs do not quantify) and assessment of parasite maturity/pigment for prognostic stratification
G6PD status (knowledge basis for safe hypnozoite-directed therapy of the vivax component) — testing rationale only

Sporozoites inoculated by anopheline mosquitoes reach the liver and undergo pre-erythrocytic schizogony; a single sporozoite yields thousands of merozoites that invade RBCs and multiply (every 48 h for P. falciparum and P. vivax). In P. vivax (and P. ovale) infection, a fraction of intrahepatic forms do not divide but persist as dormant hypnozoites for weeks to a year or more, later reactivating to cause relapses — a feature absent in P. falciparum. In a mixed P. falciparum + P. vivax infection, the falciparum component drives the risk of severe disease through cytoadherence (PfEMP1 binding endothelial receptors), rosetting, and agglutination, causing sequestration of mature parasites in vital organs; only ring forms circulate, so peripheral parasitemia underestimates true burden. P. vivax preferentially invades young reticulocytes and produces lower parasitemia (seldom >2%), while P. falciparum invades RBCs of all ages and can reach very high densities. The simultaneous presence of a vivax hypnozoite reservoir means blood-stage cure of both species does not prevent later vivax relapse (p.1760-1763).

Mixed infections (most commonly P. falciparum together with P. vivax) are frequently under-detected by light microscopy and rapid antigen tests; PCR is the most sensitive method and is increasingly used specifically for speciation and genotyping in mixed infections (p.1767).

Because microscopy and RDTs may detect only the dominant species, a smear or RDT reported as single-species (especially P. falciparum) does not exclude a coexisting vivax/ovale component carrying dormant liver-stage hypnozoites.
P. vivax + P. falciparum is recognized as a distinct co-circulating pattern in endemic mapping, with roughly equal prevalence of the two species in Oceania (p.1761-1762).

Standard combination RDTs typically carry one P. falciparum-specific band plus a pan-malaria or P. vivax band; this design distinguishes falciparum from the 'less dangerous' malarias but is not optimized to flag concurrent dual infection (p.1766).

RDTs may miss low-level P. vivax (and P. ovale/P. malariae) parasitemia and PfHRP2-based tests can be falsely negative where parasites carry HRP2/3 gene deletions — both failure modes can mask one component of a mixed infection (p.1766).

The classic regularly-spaced febrile paroxysm at presentation suggests P. vivax or P. ovale (often relapse); its presence in a patient with confirmed falciparum should raise suspicion of a coexisting vivax/ovale component.
Apparent vivax/ovale relapses arising after treatment of a mixed infection reflect persistence of liver-stage hypnozoites, which are not cleared by standard blood-stage schizonticides.

Treating an apparently single-species falciparum infection as if vivax were absent: the coexisting vivax hypnozoite reservoir is not cleared by blood-stage drugs and later causes relapse — manage mixed infection as falciparum AND provide hypnozoite-directed coverage for vivax.
Relying on microscopy or RDT alone to exclude a second species — both under-detect the minor component; PCR is needed to confirm/exclude mixed infection.
Misreading PfHRP2 RDT positivity that persists for weeks after a prior infection as evidence of the current species mix.
Mistaking persistent P. falciparum gametocytemia after treatment for treatment failure or active infection.
Attributing all post-treatment fever to falciparum recrudescence when it may be a true vivax/ovale relapse from the mixed-infection liver reservoir.
Misidentifying P. knowlesi as P. falciparum on microscopy/RDT, distorting the apparent species picture.

Promptly treated uncomplicated falciparum malaria has a mortality of <0.1%, but risk rises steeply once vital-organ dysfunction occurs or parasitemia exceeds ~2%. In a mixed infection the falciparum component dictates the severe-disease prognosis; cerebral malaria carries ~20% mortality in adults and ~15% in children even with treatment, and ~10% of child survivors have residual neurologic deficits (most improving within 6 months). Poor-prognosis features include hyperparasitemia (>100,000/uL), predominance of mature pigment-containing parasites (>20%), pigment in >5% of neutrophils, hypoglycemia, hyperlactatemia, acidemia, and coagulopathy. The vivax component does not usually drive mortality but, if its hypnozoite reservoir is not addressed, predisposes to later relapse and recurrent anemia (p.1763-1767).
Coma, obtundation, delirium, or abnormal behavior (cerebral malaria) — attributable to the falciparum component
Prostration / inability to sit or stand unaided
Repeated or generalized convulsions (>2 in 24 h)
Respiratory distress / acidotic deep breathing (acidosis, lactate >=5 mmol/L)
Hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L)
Shock / hypotension with impaired perfusion
Severe normocytic anemia (Hct <15%) and/or spontaneous bleeding / DIC
Hemoglobinuria (black/brown/red urine)
Acute kidney injury (creatinine >265 umol/L)
Hyperparasitemia (>2% indicates increased risk; >5-10% defines severe disease) — a falciparum-driven marker

Severity is governed by the P. falciparum component per Harrison Table 231-2 (Manifestations of Severe Falciparum Malaria): major criteria include unarousable coma/cerebral malaria, acidosis (arterial pH <7.25 / lactate >=5 mmol/L), severe normocytic anemia (Hct <15%), renal failure (creatinine >265 umol/L), noncardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS, hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L), hypotension/shock, bleeding/DIC, and repeated convulsions; other criteria include hemoglobinuria, prostration, and hyperparasitemia (>5% nonimmune, >10% any patient). Uncomplicated disease = patient can sit/stand unaided and swallow, with no vital-organ dysfunction and parasitemia <2% (p.1763-1764).

Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin film) confirming both species — Definitive method to confirm mixed infection and quantify parasitemia of each species, directly determining treatment approach and monitoring intensity.
Rapid diagnostic test (combination P.f/P.v if available) — Can support or suggest mixed infection rapidly, though smear remains the definitive confirmatory test.
G6PD testing — Mandatory before primaquine administration to avoid precipitating hemolysis in deficient patients.
CBC, renal function, blood glucose, LFTs — Screens for organ dysfunction that would classify this as severe/complicated malaria requiring IV therapy and escalated care.
Mixed Malaria (P. falciparum + P. vivax) (infective) — Tropical Fever
veryLikely: Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax
Red flags: Urgent antimalarial therapy required (NOT an antibiotic)
Clostridial myonecrosis / gas gangrene (distinguished from clostridial NF by muscle biopsy)
Streptococcal necrotizing myositis (GAS infection extending into muscle)
Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus; localized, shock uncommon unless toxin-producing)
Synergistic nonclostridial anaerobic myonecrosis (necrotizing cutaneous myositis / synergistic necrotizing cellulitis) — a mixed aerobic-anaerobic variant
Cellulitis / erysipelas (superficial; skin more abnormal but pain mild-moderate)
Halophilic Vibrio vulnificus infection (can be as fulminant as NF; Gulf/Atlantic water exposure or raw seafood in cirrhosis)
Aeromonas soft-tissue infection (freshwater laceration exposure)
Aggressive cellulitis from Vibrio vulnificus or Aeromonas hydrophila
Ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas, neutropenic hosts)
Clostridial myonecrosis

Soft-tissue plain radiography, CT, and MRI to assess depth of infection and detect tissue gas or a localized abscess — most useful when lesions progress rapidly or SIRS is present; note imaging may show only soft-tissue swelling and is NOT specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis, where gas is typically absent
Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture of surgically excised tissue to identify GAS vs mixed flora vs MRSA vs Clostridium
Frozen-section histology of aspirate or punch biopsy (valuable in NF), though aspiration/biopsy is negative in ~80% of cases
Serum CPK (markedly elevated when myonecrosis coexists)
Lactate, d-dimer, coagulation, liver and renal function as markers of systemic toxicity/organ failure
Thrombophlebitis (a common early misdiagnosis)
Muscle strain or contusion (the minor trauma at the deep nidus)

NF is infection of the superficial and/or deep fascia investing the muscles of an extremity or trunk, with extensive necrosis of subcutaneous tissue and fascia. Infection spreads rapidly along fascial planes and via venous channels and lymphatics, typically sparing the muscle itself in pure fasciitis. Two main microbiologic patterns: a mixed aerobic-anaerobic (type I) process beginning with a breach of a mucosal barrier (GI/GU tract), and a monomicrobial group A streptococcal (type II) process. In GAS disease, organisms reach deep fascia either by transient bacteremic seeding at a site of minor non-penetrating trauma (no portal) or by spread from cutaneous infection/penetrating trauma. Thrombosis of dermal vessels produces progressive skin necrosis; infarction of cutaneous nerves causes the characteristic late anesthesia. NF caused by Clostridium perfringens or extending into muscle (clostridial/streptococcal myonecrosis) carries very high systemic toxicity with hemolysis. PVL-producing MRSA strains have been reported as a cause.

Pain out of proportion to physical findings is the classic early clue: physical signs may be minimal (only soft-tissue edema and mild erythema) while pain and fever are severe; this disparity helps distinguish NF from superficial cellulitis, where skin appearance is more abnormal but pain is only mild-to-moderate.

Early disease is frequently misdiagnosed (e.g., as thrombophlebitis) and patients may be sent home with analgesics, especially in the strep type that begins deep at a site of non-penetrating minor trauma (bruise, muscle strain) with no visible portal of entry.

Classic late signs evolve sequentially: swelling and brawny edema/tenderness, then dark-red (violaceous) induration, then bullae filled with blue/purple fluid, then friable bluish-maroon-to-black skin; thrombosis of dermal-papillae vessels is extensive by this stage.
Paradoxical decrease in pain or progression to anesthesia over the involved area is an ominous sign reflecting thrombosis of small vessels and infarction of cutaneous nerves.
GAS NF can be preceded by varicella, childbirth, or muscle strain, and most patients deny an antecedent streptococcal infection.
The inoculation site may be inapparent and remote from clinical involvement (e.g., minor hand trauma manifesting as infection over the shoulder or chest).
Myositis/myonecrosis coexists with NF in roughly 20-50% of cases and serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) may be markedly elevated, signaling deeper muscle involvement.
Early physical findings are minimal relative to pain/fever, leading to underestimation of severity and misdiagnosis as thrombophlebitis or simple cellulitis.
Absence of gas does NOT exclude NF: gas is usually absent when the cause is GAS or MRSA and is seen mainly with mixed/clostridial infection.
Normal or nonspecific imaging does NOT rule out NF — CT/MRI may show only soft-tissue swelling and are not specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis.
A negative aspirate or frozen-section biopsy does NOT exclude NF (negative in ~80% of cases).
Decreasing pain should not be reassuring — it can signal nerve infarction and disease progression rather than improvement.
Do not wait for imaging or cultures when NF is suspected with systemic toxicity; surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Mortality for NF is roughly 11-34% overall and rises substantially when associated with toxic shock syndrome. GAS/clostridial fascial-muscle infection historically carried 20-50% mortality with penicillin alone. Survivors of GAS NF often require repeated surgeries including amputation. Clostridial NF/myonecrosis is far more lethal: spontaneous (nontraumatic) myonecrosis mortality exceeds 65% (often C. septicum with underlying malignancy); trunk infection ~63% vs limb ~12% mortality. Any delay in surgery increases the risk of death; early aggressive surgery markedly improves outcomes.
Pain out of proportion to examination findings
Rapidly progressing lesion with signs of systemic inflammatory response / toxicity
Violaceous (blue/purple) bullae, skin sloughing, dusky/mottled erythema
Progression of tenderness to anesthesia over the lesion (cutaneous nerve infarction)
Crepitus or gas in deep tissue (suggests mixed/clostridial infection)
Renal impairment that may precede shock, plus hypotension/multiorgan failure
Urgent surgical exploration supersedes other diagnostic or therapeutic maneuvers — debridement is life-saving and must not be delayed

Microbiologic/clinical typing: Type I = mixed aerobic-anaerobic, begins at a mucosal-barrier breach (GI/GU), common in diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, malignancy, surgery, or abdominal penetrating injury; Fournier gangrene is the perineal/scrotal form. Type II = monomicrobial group A streptococcal (GAS implicated in ~60% of NF cases), can occur in otherwise healthy hosts, two presentations (with vs without a defined portal of entry). PVL-producing MRSA is a recognized monomicrobial cause. NF qualifies as soft-tissue necrosis under the CDC streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (hypotension plus >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, hepatic impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous desquamating rash, soft-tissue necrosis/NF/myositis/gangrene). (LRINEC score not described in this source.)

Urgent surgical exploration (diagnostic AND therapeutic) — The definitive diagnostic test — direct visualization of necrotic fascia confirms the diagnosis and simultaneously allows debridement; imaging should not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high.
Blood cultures and intraoperative tissue/fluid cultures — Identifies the causative organism(s) to guide de-escalation.
CT or MRI (only if diagnosis uncertain and patient stable enough to tolerate delay) — May show fascial thickening/gas, but should never delay surgery in a patient with high clinical suspicion.
CPK — Markedly elevated levels suggest muscle involvement (myonecrosis), affecting the extent of surgical debridement needed.

LRINEC score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis) — Can support clinical suspicion using CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose, though it should not override strong clinical suspicion if score is low.
Necrotizing Fasciitis (infective) — Skin & Soft Tissue

veryLikely: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) — monomicrobial type II, Polymicrobial flora including anaerobes and Enterobacteriaceae — type I (more common, often in diabetics/immunocompromised); likely: Staphylococcus aureus (including community-associated MRSA), Clostridium species (if gas gangrene/myonecrosis); possible: Vibrio vulnificus (if marine/brackish water exposure), Aeromonas species (if freshwater exposure)
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Piperacillin-tazobactam + Clindamycin + Vancomycin This combination covers polymicrobial type I infection (pip-tazo), provides antitoxin effect against streptococcal/staphylococcal toxin production (clindamycin, via protein synthesis inhibition), and covers MRSA (vancomycin) — maximal reasonable empiric coverage is justified given the extreme mortality risk.
[guideline] alternative → Meropenem + Clindamycin + Vancomycin (broader gram-negative coverage if indicated)
[guideline] alternative → IVIG (adjunctive, for confirmed streptococcal toxic shock features)
Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) or throat culture — Confirms or excludes Group A Streptococcus before committing to antibiotics, directly preventing unnecessary use in viral pharyngitis.
Acute Pharyngitis (infective) — Respiratory

veryLikely: Respiratory viruses (most common overall); likely: Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) — when Centor score is high; possible: Fusobacterium necrophorum (consider in older adolescents/young adults with severe symptoms)

[guideline] empiric → Penicillin V (only if GAS confirmed or very high pretest probability) Penicillin remains first-line for confirmed Group A Streptococcal pharyngitis — narrow spectrum, no resistance reported, and prevents rheumatic fever when given for a full 10-day course.
[guideline] alternative → Amoxicillin
[guideline] alternative → Azithromycin (penicillin allergy)
Urinalysis and urine culture — Identifies the causative organism; this is preferred over prostatic secretion sampling in the acute setting given bacteremia risk with prostatic massage.
Blood cultures (if febrile/systemically unwell) — Bacteremia is not uncommon in acute prostatitis and positive cultures help confirm the organism.

Post-void residual / bladder scan (if retention suspected) — Urinary retention is a recognized complication requiring catheterization (suprapubic preferred over urethral if prostatitis is causing obstruction).
STI testing (NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia) if risk factors present — Identifies sexually transmitted causes requiring different management and partner notification.
Acute Bacterial Prostatitis (infective) — Genitourinary

veryLikely: Escherichia coli; likely: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus species; possible: Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis (younger sexually active men — different management)

[guideline] empiric → Ciprofloxacin Fluoroquinolones achieve excellent prostatic tissue penetration, which is essential since many antibiotics with good urinary concentration do not adequately penetrate prostatic tissue; prolonged duration (longer than typical UTI) reduces the risk of chronic prostatitis.
[guideline] alternative → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (if susceptible)
[guideline] alternative → Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin/Doxycycline (if STI risk in younger sexually active men)
Sputum smear for AFB (at least 2 samples) — Rapid, widely available test; positive smear supports diagnosis and indicates infectiousness for public health purposes.

CBNAAT / Xpert MTB-RIF (or equivalent rapid molecular test) — Provides faster diagnosis than culture and simultaneously detects rifampicin resistance, directly informing regimen choice — should be prioritized where available.
Sputum culture (liquid or solid media) — Gold standard for diagnosis and allows full drug-susceptibility testing if initial molecular testing suggests resistance or treatment failure occurs.
Chest X-ray — Supports diagnosis (upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation) and provides a baseline for treatment response monitoring.
HIV testing — TB-HIV co-infection changes management (ART timing, drug interactions) and is a standard part of TB workup per national guidelines.
Pulmonary Tuberculosis (infective) — Respiratory / Tuberculosis
veryLikely: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; possible: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (if AFB smear positive but culture/PCR does not confirm M. tuberculosis)

[guideline] empiric → Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol (HRZE) Standard first-line four-drug regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, started ONLY after microbiological confirmation (or strong programmatic criteria per national guidelines) — not empirically on clinical suspicion alone.
[guideline] alternative → Modified regimens per drug-susceptibility testing

Infective endocarditis (including culture-negative endocarditis from fastidious organisms - nutritionally variant streptococci, HACEK group, Coxiella burnetii, Tropheryma whipplei, Bartonella) - one of the more common infectious causes (pp.150-151)
Adult-onset Still's disease (NIID, relatively common in FUO) (p.150)
Large-vessel vasculitis and giant cell arteritis / polymyalgia rheumatica (pp.150, 153)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (p.150)
Sarcoidosis (p.150)
Familial Mediterranean fever and other autoinflammatory syndromes (rare except in specific regions) (p.150)
Schnitzler's syndrome - urticaria, bone pain, monoclonal gammopathy (p.150)

VEXAS syndrome - adult-onset, middle-aged/elderly males, recurrent inflammation, chondritis, skin lesions, lung disease, venous thrombosis, arthritis, MDS; bone-marrow vacuoles in myeloid precursors; somatic UBA1 variants (p.150)
Malignant lymphoma - by far the most common neoplastic cause; fever may precede detectable lymphadenopathy (p.150)
Common solid tumors causing fever: breast, colon, hepatocellular, lung, pancreatic, renal cell carcinoma (p.151)
Extrapulmonary and miliary tuberculosis - up to half of infections in non-Western FUO are M. tuberculosis; miliary TB is especially hard to diagnose (pp.150, 153)
Diverticulitis (p.150)
Vertebral osteomyelitis / spondylodiscitis (pp.150-151)
Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) - consider with rural exposure, animal contact, valve disease, aortic aneurysm, or vascular prosthesis; test by immunofluorescence assay (pp.150-151)
Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei) - consider with unexplained CNS, GI, or joint symptoms; PCR on stool and blood early (p.150)
Intraabdominal / hepatic / renal / pelvic abscesses (p.151)
Endemic infections after relevant travel/residence: malaria, visceral leishmaniasis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis (p.150)
Acute HIV infection (p.150)
Culture-negative endocarditis - sterile cultures may simply reflect ongoing antibiotic therapy rather than a noninfectious cause (pp.151-152)
Marantic (nonbacterial thrombotic) endocarditis - sterile, paraneoplastic, especially with adenocarcinomas, mimics infective endocarditis (p.151)
Sterile endocarditis of SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome (p.151)

Obligatory baseline panel: ESR and CRP, platelet count, leukocyte count with differential, hemoglobin, electrolytes, creatinine, total protein, alkaline phosphatase, ALT, AST, LDH, creatine kinase, ferritin, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, protein electrophoresis, urinalysis, three blood cultures, urine culture, chest x-ray, abdominal ultrasonography, and TST or IGRA (p.149)

Specialized blood cultures held long enough for fastidious organisms (e.g., HACEK); inform the lab and use special media for Histoplasma or Legionella; >3 blood cultures or >1 urine culture is useless without PDCs (p.153)
Q fever serology by immunofluorescence assay; T. whipplei PCR on stool/blood (pp.150-151)
Temporal artery biopsy in patients >=55 years for suspected giant cell arteritis (p.153)
CSF examination (HSV especially type 2, Cryptococcus, M. tuberculosis) when FUO is accompanied by headache (p.153)
Later-stage PDC-driven biopsies for pathology and/or microbiology (p.154)
Cryoglobulins - useful low-cost screening test (p.153)
Fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist - early, to exclude retinal vasculitis when PDCs are absent or misleading (p.153)

18F-FDG-PET/CT - established next step when PDC-guided tests are unrevealing; ~50% total diagnostic yield; best performed during active inflammation (elevated CRP/ESR or fever) and before glucocorticoids; outperforms gallium and labeled-leukocyte scintigraphy (pp.152-154)
Gallium-67 citrate or 111In/99mTc-labeled leukocyte scintigraphy - alternatives when PET/CT unavailable (lower yield; gallium localizes ~1/3, leukocyte ~1/5 of cases) (p.154)
Whole-body MRI - one study reported yield comparable to PET/CT (needs confirmation) (p.154)
Echocardiography - low yield without PDCs; reserve for high suspicion of endocarditis (p.153)
Liver biopsy (acid-fast smear, culture, PCR) - highest yield if miliary TB suspected; bone marrow / lymph node biopsies are alternatives (p.153)
Mycobacterial PCR alongside cultures - may shorten time to TB diagnosis (p.153)

Drug-induced fever - virtually any drug, even after long-term use; common culprits include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfasalazine, furosemide, and antimicrobials (sulfonamides, minocycline, vancomycin, beta-lactams, isoniazid); fever persisting >72h after stopping the drug makes it an unlikely cause (pp.150, 153)
DRESS / drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome - often with eosinophilia and extensive lymphadenopathy (p.150)

Benign or exercise-induced hyperthermia - elevated temperature WITHOUT raised CRP/ESR or other inflammation; may be postinfectious (triggers similar to chronic fatigue syndrome: EBV, Q fever, COVID-19) (p.150)
Factitious fever - artificially induced (e.g., IV injection of contaminated water); suspect with access to medical equipment (p.150)
Fraudulent fever - patient is normothermic but manipulates the thermometer; simultaneous multi-site measurement (rectum/ear/mouth) and pulse-temperature dissociation are clues (p.150)
Central thermoregulatory disorders - brain tumor, stroke, encephalitis, hypothalamic dysfunction (p.151)
Peripheral thermoregulatory causes - hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, heat stroke (p.151)

FUO is a syndrome, not a single disease - a final prolonged febrile illness in which intensive standard evaluation has failed to localize a cause. Etiologies cluster into four groups: infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs: autoimmune, autoinflammatory, granulomatous, and vasculitides), malignancy, and miscellaneous, with a substantial undiagnosed fraction. The spectrum has shifted over time: intraabdominal abscesses, tumors, and infective endocarditis have declined as CT, ultrasound, blood culture, and echocardiography improved, while entities such as acute HIV and autoinflammatory syndromes are now recognized. NIIDs may precede their typical clinical or laboratory features by months, requiring prolonged observation. The 'FUO paradox' describes how, despite better imaging (CT/MRI/PET-CT), the undiagnosed proportion is now higher (>50% in some Western cohorts) because most febrile illnesses are diagnosed before 3 weeks elapse, leaving only the most difficult cases to meet FUO criteria (pp.149-150).

Current (post-Petersdorf) FUO definition requires all of: fever >=38.3C (101F) on at least two occasions, illness lasting at least 3 weeks, no known immunocompromised state, and a diagnosis still uncertain after thorough history, examination, and a defined set of obligatory investigations (p.149).

Geography shapes the differential: infections (especially TB) dominate non-Western cohorts, while noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs) are the most common cause in Western cohorts, accounting for up to one-third of cases (p.150).
Investigation of cryoglobulins is a useful low-cost screening test in FUO given the frequent absence of specific symptoms (p.153).
Inflammation of unknown origin (IUO) shares the FUO definition but lacks the temperature criterion (elevated CRP/ESR with normal temperature); its causes and workup are identical to FUO (p.149).
FUO usually reflects an ATYPICAL presentation of a COMMON disease rather than a rare disease; pattern recognition explains the higher diagnostic yield at expert centers (pp.150, 153).

The cornerstone of the workup is the search for potentially diagnostic clues (PDCs) - all localizing signs, symptoms, and abnormalities pointing toward a diagnosis - via repeated history, examination, and obligatory tests; further testing should be PDC-driven (pp.152-153).
Examination should pay special attention to the eyes, lymph nodes, temporal arteries, liver, spleen, prior surgical sites, the entire skin surface, and mucous membranes (p.152).

History should capture fever pattern (continuous vs recurrent) and duration, prior medical history, current/recent drugs, family and sexual history, country of origin, recent and remote travel, environmental/hobby exposures, and animal contacts (p.152).
Giant cell arteritis is notably prevalent among FUO patients, with rates up to 17% in the elderly; temporal artery biopsy is still recommended for patients >=55 years (p.153).
FUO with headache should prompt CSF microbiologic examination for herpes simplex virus (especially type 2), Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, and M. tuberculosis (p.153).

In patients with recurrent/episodic FUO, ask the patient to return DURING a febrile episode; further tests should be done during an inflammatory episode since abnormalities may be absent between episodes (pp.152-153).
Starting empirical therapeutic trials before a diagnosis - should be AVOIDED except when the patient is rapidly deteriorating, because most undiagnosed patients resolve spontaneously (p.154).

Continuing antibiotics/glucocorticoids during workup - they mask disease: cultures become unreliable and glucocorticoids shrink lymph nodes regardless of cause; stop them before further testing (p.152).

Early empirical glucocorticoids - can mask fever while infection or lymphoma spreads and reduce the chance of diagnosing a treatable malignancy; avoid until infection and lymphoma are sufficiently excluded (p.155).

Ordering more screening tests without PDCs - low yield; immunologic and microbiologic serologies without PDCs more often give false-positives; better to wait for new PDCs unless the patient deteriorates (pp.153-154).
Over-culturing - performing >3 blood cultures or >1 urine culture is useless absent PDCs (p.153).
Failing to recognize PDCs already present in available information is a frequent cause of diagnostic delay (p.154).
Interpreting a negative TST/IGRA as excluding TB - it does not; results may be indeterminate in miliary TB, malnutrition, immunosuppression, or with anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies (p.153).

Misreading PET/CT - physiologic FDG uptake in brain, heart, bowel, kidneys, and bladder can obscure pathology (e.g., cardiac uptake masking endocarditis - mitigate with a pre-scan low-carbohydrate diet) (p.153).
Not excluding factitious/fraudulent fever and drug fever early, especially when inflammatory markers are normal (pp.150, 153).

Prognosis depends chiefly on the underlying diagnosis. When FUO remains unexplained after extensive evaluation, outlook is favorable: large cohorts report high rates of spontaneous fever resolution and mortality of 8% or less over several years of follow-up. The greatest mortality risk is during the early diagnostic phase. A normal 18F-FDG-PET/CT is associated with higher rates of spontaneous resolution and may help predict who will resolve. A symptom duration >12 months and a normal PET/CT both lower the chance of ever reaching a final diagnosis (pp.150, 154).
Clinical deterioration without new PDCs - the trigger to escalate workup (rather than wait) and the situation where empirical therapy may be justified (pp.152-153)
Hemodynamic instability or neutropenia - good indications for empirical antibiotic therapy (p.155)
Granulomatous disease on liver or bone marrow biopsy - should prompt (re)consideration of miliary tuberculosis (p.153)
Early phase of evaluation carries the highest FUO-related mortality risk (deaths occurred during index admission in cohort data; intravascular lymphoma and pneumonia found at autopsy) (p.154)

FUO categories (by host/setting), each requiring a distinct approach: (1) classic FUO - the immunocompetent adult per the formal definition; (2) nosocomial FUO; (3) neutropenic FUO; and (4) HIV-associated FUO. The contemporary Harrison definition explicitly EXCLUDES immunocompromised states, which need a different, more aggressive approach. Etiologies are grouped into four diagnostic categories - infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs), malignancy, and miscellaneous - with a large 'no diagnosis' fraction (pp.149-150).
Repeat detailed history and serial examinations — New localizing signs often emerge over time and are the single most valuable step in PUO workup.
CBC, ESR, CRP, LFTs, RFTs, urinalysis — First-tier screening tests that can reveal a localizing clue (e.g., abnormal LFTs pointing to liver abscess or biliary source).
Blood cultures (multiple sets, including for fastidious organisms if endocarditis suspected) — Identifies bacteremic causes including culture-negative endocarditis pathogens with extended incubation.
Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound — First-line imaging to screen for occult infection (TB, abscess) or malignancy.
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (second-tier) — More sensitive for occult abscess, lymphadenopathy, or malignancy if first-tier workup is unrevealing.
Echocardiography (if any murmur, risk factors, or persistent bacteremia) — Screens for infective endocarditis as a cause of prolonged fever.
Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (infective) — Systemic
veryLikely: Diagnosis-dependent — broad differential includes infective (TB, enteric fever, infective endocarditis, abscess), neoplastic (lymphoma), and autoimmune/rheumatologic causes
Urine culture and sensitivity — Confirms organism and susceptibility, essential for targeted therapy and de-escalation.
Blood cultures — Pyelonephritis carries meaningful bacteremia risk; positive cultures confirm systemic involvement and guide duration.
Renal ultrasound or CT (if no improvement in 48-72 hours) — Evaluates for obstruction or abscess if the patient fails to improve on appropriate therapy.
Acute Pyelonephritis (infective) — Genitourinary
veryLikely: Escherichia coli; likely: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis; possible: Enterococcus species, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (catheter/structural risk)

chunks.text: Rickettsiae and Orientia are obligately intracellular gram-negative coccobacilli that primarily infect vascular endothelial cells. After tick saliva inoculates organisms into the dermis (in RMSF after roughly 6 h of feeding), they spread lymphohematogenously and infect contiguous foci of endothelium throughout the body, producing a widespread infectious vasculitis with increased vascular permeability. The resulting edema, hypovolemia, and tissue ischemia (rather than occlusive thrombosis) drive the organ injury: prerenal azotemia, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and CNS dysfunction. Platelet consumption causes thrombocytopenia in about a third to half of RMSF cases, but frank DIC with hypofibrinogenemia is rare; the coagulation changes appear to be homeostatic responses to endothelial injury forming nonocclusive hemostatic plugs (p.1454, p.1456).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.137-141 (Ch.21 Fever and Rash); p.1454-1459 (Ch.192 Rickettsial Diseases); p.1488 (Ch.189 Leptospirosis differential)

chunks.text: All acute rickettsial illnesses look alike for roughly the first 5 days: fever, headache, and myalgias, often with nausea, vomiting, or cough; the distinguishing features (rash, eschar, pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis) emerge only as the illness progresses (p.1454).

chunks.text: Outcome is strongly time-dependent: untreated RMSF carries mortality of roughly 20-25% (historic) with confirmed-case fatality around 9-10% where R. rickettsii is the sole agent, versus ~3-5% when treated early; delayed recognition and treatment markedly increase death. For unclear reasons RMSF case-fatality approaches 50% in Mexico and Brazil. Severe Mediterranean spotted fever has mortality near 50% without treatment but improves dramatically with even a single day of appropriate therapy. Untreated epidemic typhus historically killed up to 60% and still exceeds 10-15% in outbreaks. Many survivors of severe RMSF recover fully, but permanent neurologic deficits and gangrene requiring amputation can follow severe illness (p.1456-1457; p.1488 / Ch.21).

Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular organism placed in a separate genus within the family Rickettsiaceae. It differs substantially from Rickettsia species both genetically and in cell-wall composition, notably lacking lipopolysaccharide. Disease results from infection of vascular endothelial cells with increased vascular permeability (a mechanism shared across the rickettsioses). The organism is maintained in nature by transovarial transmission within trombiculid mites; infected larval mites (chiggers, the only mite stage that feeds on a vertebrate host) inoculate the organism into the skin during feeding. Severe disease reflects widespread vascular injury, producing the encephalitis and interstitial pneumonia that characterize advanced cases. Closely related Orientia species (O. chuto, Candidatus O. chiloensis) cause scrub typhus-like illness in newly recognized foci (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456, p.1460, p.3773).

The classic triad of an inoculation eschar at the chigger feeding site, regional lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash is the textbook description, but these signs are seldom seen in indigenous (local endemic) patients (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Among returning travelers, fewer than 50% develop an eschar and fewer than 40% develop a rash; when a rash does appear it typically emerges on day 4-6 of illness (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Eschar formation occurs at the site of mite/chigger feeding and may develop during the incubation period; an eschar is a useful diagnostic clue that should prompt consideration of scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1455).

Onset after a 6-21 day incubation is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, cough, and gastrointestinal symptoms; some patients recover spontaneously after a few days while others progress to severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Chigger bites may be asymptomatic, so the absence of a recalled bite does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3773).

Immunity to scrub typhus is short-lived: protection against the homologous strain wanes over 1-3 years, and the organism's marked antigenic diversity means cross-protective immunity can be lost in as little as 1 month, so reinfection is possible (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Relying on the classic triad: eschar, rash, and lymphadenopathy are frequently absent (eschar <50% and rash <40% of travelers; signs seldom seen in indigenous patients), so a negative skin exam does not exclude scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Expecting a recalled bite: chigger bites may be asymptomatic and the mites are tiny and rarely noticed (Harrison 22e p.3773).

Assuming geographic exclusion: although classically eastern/southern Asia, northern Australia, and Pacific/Indian Ocean islands, emerging and reemerging foci (e.g., Chile, parts of South/Central America, Africa, Arabian peninsula via related Orientia species) challenge the traditional epidemiology (Harrison 22e p.1460, p.3773).
Note that PCR on blood is less sensitive than PCR on eschar material (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Some Thai isolates are poorly responsive to doxycycline or chloramphenicol (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Illness ranges from mild and self-limiting to fatal. The case-fatality rate for untreated classic cases is about 6% and would likely be lower if all mild cases were captured; overall reported mortality varies widely by location (cited as 1% to 70%). Risk of death rises with increasing age and with the presence of myocarditis, delirium, pneumonitis, or signs of hemorrhage. Recognized in time, the disease responds well to appropriate antibiotic therapy (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460).
Altered mental status / encephalitis (meningoencephalitis is a feature of severe disease) (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455).
Interstitial pneumonia / pneumonitis with dyspnea or progression toward respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460).
Myocarditis (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation or hemorrhage (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Renal failure (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (a severe-disease pattern shared by the rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455).

Harrison does not give a formal severity score; it contrasts mild/self-limiting illness with severe disease. Severe scrub typhus is marked by encephalitis/meningoencephalitis and interstitial pneumonia due to vascular injury, and may progress to myocarditis, DIC, renal failure, hypotension, and multiorgan failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455, p.1460).

Careful skin examination for eschar — Eschar (a painless, often overlooked necrotic lesion at the chigger bite site) is highly specific for scrub typhus when found — actively look in skin folds, axillae, groin.
Scrub typhus IgM ELISA / Weil-Felix (less specific) — Confirms diagnosis serologically, though treatment should not wait for results when clinical suspicion is high.
CBC, LFTs, renal function — Assesses organ involvement; transaminitis and thrombocytopenia are common supportive findings.
Chest X-ray (if respiratory symptoms) — Screens for ARDS, a recognized complication of severe/delayed scrub typhus.

chunks.text: Sepsis arises when an infection provokes a dysregulated, self-amplifying host response rather than a contained local one. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g., LPS, bacterial cell-wall components, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g., histones, HMGB1, S100 proteins, mitochondrial/double-stranded DNA, ATP released from injured cells) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD-like receptors) on innate immune and parenchymal cells. This triggers exuberant release of cytokines and chemokines and upregulation of vascular adhesion molecules. Myeloid cells (neutrophils, monocytes, M1 macrophages, dendritic cells) drive injury through phagocytosis, degranulation, reactive oxygen/nitrogen species, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), while emergency granulopoiesis releases immature neutrophils (a poor-prognosis marker). Lymphoid responses are dysregulated, with lymphocyte apoptosis, exhaustion, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells producing a state of immunosuppression that predisposes survivors to secondary infection. The endothelium is activated and injured: glycocalyx breakdown, loss of VE-cadherin/tight junctions, and apoptosis cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and a widened oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic shift (increased tissue factor, vWF, PAI-1; depleted antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and protein C; complement activation with C3a/C5a and the C5b-9 membrane attack complex) generates microvascular thrombi and, once clotting factors and platelets are consumed, bleeding. Excess nitric oxide drives systemic vasodilation. The net result is impaired oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization; even when oxygen delivery is adequate, mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction impairs ATP generation and ion homeostasis, producing multiorgan cellular injury and dysfunction (p.2317-2319).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Sepsis-3 (2016) reframes sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, not merely a systemic inflammatory state; the older SIRS-based criteria and the term 'severe sepsis' were discarded for poor specificity (p.2316).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Lactate is central to risk-stratifying sepsis: elevation reflects tissue hypoperfusion/anaerobic metabolism, correlates with worse outcome, and serial measurements help track response to resuscitation (p.2313).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Most sepsis is community-onset (~88%); the urinary tract is the single most common primary site, followed by respiratory, intra-abdominal, and skin/soft-tissue sources (p.2316).

chunks.text: Hospital-onset sepsis tends to involve sicker, more comorbid patients with more intra-abdominal infection and bacteremia from Enterococcus, Candida, and Pseudomonas, and carries higher ICU admission and mortality (p.2317).

chunks.text: Operationally, sepsis is identified by an acute rise of >=2 points in the SOFA score over baseline in a patient with suspected or confirmed infection (p.2320).

chunks.text: Septic shock is the subset of sepsis with persistent hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP >65 mmHg PLUS lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, reflecting circulatory, cellular, and metabolic derangement that markedly raises mortality (p.2310, 2320).

chunks.text: Overall in-hospital mortality is roughly 15% among hospitalized adults with sepsis, rising to up to ~40% with septic shock; globally an estimated ~11 million sepsis-related deaths occur yearly (about one in five deaths worldwide). Mortality climbs with age and is higher in men. Elevated SOFA scores and machine-learning-defined phenotypes track population-level outcome (e.g., alpha/beta/gamma/delta phenotypes with ~2%/5%/15%/32% mortality) but cannot reliably predict an individual patient's outcome. Survivorship carries a heavy long-term burden: physical (prolonged fatigue, muscle loss, weakness, reduced functional capacity), cognitive (cognitive decline, dementia), and psychological (depression, reduced quality of life) sequelae, plus increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. About half of survivors are rehospitalized within a year and roughly one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated death risk persisting up to ~2 years (p.2316-2317, 2324). No FDA-approved host-targeted/immunomodulatory therapy exists for sepsis (p.2324).

chunks.text: Sepsis-3 (Singer et al., JAMA 2016) is the current framework: (1) Infection (suspected or confirmed) without organ dysfunction is not sepsis. (2) Sepsis = suspected/confirmed infection with an acute increase of >=2 points in the SOFA score from baseline (life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response). The SOFA score grades six systems 0-4: respiratory (PaO2/FiO2), coagulation (platelets), liver (bilirubin), cardiovascular (MAP / vasopressor requirement), CNS (Glasgow Coma Scale), and renal (creatinine / urine output). (3) Septic shock = sepsis with vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP >65 mmHg AND serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. qSOFA (>=2 of RR >=22/min, altered mentation, SBP <=100 mmHg) is a rapid bedside risk-stratification prompt for poor outcome in suspected infection, not a diagnostic criterion. The prior 1991/1992 SIRS-based definitions and the term 'severe sepsis' are obsolete under Sepsis-3 (p.2292, 2316, 2320).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Blood cultures (x2, before antibiotics if feasible) — Identifies the causative organism and susceptibility for de-escalation.
Lactate — Core Sepsis-3/Surviving Sepsis Campaign marker of tissue hypoperfusion; guides resuscitation and risk-stratification toward septic shock.
Source-specific cultures (urine, sputum, wound, CSF as guided by clinical exam) — Identifies and confirms the infectious source to allow targeted therapy.
CBC, renal function, liver function, coagulation profile — Assesses organ dysfunction (SOFA components) and supports staging severity.
Imaging directed by suspected source (CXR, abdominal ultrasound/CT) — Localizes the source and identifies any need for source control (drainage, debridement).
Sepsis (infective) — Systemic

veryLikely: Organism depends entirely on the suspected source (e.g., E. coli for urosepsis, S. pneumoniae for pulmonary sepsis); likely: Polymicrobial flora if source is intra-abdominal; possible: Resistant organisms if healthcare-associated or recent antibiotic exposure
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Piperacillin-tazobactam (broad empiric, source unclear) / Add Vancomycin if MRSA risk, line-associated, or skin/soft tissue source Broad empiric gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic coverage is reasonable when the source is not yet localized, pending rapid source identification to allow narrowing.
[guideline] alternative → Source-directed narrow-spectrum therapy (preferred once source identified)
Other causes of distributive shock: pancreatitis, severe burns, liver failure, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock from brain/spinal cord injury, and adrenal insufficiency/adrenal crisis (p.2353-2354)

chunks.text: Septic shock is the most common form of distributive shock, in which the primary hemodynamic derangement is a fall in systemic vascular resistance (vasoplegia) rather than a primary loss of preload or pump function. The vasodilatory profile is distinctive: SVR is reduced, cardiac output is typically increased as a compensatory response, and both central venous pressure (CVP) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) tend to be low (p.2353-2354). Arterial and venous vasodilation is mediated in part by excess nitric oxide; vasopressin deficiency may also contribute to refractory hypotension. The dysregulated host response begins when pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g. LPS, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g. histones, HMGB1, mitochondrial DNA, ATP) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD receptors) on neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and parenchymal cells, triggering proinflammatory cytokine/chemokine release and upregulation of endothelial adhesion molecules. Activated neutrophils release reactive oxygen species and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); endothelial activation/injury, glycocalyx degradation, and loss of VE-cadherin tight junctions cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and increased oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic state arises from tissue-factor-driven coagulation, platelet/vWF microthrombi, complement activation (C3a, C5a, C5b-9 membrane attack complex), reduced anticoagulants (antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, activated protein C), and impaired fibrinolysis (elevated PAI-1); consumption of clotting factors and platelets can then produce hemorrhage. The net effect is hypotension (from vasodilation, myocardial depression, and hypovolemia), microcirculatory dysfunction, and mitochondrial/metabolic failure, so that oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization are all impaired and cellular injury occurs even when bulk oxygen delivery appears adequate (p.2317-2320). Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy can add a cardiogenic component, producing mixed shock (p.2355).

chunks.text: Septic shock carries up to ~40% mortality, far higher than the ~15% overall mortality among US hospitalized adults with sepsis (p.2316). In emergency-department shock cohorts, septic and cardiogenic shock have the highest 90-day mortality (reported ~56% and ~52% respectively), and septic shock predominates among ICU shock (~62% of ICU shock patients in one multicenter series), whereas hypovolemic shock has lower mortality (p.2355). Mortality rises with age and is higher in men; comorbidities such as diabetes, obesity, neurologic/respiratory/cardiac disease, renal or hepatic insufficiency, cancer, and immunosuppression worsen outcomes (p.2317). SOFA scores predict mortality at the population level but not for individual patients; proposed clinical 'phenotypes' (alpha/beta/gamma/delta) carried roughly 2%, 5%, 15%, and 32% mortality (p.2317). Survivors face substantial long-term sequelae: physical (fatigue, muscle loss, weakness), cognitive and psychological (cognitive decline, dementia, depression), and increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. Roughly half of survivors are rehospitalized within 1 year and about one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated risk persisting up to 2 years (p.2321).

chunks.text: Acute leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of immature, poorly differentiated haematopoietic precursors (blasts) that infiltrate marrow, blood and other tissues; AML arises from myeloid progenitors and ALL from lymphoid (B- or T-lineage) progenitors. Genome sequencing indicates most AML arises from a small number of mutations that accumulate with age - up to 5-6% of normal people over 70 carry premalignant clones (clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, CHIP, commonly DNMT3A/TET2/ASXL1), which carries a ~10-fold increased risk of haematologic malignancy though additional 'hits' are required to progress to overt leukaemia. Genetic lesions drive both phenotype and behaviour: for example t(15;17)/PML-RARA defines APL and predisposes to DIC, while NPM1 and FLT3 mutations associate with high leukocyte counts. Marrow replacement by blasts produces anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, accounting for the dominant clinical features (Harrison 22e p.825-828, p.844).

Acute adrenal insufficiency reflects an absolute or relative deficiency of cortisol, in primary disease compounded by loss of aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). Glucocorticoid deficiency impairs vascular tone, gluconeogenesis and loss of feedback inhibition of AVP release (contributing to hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia), while mineralocorticoid deficiency causes renal salt wasting with volume depletion, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and rising creatinine. The result is hypotension that may decompensate into hypovolaemic shock. Crisis is usually unmasked by a stressor that exceeds the inadequate cortisol reserve — intercurrent illness, surgery or other stress, or increased glucocorticoid inactivation as in hyperthyroidism (p.3111).
Adrenal crisis typically emerges after a prolonged prodrome of nonspecific complaints rather than appearing out of the blue (p.3111).
Crisis is more frequent in PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency because both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid secretion are lost (p.3111).
Postural hypotension can progress to frank hypovolaemic shock (p.3111).
Prospective data: about 8.3 adrenal crises per 100 patient-years and roughly 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years (p.3111).
Adrenal crisis is classified as a form of endocrine/distributive shock (p.2353).
In suspected crisis, it is reasonable to draw a baseline cortisol (and ACTH), start replacement, and defer formal stimulation testing — diagnostic testing must never delay treatment (p.3111).

Starting thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient can precipitate adrenal crisis, because thyroid hormone shortens cortisol half-life; screen for adrenal insufficiency before treating hypothyroidism in possible polyendocrine syndrome (p.3133).
Do NOT let diagnostic testing delay treatment in suspected crisis (p.3111).

Random/baseline serum cortisol has limited diagnostic value because levels may be coincidentally low from normal diurnal rhythm, and many secondary cases have near-normal baseline cortisol that only fails on stimulation testing (p.3111).
Do NOT start thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency — it can precipitate crisis (p.3133).
Hyperthyroidism increases glucocorticoid inactivation and can trigger crisis (p.3111).
Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by concurrent primary hypothyroidism, which prolongs cortisol half-life (p.3133).
Acute adrenal insufficiency is potentially lethal (p.636). Even with established care, crises and crisis-related deaths continue to occur (~8.3 crises and ~0.5 deaths per 100 patient-years) (p.3111).

chunks.text: Anemia results from a defect in any of the three requirements for normal red-cell production: renal erythropoietin (EPO) output, a functioning erythroid marrow, and adequate substrate (especially iron). EPO rises logarithmically once haemoglobin falls below ~100-120 g/L, but in chronic kidney disease and chronic inflammation EPO is inappropriately low for the degree of anemia. With adequate EPO and substrate, marrow red-cell output can rise four- to fivefold over 1-2 weeks. Mechanistically anemia is either hyperproductive/regenerative (blood loss or haemolysis, with reticulocytosis) or hypoproliferative (nutritional deficiency, marrow replacement, absent precursors, stem-cell defects, or EPO deficiency). Inflammatory cytokines such as TNF lower EPO and raise hepcidin, which blocks iron absorption and release from stores, producing the anemia of inflammation (p.443-450).

Psoriatic arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2958)

Polarized light microscopy of synovial fluid - MSU: needle/rod-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent; CPP: rhomboid/rod-shaped, weakly positively or non-birefringent; apatite: non-birefringent (requires alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy); calcium oxalate: bipyramidal, variable/strong birefringence, alizarin red S positive (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961-2962)

Arthrocentesis of an unaffected first MTP joint or knee between flares can still demonstrate MSU crystals (Harrison 22e p.2959)

Plain radiographs - advanced gout: well-defined erosions with sclerotic/overhanging margins, soft tissue tophi; CPPD: punctate/linear chondrocalcinosis in fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961)
Musculoskeletal ultrasound - double-contour sign over articular cartilage indicating MSU deposition; can also reveal chondrocalcinosis in CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961)
Dual-energy CT - identifies MSU crystals by chemical composition (Harrison 22e p.2959)

In CPPD patients under 50, evaluate for metabolic/familial causes: serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, iron, transferrin (Harrison 22e p.2960)

Gout arises from an increased body urate pool due to chronic hyperuricemia, leading to supersaturation and crystallization of monosodium urate (MSU) within joints and connective tissue. Hyperuricemia is predominantly due to impaired renal urate excretion (~90%) and less often urate overproduction (~10%); a minority (~10%) of cases reflect inherited metabolic disorders (PRPP synthetase superactivity, HPRT deficiency). Crystal shedding from inert synovial deposits, triggered by metabolic factors, diuresis, rapid urate changes (including urate-lowering therapy initiation), local trauma, or medical illness, activates resident synovial phagocytes (monocytes/macrophages, mast cells) and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta and other proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha). Phagocytosis of MSU crystals by neutrophils with a respiratory burst amplifies the acute inflammatory response. Persistent MSU deposition produces tophi (granulomatous inflammation around crystals) and chronic erosive gouty arthritis. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals; their release similarly drives inflammasome-mediated inflammation, analogous to hyperuricemia in gout. Apatite and calcium oxalate crystals can likewise stimulate synovial cell proliferation and release of proteases, collagenases, and prostaglandin E2, contributing to joint destruction (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962).

Initial gout flares are usually monoarticular; the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases, followed by tarsal joints, ankles, and knees. Oligo- and polyarticular flares emerge over time (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) arthropathy can cause an extremely destructive arthropathy of the elderly, classically the shoulder (Milwaukee shoulder), with low synovial fluid leukocyte counts despite dramatic symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2961).

Hyperuricemia and gout are part of the insulin-resistance syndrome and associate with cardiometabolic-kidney comorbidities: obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, CKD, and urate nephrolithiasis (Harrison 22e p.2956).

Gout flares often begin at night to early morning, are among the most painful conditions humans experience, and the affected joint becomes warm, red, tender, and very swollen, frequently mimicking cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.2958).
Untreated flares usually subside spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, with symptom-free intervals (intercritical gout) until the next episode (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Serum urate can be normal or low during an acute flare because inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 are uricosuric and can lower urate by about 2 mg/dL; seek historical or post-flare urate values instead (Harrison 22e p.2959).

In CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) the knee is most commonly affected, followed by the wrist; the first MTP joint (podagra) is rarely involved, a useful distinguishing clue from gout (Harrison 22e p.2960).
Initial acute CPPD attacks tend to last longer than typical gout flares, sometimes weeks to months (Harrison 22e p.2960).
Acute CPPD can be precipitated by trauma, severe medical illness, or surgery (especially parathyroidectomy, which rapidly lowers serum calcium and magnesium and sheds crystals) (Harrison 22e p.2960).

Women account for only about 5-20% of gout patients; most are postmenopausal, elderly, and often on diuretics with coexisting osteoarthritis, hypertension, or mild renal insufficiency. Premenopausal gout is rare (Harrison 22e p.2958).
Hyperuricemia in a prepubertal boy should prompt consideration of inherited enzyme defects such as HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan spectrum) or PRPP synthetase superactivity (Harrison 22e p.2958).
Relying on a normal serum urate during an acute flare to exclude gout - urate is often normal or low at flare onset (Harrison 22e p.2959).
Attributing a destructive 'osteoarthritis' in atypical joints (MCP, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle) to primary OA rather than recognizing pseudo-osteoarthritis from CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2961).
Assuming chondrocalcinosis on imaging is always CPPD - calcium oxalate deposition in chronic renal failure is an exception (Harrison 22e p.2961).
Missing apatite arthropathy because individual apatite crystals are not visible on routine polarized light microscopy and need alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy (Harrison 22e p.2961).
Overlooking inherited enzyme defects when hyperuricemia/gout presents in a young patient, particularly a prepubertal boy (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Untreated gout flares typically resolve spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, but recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, joint deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Controlling the underlying chronic hyperuricemia (urate-lowering therapy to a subsaturation target) can prevent recurrent flares and dissolve tophi, generally requiring lifelong therapy. For chronic CPPD there is no means to remove established CPP crystal deposits from cartilage and synovium (unlike urate lowering in gout), and progressive destructive large-joint disease may require joint replacement. Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) progresses indolently and may also lead to joint replacement (Harrison 22e p.2958-2962).

Crystal-proven arthritis does not exclude concurrent septic arthritis - bacterial infection can coexist with MSU or CPP crystals in synovial fluid; always Gram stain and culture (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961)

Acute CPPD can produce systemic features (fever, chills, raised acute-phase reactants), with low-grade fever in up to 50% and temperatures occasionally as high as 40C - mandates microbial culture to exclude infection (Harrison 22e p.2960, p.2961)
CPPD onset before age 50 warrants workup for underlying metabolic disease (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) or hereditary CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2960)

chunks.text: DIC arises from uncontrolled thrombin generation triggered by multiple mechanisms, with simultaneous disruption of physiologic anticoagulant pathways and abnormal fibrinolysis. In sepsis and trauma, activation of inflammatory pathways increases tissue factor expression, activates neutrophils and monocytes with cytokine release and neutrophil extracellular trap formation, and releases polyphosphates that cross-talk with the coagulation system (thrombo-inflammation); endothelial damage causes loss of native antithrombotic properties. The result is systemic fibrin deposition in small and mid-size vessels causing microvascular occlusion, ischemic organ damage, and red cell fragmentation/hemolysis. Sustained activation consumes platelets and clotting factors, producing systemic bleeding that is aggravated by secondary hyperfibrinolysis in late stages. Purpura fulminans is a severe form of DIC with extensive cutaneous thrombosis, predominantly in young children after viral or bacterial infection, especially with inherited or acquired protein C pathway deficiency (p.976).

Alcoholic ketoacidosis — high-anion-gap acidosis (predominantly beta-hydroxybutyrate) without hyperglycaemia, usually with preserved renal function, in chronic alcohol use with vomiting and poor intake (p.413).
Starvation ketoacidosis — ketoacidosis with normal or low glucose (p.413).
Other high-anion-gap acidoses: lactic acidosis, toxic ingestions (e.g. salicylates), and renal failure/uraemia (p.413).
Plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate measured directly (more reliable than urine nitroprusside ketones) (p.413).
Anion gap calculation, including assessment for a mixed non-anion-gap / high-anion-gap acidosis when the change in bicarbonate exceeds the change in anion gap (p.413).
Acute pancreatitis can mimic DKA (and vice versa), with overlapping abdominal pain; DKA may itself be accompanied by amylase elevation, complicating the distinction (p.2788).

DKA results from increased fatty acid metabolism with accumulation of the ketoacids acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, producing hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. It typically occurs in insulin-dependent diabetes when insulin is stopped or when an intercurrent illness (e.g. infection, gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, myocardial infarction) acutely raises insulin requirements. In euglycaemic DKA caused by SGLT2 inhibitors, glycosuria drives an osmotic diuresis and volume depletion while plasma glucose stays in the normal range despite the ketoacidosis (p.413).
An acetone-like fruity odour on the breath is a classic bedside clue to ketoacidosis (p.93).
Urine dipstick (nitroprusside reaction) detects acetoacetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate, so it can underestimate the true degree of ketosis; measure plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate directly (p.413).

As the circulation is restored with fluids, beta-hydroxybutyrate is converted to acetoacetate, so the nitroprusside ketone reading may paradoxically become more positive during treatment rather than reflecting worsening disease (p.413).
Glucose may be normal or only mildly raised in euglycaemic DKA (SGLT2-inhibitor associated) and in starvation ketoacidosis, so a normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis (p.413).
Excretion of ketoacids obligates loss of cations (sodium, potassium), worsening volume depletion and promoting chloride retention (p.413).
Relying on urine ketone dipstick, which misses beta-hydroxybutyrate and underestimates ketosis (p.413).
Interpreting a rising nitroprusside ketone result during fluid resuscitation as deterioration, when it reflects the beta-hydroxybutyrate-to-acetoacetate shift (p.413).
Assuming a normal/near-normal glucose excludes DKA, missing euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors (p.413).
Over-resuscitation with isotonic saline causing volume overload and/or hyperchloraemic acidosis (p.413).

Mucormycosis risk: DKA patients are at high risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis; acidosis frees iron from carrier proteins and beta-hydroxybutyrate upregulates fungal adherence/penetration receptors — consider in a DKA patient with sinus/orbital/facial signs (p.1761).
Severe acidaemia (pH <7.00) or shock identifies the small subset where bicarbonate may be considered; cerebral oedema risk limits its use (p.413).
Hyperchloraemic (non-anion-gap) acidosis and volume overload can be precipitated by aggressive isotonic saline during treatment (p.413).

Characterise overall physiologic state and toxidrome from vital signs and neuromuscular exam (p.3704)
Anion gap (raised AGMA in methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate, or any poisoning causing organ failure, seizures or shock; low anion gap with bromide, calcium, iodine, lithium, magnesium) (p.3705)
Osmolal gap (>10 mmol/L suggests a low-molecular-weight solute such as an alcohol or glycol) (p.3705)
Serum lactate (low relative to anion gap in alcohol/glycol intoxication, high and near the anion gap in hypoperfusion) (p.3705)
Glucose, electrolytes, ketones (hypo-/hyperglycaemia and hypo-/hyperkalaemia patterns can implicate specific agents) (p.3705)
ECG (bradycardia/AV block, QRS and QT prolongation, ventricular tachyarrhythmias suggest specific agent classes) (p.3706)
Abdominal/chest radiograph (radiopaque densities suggest heavy metals, drug packets, iron, enteric-coated or salicylate tablets; CXR for pulmonary edema/aspiration) (p.3706)

Quantitative serum levels (acetaminophen, alcohols incl. ethylene glycol/methanol, anticonvulsants, barbiturates, digoxin, iron, lithium, salicylate, theophylline, carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin) guide management (p.3706)
Coagulation (PT/INR) for warfarin/rodenticide risk stratification, though unreliable for direct oral anticoagulant overdose (p.3705)
Psychogenic illness / anxiety reaction (mass hysteria, fear of poisoning) producing symptoms inconsistent with the exposure history (p.3705)
Structural CNS lesion - focal neurologic findings are uncommon in poisoning and should prompt evaluation for a structural cause (p.3703)

Poisoning is a dose-related adverse effect from exposure to a chemical, drug or other xenobiotic. Responses to a given dose vary with genetic polymorphism, enzyme induction or inhibition by co-ingestants, and acquired tolerance. Toxicity may be local or systemic depending on route, the agent's physicochemical properties and mechanism, and its severity/reversibility depends on the functional reserve of the patient or target organ (influenced by age and pre-existing disease) (p.3703).

Diagnosis of an unknown poisoning rests on pattern recognition: first classify the overall physiologic state as stimulated, depressed, discordant, or normal, then look for a recognizable toxidrome (p.3704).

Most patients who are or become asymptomatic by 6 h after ingestion are unlikely to develop later toxicity and may be discharged, but longer observation is required after 'toxic time-bomb' ingestions (p.3707).

Core temperature is the single most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant (e.g. cocaine) poisoning or in drug/alcohol/GHB withdrawal, so it must be measured even in difficult or combative patients (p.3704).

Mydriasis is common to all stimulant states but is most marked with anticholinergics (muscarinic loss of pupil reactivity); cocaine and other sympathomimetics enlarge pupils yet retain some light reactivity (p.3704).

The anticholinergic toxidrome is distinguished from other stimulant states by hot, dry, flushed skin, decreased bowel sounds and urinary retention, whereas sympathomimetic states cause diaphoresis and increased bowel activity (p.3704).
Miosis points to a depressed state from opioids or cholinergic agents; muscarinic/nicotinic features separate cholinergic poisoning from opioid poisoning (p.3704-3705).

In opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign derangements are secondary to CNS depression and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression); marked cardiovascular depression with preserved consciousness instead suggests a peripherally acting sympatholytic (p.3705).
Rotatory nystagmus among stimulated patients is essentially specific to phencyclidine and ketamine (p.3704).

A near-normal exam may reflect a nontoxic exposure, psychogenic illness, or a 'toxic time-bomb' (slowly absorbed, slowly distributed, requiring metabolic activation, or disrupting metabolism); once-daily reformulations have made these increasingly common (p.3705).
Rapid response of altered mental status to IV dextrose, naloxone or flumazenil is virtually diagnostic of hypoglycemia, opioid poisoning and benzodiazepine intoxication respectively (p.3706).

Rapid hospital urine drug-of-abuse screens are screening tests only, cannot confirm the exact substance, and are not diagnostic or forensic; false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones triggering false-positive opiate screens) and false negatives are common (p.3706).

A negative drug screen does not exclude poisoning - the agent may be undetectable by the assay (e.g. synthetic cannabinoids/spice, cathinones/bath salts, kratom) or present below the limit of detection at the time of sampling; repeat testing later may turn positive (p.3706).

Qualitative drug screens are not clinically useful or cost-effective when the patient is asymptomatic or the picture fits the reported history; reserve them for severe or unexplained toxicity (coma, seizures, cardiovascular instability, acidosis, nonsinus rhythms) (p.3706).
Blood levels obtained during absorption/distribution may exceed tissue levels and may not correlate with toxicity (p.3707).
In polydrug overdose a clear toxidrome may be obscured when different drug classes counteract each other's physiologic effects (p.3704).
Physostigmine fully reverses anticholinergic poisoning but can also produce some arousal in CNS depression of any cause, so arousal alone is not specific (p.3706).
Overdose effects begin sooner, peak later and last longer than therapeutic-dose effects, and an agent's published (therapeutic) pharmacokinetics differ from its toxicokinetics in overdose (p.3707).

Overall mortality is low (<1% of all poison exposures) but rises to 1-2% among hospitalised patients with intentional (suicidal) overdose or complications of drugs of abuse, who account for most serious poisonings. About 20-25% of exposures need bedside professional evaluation and ~5% need hospitalisation. Acetaminophen is the pharmaceutical most often implicated in fatal poisoning, while carbon monoxide is the leading overall cause of poisoning death (often fatal before discovery). Most patients asymptomatic at 6 h are unlikely to deteriorate (p.3703, p.3707).
Temperature elevation (grade 4 stimulation) - most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant poisoning and withdrawal (p.3704)
Coma, seizures or cardiovascular collapse (grade 4 physiologic stimulation or depression) (p.3705)

Depression - grade 1 lethargic but arousable to voice/touch; grade 2 responds to pain not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; grade 3 unresponsive to pain, depressed brainstem reflexes, reduced tone/respiration/temperature; grade 4 flaccid, absent brainstem reflexes and respirations, depressed cardiovascular signs (p.3705).

[guideline] management
Diabetic ketoacidosis (and the DKA/HHS overlap presentation) (p.3216).
Other causes of an altered/hyperosmolar sensorium - the differential for hyperosmolar coma includes uremia, nonketotic hyperosmolar states and other metabolic derangements (p.3216, general).
Plasma glucose - typically markedly elevated, may be >55.5 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) (p.3219).
Serum osmolality - characteristically >300 mOsm/L (p.3219).
Corrected serum sodium - measured Na may be normal or low, but corrected Na (add ~1.6 meq/L for each 5.6 mmol/L [100 mg/dL] rise in glucose) is usually elevated (p.3219).
Renal function (BUN/creatinine) - prerenal azotaemia from volume depletion; creatinine typically moderately raised (p.3219).
Ketones/beta-hydroxybutyrate - absent or only mild; serum beta-hydroxybutyrate <1.0 mmol/L; any moderate ketonuria is usually due to starvation (p.3219).
Acid-base status - acidosis absent or mild; a small anion-gap metabolic acidosis may reflect raised lactic acid (p.3219).

HHS arises from RELATIVE insulin deficiency combined with inadequate fluid intake. Insulin deficiency drives hepatic glucose overproduction (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis) and impairs glucose uptake by skeletal muscle. The resulting hyperglycaemia causes an osmotic diuresis with intravascular volume depletion that is worsened by inadequate fluid replacement. The reason ketosis is absent is not fully understood; the insulin deficiency is presumed to be only relative and less severe than in DKA, and some studies show lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels in HHS than in DKA, with possibly reduced hepatic ketone synthesis or an insulin/glucagon ratio that does not favour ketogenesis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated in both HHS and DKA (p.3217-3219).
Typical patient is an older adult with type 2 diabetes presenting after a several-week prodrome of polyuria, weight loss and falling oral intake, progressing to confusion, lethargy or coma (p.3219).
Examination reflects profound dehydration and hyperosmolality: hypotension, tachycardia and altered mental status (p.3219).
Features classically ABSENT in HHS that are seen in DKA: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and Kussmaul respirations (p.3219).
HHS and DKA lie on a continuum of hyperglycaemia; up to one-third of patients have overlapping features of both (p.3216).
Plasma glucose in HHS is usually markedly higher than in DKA and may exceed 55.5 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) (p.3219).
A debilitating condition (e.g. prior stroke, dementia) or a social situation that limits access to water frequently contributes to HHS by impairing water intake (p.3218-3219).
Worldwide reported cases of both HHS and DKA are rising for reasons that are not clear (p.3216).
A normal or low measured serum sodium can be falsely reassuring - it must be corrected for hyperglycaemia, after which it is usually elevated and reveals a profound water deficit (p.3219).
Mild ketonuria may be present but is typically from starvation, not from ketoacidosis - it should not redirect the diagnosis away from HHS (p.3219).
Fever may be absent even when infection is the precipitant; signs of infection should be sought regardless (p.3217, DKA section, applicable to acute hyperglycaemic crises).

Even with appropriate treatment, HHS has a substantially higher mortality rate than DKA, reported up to about 15% in some clinical series. The worse outlook reflects that HHS patients are usually older, have more profound fluid losses and dehydration (developed over days to weeks), are more likely to have mental status changes, and more often have a life-threatening precipitating event with accompanying comorbidities (p.3219).
HHS carries a substantially higher mortality than DKA (up to ~15% in some series), reflecting older patients, more pronounced dehydration and serious precipitating events with comorbidities (p.3219).
Hyperosmolar state must be reversed gradually - too-rapid correction risks worsening neurologic function (p.3219).
Precipitant is often a serious concurrent illness - myocardial infarction, stroke, sepsis, pneumonia or other severe infection - which must be actively sought (p.3219).

Harrison does not give a graded severity classification specific to HHS (unlike DKA, which is graded mild/moderate/severe by pH, bicarbonate and mental status). HHS is instead defined by marked hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality (>300 mOsm/L) and the relative absence of ketosis/acidosis, on a continuum with DKA (p.3218-3219).
