Tertiary hyperparathyroidism; rare ectopic PTH secretion (p.362-363)
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) — autosomal dominant, inactivating CASR mutations; calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01, parathyroid surgery ineffective (p.363)
Multiple myeloma (consider in malignant setting; can also cause chronic hypercalcaemia) (p.363-364)
Granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, leprosy, fungal infection, foreign-body reaction) via extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D (p.362-363)
Vitamin D intoxication (excess 25(OH)D or 1,25(OH)2D; CYP24A1 deficiency) (p.362-363)
Thyrotoxicosis, Paget's disease, prolonged immobilisation (increased bone resorption) (p.363)
Milk-alkali syndrome / excess calcium intake or TPN (p.362-363)
Drugs: thiazides, vitamin A, lithium, foscarnet, teriparatide, aromatase inhibitors; rebound resorption after denosumab discontinuation (p.362)

Tuberculosis — can cause hypercalcaemia through granulomatous extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D production, mimicking a malignant cause (p.362-363)
Other granulomatous infections (leprosy, fungal infections) via the same macrophage CYP27B1 mechanism (p.362-363)
Intact PTH by two-site assay — the key second test; suppressed in HHM, inappropriately normal/elevated in primary hyperparathyroidism (p.363-364)
PTHrP level — to confirm hypercalcaemia of malignancy when needed (p.364, 738)
Serum phosphate — low/hypophosphataemia with PTHrP and primary hyperparathyroidism; high-normal/elevated with vitamin D-mediated hypercalcaemia (p.363-364, 738)
Serum 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D — 1,25(OH)2D raised/inappropriately normal in lymphoma and granulomatous causes (p.364)
Serum free light chains plus protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to evaluate for myeloma (p.364)
Albumin to calculate corrected calcium (p.363)
Urinary calcium / calcium-creatinine clearance ratio (<0.01 suggests FHH; >0.02 fractional excretion supports pHPT) (p.363)
Genetic testing (CASR, GNA11, AP2S1) if FHH suspected and urine studies inconclusive (p.363)
ECG — may show shortened QTc/ST segments, bradyarrhythmias, AV block, QRS widening, bundle branch block (p.364, 738)
Primary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism — PTH-driven hypercalcaemia mimicking malignant hypercalcaemia (p.362-364)
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia — benign mimic where surgery is ineffective (p.363)
Sarcoidosis and other non-infectious granulomatous/foreign-body reactions (p.362-363)
Pseudohypercalcaemia (e.g. calcium-binding IgM in Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia, or spuriously high reading from altered albumin binding) (p.362-363)

Calcium balance is governed by PTH and the vitamin D metabolites 1,25(OH)2D and 25(OH)D acting across parathyroid, kidney, intestine and bone. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy arises mainly through three mechanisms. (1) PTHrP overproduction by solid tumours (squamous head/neck, lung, skin; breast; genitourinary; gastrointestinal) — PTHrP mimics PTH at the PTH receptor, raising bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. (2) Local osteolysis from skeletal metastases (breast, myeloma), where metastatic deposits secrete PTHrP and chemokines driving bone breakdown. (3) Excess 1,25(OH)2D production, notably by lymphomas (and granulomatous disease) via macrophage CYP27B1 converting 25(OH)D to active 1,25(OH)2D, enhancing intestinal calcium absorption. PTHrP induction is linked to PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli signalling, TGF-beta, oncogene activation (e.g. Ras) and p53 loss. In all these malignant mechanisms, the high serum calcium activates the parathyroid CaSR and appropriately suppresses endogenous PTH (p.363, 737).

Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HHM) occurs in up to ~20% of cancer patients; the typical picture is a patient with known malignancy found hypercalcaemic on routine labs, though occasionally hypercalcaemia is the presenting feature of an undiagnosed cancer (p.737).
Most malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia runs a relatively acute course, in contrast to the chronic, fluctuating high-normal pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism or occasionally myeloma (p.363).
An elevated PTHrP level confirms HHM and is raised in roughly 80% of hypercalcaemic cancer patients; PTH should be suppressed in true HHM (p.738).
Features favouring HHM over primary hyperparathyroidism: known malignancy, recent onset, and very high serum calcium levels (p.738).
PTHrP shares homology with the first ~13 amino acids of PTH and binds the PTH receptor, explaining the PTH-like biochemical effects on bone and kidney (p.363, 737).
Serum free light chains should be checked when myeloma is suspected, since ~3% of myeloma is missed by serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (p.364).

Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is one of the few clinical settings where measuring serum 1,25(OH)2D is genuinely useful — it is elevated or inappropriately normal in lymphoma- and granulomatous-mediated hypercalcaemia (p.364).
Always confirm true hypercalcaemia first by correcting for albumin (add ~0.8 mg/dL to total calcium per 1.0 g/dL fall in albumin below 4.0 g/dL) to exclude pseudohypercalcaemia (p.363).
Failing to correct calcium for albumin can produce pseudohypercalcaemia or pseudohypocalcaemia and a false diagnosis (p.363).
FHH may present with mildly elevated PTH and hypercalcaemia and be mistaken for primary hyperparathyroidism — parathyroid surgery is ineffective in FHH and must be excluded (p.363).
Mild hypercalcaemia (10.5-11.9 mg/dL) is often asymptomatic or causes only vague neuropsychiatric or constitutional symptoms, so it may be overlooked (p.363).
Ionised calcium measurement is easily distorted by collection technique (e.g. prolonged tourniquet); corrected total calcium is generally preferable (p.363).
Up to ~3% of myeloma is undetected by serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation — check free light chains (p.364).
In immobilisation-related hypercalcaemia, an unrecognised underlying driver (pHPT, Paget's, myeloma) may coexist and should be sought, especially in older patients (p.363).
Markedly elevated calcium (>14 mg/dL / >3.5 mmol/L) with progressive lethargy, stupor or coma (p.363-364, 737)
Severe GI involvement — nausea, vomiting, anorexia, peptic ulcer or pancreatitis (p.364)
Acute renal failure and volume depletion from hypercalcaemia-induced nephrogenic concentrating defect and polyuria (p.364)
Cardiac conduction abnormalities — bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc (p.364)

By total serum calcium: mild 10.5-11.9 mg/dL (often asymptomatic); moderate >=12-14 mg/dL; severe >=14 mg/dL (progressive lethargy, stupor or coma, prominent GI symptoms and acute renal failure) (Harrison 22e p.363-364).

Graves' hyperthyroidism is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs, detected as TSH-receptor antibodies/TRAb) that activate the TSH receptor. Susceptibility involves genetic (HLA-DR, CTLA-4, CD25, CD40, PTPN22, TSH-R gene) and environmental factors; concordance is 20-30% in monozygotic vs <5% in dizygotic twins. Triggers/risk factors include stress, smoking (moderate for Graves', major for ophthalmopathy), sudden iodine intake increases, the postpartum period (threefold rise), and immune reconstitution after HAART, alemtuzumab, or immune checkpoint inhibitors. Coexisting lymphocytic thyroiditis and TPO/Tg antibodies (up to 80%) mean there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels. Ophthalmopathy is driven by cytokine-mediated (IFN-gamma, TNF, IL-1) infiltration of extraocular muscles by activated T cells, fibroblast activation, glycosaminoglycan deposition trapping water, and aberrant IGF-1R signalling; the TSH-R is expressed in orbital tissue (p.3032-3033).

Thyrotoxicosis (state of thyroid hormone excess) is NOT synonymous with hyperthyroidism (excessive thyroid gland function); destructive thyroiditis and ingestion of exogenous hormone cause thyrotoxicosis without true hyperthyroidism (p.3032).

Graves' ophthalmopathy specific signs (proptosis, periorbital oedema, conjunctival injection, diplopia) occur in ~one-third of Graves' patients clinically; ~10% of ophthalmopathy is unilateral (p.3033-3034).
Graves' ophthalmopathy can occur in the absence of hyperthyroidism in ~10% (euthyroid ophthalmopathy); onset is within a year before/after thyrotoxicosis diagnosis in 75% (p.3034).
A diffuse, firm (non-nodular) goitre with a thrill or bruit at the inferolateral margins points to Graves' disease (p.3033).
Thyrotoxic hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is a recognised association, particularly common in Asian males (p.3033).

Mild hypercalcaemia occurs in up to 20% of patients (hypercalciuria more common) from thyroid-hormone-driven bone resorption; long-standing disease causes osteopenia and a small increased fracture rate (p.3033).
Graves' disease accounts for 60-80% of thyrotoxicosis; affects up to 2% of women, ~10x less common in men, typically ages 20-50 (p.3032).
In the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss ('apathetic thyrotoxicosis'), and may be mistaken for depression (p.3033).
Weight loss occurs despite increased appetite due to raised metabolic rate, but ~5% of patients GAIN weight due to increased food intake (p.3033).
Atrial fibrillation is more common in patients >50 years; treating the thyrotoxic state alone reverts AF to sinus rhythm in up to 75% of those without underlying cardiac disease (p.3033).

Symptoms in descending frequency: hyperactivity/irritability, heat intolerance/sweating, palpitations, fatigue/weakness, weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhoea, polyuria, oligomenorrhoea/loss of libido (p.3033 Table 396-2).
Signs: tachycardia (AF in elderly), fine tremor, goitre, warm moist skin, proximal myopathy, lid retraction/lag (p.3033 Table 396-2).
Fine tremor is best elicited by having the patient stretch out the fingers while feeling the fingertips with the palm (p.3033).
Lid retraction (staring appearance) results from sympathetic overactivity and occurs in ANY form of thyrotoxicosis; it is distinct from the specific eye signs of Graves' ophthalmopathy (p.3033).

Do NOT assume thyrotoxicosis means hyperthyroidism - low radionuclide uptake indicates destructive thyroiditis, iodine excess or factitia rather than gland overactivity, which changes management (p.3032, 3037).

T3 toxicosis: 2-5% have suppressed TSH with elevated T3 but normal T4, so a normal T4 does not exclude thyrotoxicosis; conversely iodine-induced T4 toxicosis can show elevated T4 with normal T3 (p.3034).
Diagnostic confusion: thyrotoxicosis can elevate bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, and cause microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia (p.3034).

Antithyroid drug agranulocytosis (<1%) is idiosyncratic and abrupt - routine prospective blood-count monitoring is NOT useful; instead warn patients to stop the drug and obtain an urgent FBC for sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers (p.3036).

Suppressed TSH may persist for several months after starting antithyroid drugs, so TSH is not a reliable early index of response - titrate on unbound T4; euthyroidism is usually not reached until 6-8 weeks (p.3035).
Thyroid acropachy/clubbing without coincident dermopathy and ophthalmopathy in a Graves' patient should prompt a search for an alternative cause of clubbing (p.3034).
A normal TSH with normal unbound T4/T3 excludes thyrotoxicosis and excludes Graves' as the cause of a diffuse goitre (p.3034).

Untreated, clinical features generally worsen; historical mortality was 10-30% before effective therapy. Mild Graves' may show spontaneous relapses and remissions, and rarely fluctuates between hypo- and hyperthyroidism with changing TRAb activity. About 15% of treated patients in remission develop hypothyroidism 10-15 years later from the destructive autoimmune process. Ophthalmopathy runs an independent course: typically worsens over 3-6 months, plateaus over 12-18 months, then partially improves (soft-tissue changes especially); fulminant in up to 5% requiring acute intervention. Thyrotoxic crisis carries 4-17% mortality even with treatment (p.3034-3036).
Optic nerve compression at the orbital apex -> papilloedema, peripheral field defects and permanent vision loss; sight-threatening ophthalmopathy is an emergency (p.3034, 3036)
Corneal exposure/ulceration when lids fail to close during severe proptosis (p.3034)
Atrial fibrillation or worsening angina/heart failure, especially in elderly or pre-existing cardiac disease - high cardiac output can precipitate high-output failure (p.3033)
Features suggesting thyroid storm: fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice (p.3036)

Subclinical hyperthyroidism = low TSH with normal free T3 and free T4; treatment is increasingly recommended in the elderly to reduce atrial fibrillation and bone-loss risk (p.3034, 3041). Graves' ophthalmopathy severity is graded by the NO SPECS mnemonic (0 no signs/symptoms; 1 only signs e.g. lid retraction/lag; 2 soft tissue involvement; 3 proptosis >22 mm; 4 extraocular muscle involvement/diplopia; 5 corneal involvement; 6 sight loss), though activity-based systems such as EUGOGO are preferred for monitoring/treatment decisions (p.3034).

Severe falciparum malaria — hypoglycemia is a common complication and its neurologic effects are indistinguishable from cerebral malaria; usual adrenergic signs (sweating, gooseflesh, tachycardia) are often absent (p.1807)
Fasting insulin level (p.721)
Proinsulin level (p.721)
C-peptide level — helps separate endogenous from exogenous insulin (p.721)
Serum/plasma sulfonylurea assay when surreptitious agent use suspected (p.721)
IGF-II level and IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (ratio >10:1 suggestive of non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia; standard IGF-II assays may miss precursors) (p.782)
Endoscopic ultrasound for localization of insulinoma (typically small, <2 cm) (p.721)
Syncope and seizure — hypoglycemia-related loss of consciousness can be mistaken for either (p.204)
Psychiatric illness — neuroglycopenic behavioral symptoms of insulinoma can be misdiagnosed as psychiatric disease (p.721)

Pseudohypoglycemia — artifactually low glucose from in vitro glucose consumption by markedly elevated leukocytes (hyperleukocytosis in leukemia, myeloproliferative disease, leukemoid reaction, or after colony-stimulating factor) (p.635-636)

Falling glucose triggers counterregulatory autonomic activation (catecholamines) producing adrenergic warning symptoms, while inadequate glucose supply to the brain produces neuroglycopenia. Endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma) drives fasting hypoglycemia with elevated insulin, proinsulin, and C-peptide. Non-islet-cell tumors can cause hypoglycemia chiefly through secretion of incompletely processed IGF-II ('big' IGF-II), which weakly activates insulin receptors and more strongly IGF-I receptors; reduced IGFBP-3 and acid-labile subunit increase IGF-II bioavailability to target tissues, and large tumors may also impair hepatic gluconeogenesis or consume glucose. In severe malaria, hypoglycemia arises from failed hepatic gluconeogenesis combined with increased host (and to a lesser extent parasite) glucose consumption, and may be worsened by quinine-induced insulin secretion (p.204, p.635-636, p.721, p.782, p.1807).

Symptoms fall into two groups: autonomic/adrenergic features (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, sweating, hunger, paresthesias) driven by counterregulatory activation, and neuroglycopenic features (fatigue, weakness, dizziness, confusion, behavioral change, cognitive impairment) from impaired neuronal function (p.204).
Hypoglycemia can cause transient loss of consciousness and may mimic syncope or seizure; hunger as a premonitory symptom and absence of immediate reorientation help distinguish it (p.204).
Insulinoma may first be misattributed to psychiatric illness, with symptoms (confusion, irrational behavior, visual difficulty, coma) recognized as neuroglycopenic only in retrospect (p.721).

Distinguish endogenous insulin excess (insulinoma) from surreptitious exogenous insulin use: C-peptide and proinsulin are elevated with insulinoma but suppressed with exogenous insulin injection (p.721).

A non-islet-cell tumor cause is suggested by hypoglycemia with suppressed insulin and C-peptide plus an elevated IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (>10:1) and inappropriately low GH and beta-hydroxybutyrate (p.635-636, p.782).
Repeated hypoglycemia produces hypoglycemia unawareness by impairing the counterregulatory response, so the absence of adrenergic warning symptoms does not exclude dangerous hypoglycemia (p.204).

In severe malaria the clinical signs of hypoglycemia (sweating, gooseflesh, tachycardia) are typically absent and its neurologic effects mimic the underlying disease, so it is easily missed without glucose measurement (p.1807).
Failing to measure C-peptide/proinsulin can miss surreptitious exogenous insulin use, which mimics insulinoma (p.721).
Circulating IGF-II may not be overtly elevated in tumor-induced hypoglycemia, so a normal IGF-II level does not exclude it; the IGF-II/IGF-I ratio is more informative (p.635-636, p.782).
A markedly raised leukocyte count can cause artifactual low glucose (pseudohypoglycemia) if the sample is not processed promptly (p.635-636).
Hypoglycemia is rapidly reversible with glucose, but in severe malaria it independently signals a poor prognosis, particularly in children and pregnant women (p.1807).
Hypoglycemia complicating severe malaria carries a poor prognosis, especially in children and pregnant women, and the usual warning signs may be absent (p.1807)
Recurrent hypoglycemia blunts counterregulation, causing hypoglycemia unawareness — loss of the warning symptoms that normally prompt correction (p.204)
Coma or seizures from neuroglycopenia indicate severe, potentially irreversible CNS compromise (p.721, p.782)
Capillary & lab glucose
Give IV dextrose
Hypoglycemia (non-infective) — Endocrine
Altered sensorium with low glucose is rapidly reversible and must be excluded first.
Red flags: Rapidly reversible — check glucose first in any altered patient
[guideline] management
Hypovolaemic: GI losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, tube drainage) and insensible loss (sweating, burns) with inadequate replacement — urine Na+ typically <20 mM (p.390).
Hyperglycaemia-related ('true') hyponatraemia — plasma Na+ falls ~1.6-2.4 mM per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose; resolves after correcting hyperglycaemia (p.393).

Hypovolaemic renal: thiazide diuretics, mineralocorticoid/aldosterone deficiency (primary adrenal insufficiency, hypoaldosteronism), salt-losing nephropathies (reflux nephropathy, interstitial nephropathies, post-obstructive uropathy, medullary cystic disease, recovery phase of ATN) — urine Na+ typically >20 mM (p.390-391).
Osmotic/solute-driven hypovolaemic: glycosuria, ketonuria (starvation, diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis), bicarbonaturia (RTA, metabolic alkalosis) (p.391).
Cerebral salt wasting (subarachnoid haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, craniotomy, encephalitis, meningitis) (p.391).
Hypervolaemic: congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and acute or chronic renal failure (the latter uniquely with raised urine Na+) (p.391).
Euvolaemic: SIAD, moderate-to-severe hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease (glucocorticoid deficiency) (p.391).
Low solute intake: beer potomania (alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer) and nutrient-restricted/extreme vegetarian diets — urine osmolality <100-200 mOsm/kg, urine Na+ <10-20 mM (p.391-392).

SIAD causes (Table 56-1): malignancy (especially small-cell lung carcinoma — 75% of malignancy-associated SIAD; ~10% present with Na+ <130 mM), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, TB, abscess, pleural effusion), CNS disease (tumour, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, head trauma, hydrocephalus), drugs, and transient causes (pain, nausea, stress, endurance exercise, general anaesthesia) (p.391-392).
Pseudohyponatraemia — hyponatraemia coexisting with normal/increased plasma tonicity, from extreme hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia (p.393).

Serum osmolality, converted to effective osmolality/tonicity by subtracting urea (in mg/dL divided by 2.8) — true hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; this also excludes pseudohyponatraemia (p.393).
Imaging — chest CT in smokers/high-risk patients (screening CXR can miss small-cell lung carcinoma); CNS imaging where a central cause is suspected (p.393).
Serum glucose — to identify and correct hyperglycaemic (translocational) hyponatraemia (p.393).
Serum uric acid — low (<4 mg/dL) in SIAD physiology, often high in volume depletion (p.393).
Serum K+, BUN/creatinine — hyperkalaemia suggests adrenal insufficiency/hypoaldosteronism; raised urea/creatinine suggests renal cause (p.393).
Thyroid, adrenal and pituitary function testing, including a cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test to assess primary adrenal insufficiency, in the appropriate setting (p.393).
Urine osmolality — <100 mOsm/kg suggests primary polydipsia; >400 mOsm/kg indicates dominant AVP excess; intermediate values suggest multifactorial physiology (p.393).
Urine Na+ — <20-30 mM suggests hypovolaemia; >30 mM suggests SIAD, but values overlap, especially in the elderly (p.393).
Urine K+ — to calculate the urine-to-plasma electrolyte ratio, useful for predicting response to fluid restriction (p.393).
Demonstration that plasma Na+ corrects after isotonic saline hydration is the diagnostic gold standard for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (p.393).
Pseudohyponatraemia from severe hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia: measured Na+ is low but plasma tonicity is normal or high; exclude by measuring serum osmolality (p.393).
Hyperglycaemic hyponatraemia: a translocational, true hyponatraemia driven by glucose-induced water efflux that corrects once glucose is lowered (p.393).

Hyponatraemia reflects a relative excess of body water to sodium, almost always from increased circulating AVP (or heightened renal AVP sensitivity) together with free-water intake. Volume status modulates AVP release: hypovolaemia raises AVP at any given osmolality, and 'hypervolaemic' arterial underfilling (heart failure, cirrhosis) triggers neurohumoral activation that likewise elevates AVP, causing water retention. In hypovolaemia, AVP-mediated V2-receptor water reabsorption plus free-water intake lowers Na+. In hypervolaemic oedematous states (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), total-body Na+ rises but water rises proportionally more; reduced arterial filling drives the AVP response. In euvolaemic hyponatraemia, SIAD is the commonest cause: free-water intake persists at osmolalities below the normal thirst threshold, with patients subclinically volume-expanded (so-called 'AVP escape' limits distal tubular transport, preserving a modestly hypervolaemic steady state). Four AVP-secretion patterns occur in SIAD: erratic unregulated secretion (~1/3 of patients), failure to suppress at low osmolality, a 'reset osmostat', and a subset with undetectable AVP (gain-of-function V2-receptor mutations causing 'nephrogenic' SIAD). At the brain level, hyponatraemia causes water to move down the osmotic gradient from hypotonic ECF into cells, producing cellular swelling and cerebral oedema within the rigid skull; acute encephalopathy results when volume-regulatory mechanisms (CSF shunting, efflux of Na+/K+/Cl-) are overwhelmed. In chronic hyponatraemia, brain cells extrude organic osmolytes (creatine, betaine, glutamate, myoinositol, taurine), a process largely complete within 48 h, which mitigates but does not abolish symptoms (p.390-392).
Hyponatraemia (plasma Na+ <135 mM) is very common, affecting up to ~22% of hospitalised patients (p.390).
The absolute plasma Na+ concentration says nothing about a patient's volume status, which must be assessed separately for both diagnosis and management (p.390).

Hyponatraemia is almost always driven by excess circulating AVP and/or increased renal sensitivity to AVP combined with free-water intake; the main exception is hyponatraemia from low solute intake (p.390).
Diagnostically subdivide by ECF volume into hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, and hypervolaemic groups based on clinical history and volume status (p.390).
In hypovolaemic patients, a urine Na+ <20 mM predicts a brisk rise in plasma Na+ with isotonic saline, because AVP falls and a water diuresis ensues (p.391).
Serum uric acid helps discriminate: SIAD is typically associated with low uric acid (<4 mg/dL), whereas hypovolaemic hyponatraemia is often hyperuricaemic (p.391, p.393).
Thiazides can mimic SIAD and do not impair urinary concentrating ability, so AVP retains full effect; defer diagnosing SIAD until 1-2 weeks after stopping the thiazide (p.391, p.393).
The 48-hour mark distinguishes acute from chronic hyponatraemia and is decisive for how aggressively/cautiously sodium may be corrected (p.392).

Cerebral salt wasting (a rare hypovolaemic cause linked to intracranial disease) responds to aggressive salt-and-water repletion, so distinguishing it from SIAD is critical because their management diverges (p.391).
Hypovolaemic patients may appear clinically euvolaemic, with only a low urine Na+ to reveal the cause (p.390).
Hyponatraemia is frequently multifactorial, especially when severe — evaluate every source of excess AVP (volume status, drugs, nausea, pain) rather than settling on one (p.393).
Failing to exclude pseudohyponatraemia/hyperglycaemia before correcting; check serum osmolality and glucose first (p.393).
The 93%-water assumption used by ion-sensitive electrodes makes plasma Na+ falsely low in extreme hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia (p.393).
Urine Na+ values overlap substantially between SIAD and hypovolaemia (particularly in the elderly); the saline-challenge response is the definitive discriminator (p.393).
Diagnosing SIAD in a patient on thiazides — defer the SIAD label until 1-2 weeks after stopping the drug (p.393).
Distinguishing cerebral salt wasting from SIAD is critical because management differs (salt repletion vs fluid restriction) (p.391).

Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia carries high risk of severe neurological injury and death; encephalopathy is more severe in premenopausal women. The degree of hyponatraemia is an important prognostic indicator in hypervolaemic states, reflecting the intensity of neurohumoral activation. Chronic hyponatraemia, even when judged 'asymptomatic', is associated with subtle gait and cognitive deficits (reversible with correction), increased risk of falls, and an increased fracture risk due to neurological dysfunction and reduced bone density — so safe correction is warranted even without overt symptoms. Osmotic demyelination from overcorrection can produce permanent disabling neurological deficits (p.392-393).
Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia is a medical emergency: nausea/headache/vomiting can rapidly progress to seizures, brainstem herniation, coma and death (p.392).

Acute hyponatraemia can cause normocapnoeic or hypercapnoeic respiratory failure, typically from non-cardiogenic 'neurogenic' pulmonary oedema with normal wedge pressure; resulting hypoxia amplifies neurological injury (p.392).
Premenopausal women are far more likely than men to develop encephalopathy and severe neurological sequelae (p.392).

Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or >18 mM in 48 h) risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), classically central pontine myelinolysis — presenting days later with para-/quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, 'locked-in' syndrome, or reduced consciousness (p.393).
ODS can occur even with appropriately slow correction in high-risk patients: alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, and liver transplantation (p.393).
Plasma Na+ <125 mM is the threshold at which chronic hyponatraemia commonly becomes overtly symptomatic (nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures) (p.392).

Iatrogenic settings for acute hyponatraemia: postoperative premenopausal women given hypotonic fluids, glycine irrigation (TURP/uterine surgery), colonoscopy prep, recent thiazide initiation (Table 56-2, p.392).
MDMA ('Ecstasy'/'Molly') causes potent thirst and AVP induction leading to severe acute hyponatraemia; exercise-associated (endurance/marathon) hyponatraemia is another acute setting (p.392).

By volume status: hypovolaemic (total body water down, total body Na+ down more), euvolaemic/no oedema (total body water up, Na+ near-normal), and hypervolaemic (total body water up markedly, Na+ up) — Fig. 56-5, p.391. By chronicity: acute hyponatraemia is <48 h (osmolyte extrusion incomplete, higher cerebral-oedema risk) and chronic is >48 h (osmolytes largely extruded, lower acute symptom risk but higher ODS risk on correction), p.392. By tonicity: true hypotonic hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg, distinct from pseudohyponatraemia (normal/high tonicity) and hyperglycaemic translocational hyponatraemia, p.393. Symptomatic threshold for chronic disease is generally plasma Na+ <125 mM (p.392). SIAD diagnostic features include euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality typically >400 mOsm/kg / not maximally dilute), urine Na+ >30 mM, low serum uric acid (<4 mg/dL), and absence of thyroid/adrenal dysfunction, diuretics, hypovolaemia or hypervolaemia (p.391, p.393).

Hodgkin lymphoma (classical) - nontender cervical/supraclavicular/axillary nodes, frequent mediastinal involvement (Harrison 22e p.869)
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma - nodal and extranodal disease; B symptoms part of staging (Harrison 22e p.860)
Acute or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (can produce generalised adenopathy and constitutional symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.476)
Richter transformation of CLL - rapidly progressive focal adenopathy with night sweats, fever, weight loss and high LDH (Harrison 22e p.897)
Metastatic carcinoma to nodes (head/neck, lung, breast, thyroid, GI primaries) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Germ-cell tumour (retroperitoneal nodes in young men) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Occult solid tumours presenting with involuntary weight loss - GI/hepatobiliary, lung, breast, genitourinary, ovarian, prostate (Harrison 22e p.317)
Infectious mononucleosis (EBV or CMV) - generalised adenopathy with constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.476)
Tuberculosis - can cause unilateral mediastinal adenopathy and mesenteric lymphadenitis mimicking lymphoma, with night sweats and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.477)
Histoplasmosis - unilateral paratracheal node involvement that can mimic lymphoma in endemic regions (Harrison 22e p.477)
Toxoplasmosis - generalised reactive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476)
HIV / AIDS - generalised lymphadenopathy and a recognised lymphoma risk factor (Harrison 22e p.476, p.903)

Excisional biopsy of the largest abnormal node is preferred; fine-needle aspiration should NOT be the first procedure as it usually yields insufficient tissue and delays diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.478)
Age/sex/risk-appropriate cancer screening (e.g. faecal occult blood, colonoscopy, mammography) and abdominal ultrasound in occult-malignancy weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.318)
Serum protein electrophoresis to detect a monoclonal paraprotein (Harrison 22e p.903)
Serum beta2-microglobulin and LDH - independent prognostic markers in NHL (Harrison 22e p.903)
CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic/liver panel, uric acid and calcium (Harrison 22e p.317, p.904)
ESR and CRP as part of the constitutional-symptom / weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869)
Contrast CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging; FDG-PET/CT preferred for aggressive lymphomas and Hodgkin lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.904)
Bone marrow biopsy where indicated; lumbar puncture if CNS-risk histology or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.903-904)
HIV and hepatitis B and C serology - risk factors for NHL and relevant to hepatitis B reactivation risk (Harrison 22e p.904)
Cervical node ultrasound long-to-short axis ratio (<2.0 favours malignancy) where head/neck cancer is suspected (Harrison 22e p.478)
Sarcoidosis - mediastinal/hilar adenopathy and constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.477)
Systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease - generalised adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476)
Drug-induced (phenytoin/diphenylhydantoin and others) lymphadenopathy, including DRESS/DIHS with eosinophilia and extensive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193, p.476)
Castleman disease, Kikuchi histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy, IgG4-related disease (Harrison 22e p.476)

B symptoms in lymphoma are cytokine-mediated systemic effects of the tumour rather than direct mass effects. In classical Hodgkin lymphoma the malignant Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells are rare within a tumour mass that is largely a polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate reacting to tumour-derived cytokines; this inflammatory milieu drives constitutional symptoms and contributes to the generalised immune suppression seen in these patients. Involuntary weight loss in malignancy reflects a combination of anorexia, sarcopenia and a cytokine-driven cachexia syndrome. (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869)

B symptoms are formally defined for lymphoma staging (the Ann Arbor 'B' suffix) as unexplained fever (>38C), drenching night sweats, and/or unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869).

Half of all cancer patients lose some weight and up to 20% of cancer deaths are attributable directly to cachexia; malignancy that declares itself through marked weight loss generally carries a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.317).
The tempo of symptoms helps separate aggressive from indolent lymphoma: rapid symptomatic progression and the presence of B symptoms suggest a more aggressive process (Harrison 22e p.903).
Among malignancies, lymphoma is by far the commonest cause of malignancy-related fever of unknown origin, and the fever can precede any palpable lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193).

About one-third of patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma present with B symptoms; Hodgkin disease can even present as a fever of unknown origin, more often in older patients with abdominal mixed-cellularity disease (Harrison 22e p.869).
Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclical fever lasting days to weeks alternating with afebrile intervals) is a rare but classic Hodgkin lymphoma presentation (Harrison 22e p.869).

Node character matters: lymphomatous nodes tend to be large, firm, rubbery, mobile, symmetric and non-tender, whereas metastatic carcinoma nodes are typically hard, non-tender and fixed to surrounding tissue (Harrison 22e p.477).

Supraclavicular and scalene node enlargement is always abnormal and warrants prompt evaluation; a left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) classically reflects a gastrointestinal primary, but lung, breast, testis and ovarian cancers also seed these nodes (Harrison 22e p.477).

Examination in suspected lymphoma should systematically cover all peripheral nodal sites plus Waldeyer ring, liver and spleen size, effusions/ascites, and testicular, breast or skin involvement, since any of these can change staging and management (Harrison 22e p.903).

Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes are usually malignant (lymphoma, or germ-cell tumour in young men), in contrast to the largely benign causes of cervical adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.477).

Do NOT give glucocorticoids for undiagnosed lymphadenopathy - their lympholytic effect can obscure lymphoma, leukaemia and Castleman disease and delay/disrupt diagnosis (the rare exception is life-threatening pharyngeal obstruction from Waldeyer-ring tissue in mononucleosis) (Harrison 22e p.521).

Fine-needle aspiration is inadequate for an initial lymphoma diagnosis - obtain an excisional/core biopsy; FNA is reserved for thyroid nodules and confirming relapse of a known cancer (Harrison 22e p.478).
Antibiotics are NOT indicated for lymphadenopathy unless there is strong evidence of bacterial infection (Harrison 22e p.521).
Localized-versus-generalized adenopathy has limited discriminatory value because many causes produce either pattern; do not over-rely on it (Harrison 22e p.476).

In primary care most lymphadenopathy is benign (>two-thirds nonspecific/URI, <1% malignant) and needs only short-interval follow-up - but persistent or enlarging nodes must be re-evaluated and biopsied (Harrison 22e p.476, p.521).
If a head-and-neck primary is suspected behind a solitary cervical node, perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first before excising the node (Harrison 22e p.478).

Lymphoma prognosis is stage- and biology-dependent. For NHL the International Prognostic Index uses five factors (age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site); for DLBCL treated with R-CHOP, 0 factors gives ~94% 4-year survival versus ~53% with 3-5 factors. Across lymphomas, decreased outcome is associated with B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH and bulky disease (e.g. lymph-node mass >7 cm). In occult solid malignancy, presentation through significant involuntary weight loss generally carries a very poor prognosis, whereas when no cause is found after thorough workup the prognosis is comparatively favourable. (Harrison 22e p.317, p.861, NHL prognosis section)
Supraclavicular or scalene adenopathy - always abnormal, biopsy promptly (Harrison 22e p.477-478)
Solitary hard non-tender cervical node in an older tobacco user - prompt biopsy after ENT mucosal assessment (Harrison 22e p.478)

chunks.text: Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of a single plasma-cell clone. Myeloma cells adhere to bone marrow stromal cells and extracellular matrix, triggering cytokine loops (IL-6, IGF-1, VEGF) and signaling (Ras/Raf/MAPK, PI3K/Akt, PKC) that drive growth, survival, drug resistance, and migration. Osteoclast-activating factors (RANK ligand, MIP-1alpha, IL-1, lymphotoxin, TNF, VEGF) increase bone resorption while DKK-1 suppresses osteoblasts, producing purely lytic bone disease, hypercalcemia, fractures, and cord compression. The immune microenvironment is remodeled (expansion of MDSCs, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, TH17; suppression of effective antimyeloma T/B/NKT responses). Recurrent cytogenetic events include hyperdiploidy (trisomies) in ~half, and 14q32 IGH translocations [t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)] in the rest, plus del13q, 1q amplification/1p deletion, and del17p; KRAS/NRAS are the most frequently mutated genes (~20% each), with TP53, DIS3, FAM46C, BRAF in 5-10%. No single unifying mutation exists; subclonal heterogeneity present at diagnosis drives genomic evolution. All myeloma is preceded by MGUS (p.883-885).

[guideline] management
Sick euthyroid syndrome confounding thyroid function tests in a critically ill or hypothermic patient (p.3769).
Adrenal insufficiency / hypopituitarism, which independently increase susceptibility to hypothermia and may coexist (p.3768).
Hashimoto's encephalopathy - a steroid-responsive syndrome with TPO antibodies, myoclonus and EEG slow-wave activity (relationship to hypothyroidism not established) (p.3030).
Sepsis should be actively suspected as a precipitant; hypothermia obscures fever and leukocytosis, and infectious rigors may be mistaken for shivering (p.3032, p.3769).
Pneumonia as a respiration-impairing precipitant (p.3032).
Arterial blood gas to detect hypoxia and hypercapnia from hypoventilation (p.3032).
Glucose to detect contributing hypoglycemia (p.3032).
Septic screen / cultures, since infection is a common precipitant and is masked by hypothermia (p.3032, p.3769).
Core temperature measurement (may be very low, down to ~23 degrees C) (p.3032).
Environmental / accidental hypothermia from cold exposure, drugs (ethanol, sedatives, antipsychotics, antidepressants), or malnutrition (p.3768).
Hypoglycemia from insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, which itself causes hypothermia via neuroglycopenic hypothalamic effects (p.3768).

Long-standing thyroid hormone deficiency depresses the metabolic rate and thermogenesis, producing hypothermia, bradycardia, and reduced myocardial contractility. Dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans traps water, giving nonpitting myxedematous swelling. In myxedema coma, hypoventilation is central to pathogenesis: it leads to hypoxia and hypercapnia (CO2 retention). Dilutional hyponatremia (reduced renal perfusion with inappropriate vasopressin) and hypoglycemia further contribute. There is impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism, and impaired peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion (p.3032; p.3768).
Myxedema coma carries a 20-40% mortality despite intensive care, and outcome does not correlate with the degree of T4 or TSH abnormality (p.3032).
It occurs almost exclusively in the elderly, often in winter, and may arise either in a known hypothyroid patient with poor treatment adherence or in someone not previously diagnosed (p.3032).
Hypothermia in myxedema can be profound, reaching as low as 23 degrees C (74 degrees F) (p.3032).
Reduced consciousness is the hallmark and may be accompanied by seizures, alongside the usual signs of hypothyroidism (p.3032).
A distinguishing examination clue in hypothyroidism is a deep tendon reflex (e.g., Achilles) whose relaxation phase is prolonged out of proportion to the contraction phase (p.3769).
Hypothyroidism, especially extreme as in myxedema coma, is a recognised endocrine cause of hypothermia by reducing metabolic rate and impairing thermogenesis and behavioural responses (p.3768).

Bradycardia, reduced myocardial contractility and stroke volume, and pericardial effusion (up to ~30% of hypothyroid patients) reflect the cardiac depression that underlies the haemodynamic picture (p.3030).
Carotene accumulation can give the skin a yellow tinge, and nonpitting (myxedematous) tissue swelling distinguishes the oedema from pitting fluid overload (p.3029-3030).
Sedatives, anesthetics, and antidepressants can precipitate or worsen myxedema coma, and impaired drug metabolism means standard doses may accumulate (p.3032).
Hypothermia masks fever and leukocytosis, so infection can be missed; rigors may be misread as shivering (p.3769).
Giving parenteral levothyroxine to a euthyroid hypothermic patient is potentially hazardous, so clinical/historical evidence of hypothyroidism should be sought first (p.3769).
Sick euthyroid syndrome can confound thyroid function tests in the acutely ill patient (p.3769).

Mortality remains 20-40% even with intensive treatment, and prognosis is independent of the measured T4 and TSH levels. Hypothermia associated with concurrent sepsis is a poor prognostic sign (p.3032, p.3769).
Reduced level of consciousness with seizures in a hypothyroid patient (p.3032).
Profound hypothermia (toward 23 degrees C) (p.3032).
Hypoventilation with hypoxia/hypercapnia signalling impending respiratory failure (p.3032).
Severe dilutional hyponatremia and hypoglycemia (p.3032).
An identifiable precipitant such as infection, MI, CHF, GI bleeding, cerebrovascular accident, or respiratory-depressant drugs (p.3032).

[guideline] management
Cholinergic (muscarinic/nicotinic) poisoning — also causes miosis plus a depressed physiologic state (p.3748)
Sedative-hypnotic / GABAergic poisoning (alcohols, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, GHB) — depressed state, distinguished as naloxone-unresponsive (p.3748)
Sympatholytic poisoning (alpha-2 agonists e.g. clonidine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, cardiac glycosides) (p.3747)

Blood/urine toxicology can confirm a suspected diagnosis but must not delay clinical management (p.3690)

Chest imaging for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, a recognized complication of opioid poisoning (p.3749)
In IV users, screen for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, HIV) and bacterial complications (meningitis, osteomyelitis, abscesses, endocarditis) (p.3733)
Hypoglycemia (responds to dextrose, mimics opioid coma) (p.3748)
Benzodiazepine intoxication (responds to flumazenil) (p.3748)

Opioids act mainly through the mu receptor (also kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin), all G protein-coupled, inhibiting the cAMP system and opening GIRK potassium channels to hyperpolarize and silence neurons. Life-threatening respiratory depression results from opioid-induced insensitivity of brainstem (medullary) respiratory neurons to rising carbon dioxide; analgesia and respiratory depression are mediated by receptors in the periaqueductal grey and medulla oblongata. Untreated, progression goes to respiratory and then cardiovascular collapse and death (p.3733, p.3690).
The classic overdose picture is shallow/slow respirations, miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; toxicology can confirm but immediate management is clinical (p.3690).

Pinpoint pupils are characteristic, BUT mydriasis (dilated pupils) appears once significant cerebral anoxia supervenes — dilated pupils do not exclude opioid toxicity in a deteriorating patient (p.3690).

Hypoxia, not the drug itself, is what kills: in opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign changes are secondary to CNS depression or consequent hypoxemia and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression) (p.3748).
Aspiration pneumonia is common in overdose because of loss of the gag reflex (p.3733).
Opioids generally do NOT cause seizures, except in polydrug use, with meperidine, with high-dose tramadol, or in the newborn (p.3690).

Fentanyl and its derivatives may require severalfold higher reversal doses than other opioids, and adulteration of illicit fentanyl with xylazine markedly worsens respiratory suppression (p.3689, p.3733).

Prompt reversal of altered mental status and vital signs within minutes of IV naloxone is virtually diagnostic of opioid poisoning (alongside dextrose for hypoglycemia and flumazenil for benzodiazepine intoxication) (p.3748).
Fluoroquinolones commonly cause false-positive opiate urine screens; rapid urine drug screens are screening-only, prone to false results, and miss agents such as kratom (p.3748).
When naloxone has only a limited effect, suspect a co-ingested sedative — most commonly a benzodiazepine, which has caused fatal overdoses in combination with buprenorphine (p.3691).
Do not assume normal-sized or dilated pupils exclude opioids — mydriasis does NOT occur until significant brain anoxia supervenes (p.3690).
Significant vital-sign abnormalities do NOT occur in opioid poisoning until there is a marked decrease in level of consciousness, so early near-normal vitals are falsely reassuring (p.3748).

A negative urine drug screen does NOT rule out opioid toxicity (concentration too low, or agent such as kratom not detected); opiate screens also give false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones) (p.3748).

Primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible because it is a partial agonist with increasing antagonist activity at higher doses; failure to respond to naloxone should prompt search for a co-ingested sedative (p.3690-3691).
Be sure a patient is not also withdrawing from alcohol or sedatives, which may be more dangerous to manage than opioid withdrawal (p.3733).

Potentially lethal but rapidly reversible if respiratory depression is recognized and supported; untreated overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Opioid use disorder is chronic and relapsing, and most patients relapse during or after detoxification (p.3690, p.3691). Some opioid intoxications can leave delayed diffuse white-matter injury producing a persistent coma syndrome (p.232).
Dilated pupils in a suspected opioid overdose suggest cerebral anoxia has already occurred (p.3690)
Re-sedation: naloxone lasts only a few hours while most opioids (especially methadone, sustained-release/'toxic time-bomb' formulations) last far longer (p.3691, p.3747)
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS (p.3749)
Methadone-associated QT prolongation and sudden death (p.3733)
Necrosis and limb-loss risk with fentanyl-xylazine injection (p.3733)

Harrison frames poisoning severity by physiologic state (Tables 470-1/470-2): opioids produce a 'depressed' physiologic state (decreased pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, neuromuscular activity, with miosis). Severity is graded by depth of CNS/physiologic depression (grades 1-4); marked vital-sign abnormalities indicate grade 3-4 depression (p.3747-3748). Note: opioid WITHDRAWAL is a separate 'stimulated' syndrome — onset 8-10 h after the last dose with lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning and sweating, progressing to gooseflesh, nausea/vomiting, myalgia, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, hypertension, mydriasis over a 7-10 day acute course (p.3690).

Carbamate insecticide poisoning (aldicarb, carbaryl, propoxur) — same cholinergic mechanism (p.3712)
Other acetylcholinesterase inhibitors: medicinal agents neostigmine, physostigmine, tacrine (p.3712)
Muscarinic agonists: bethanechol, pilocarpine, and muscarine-containing mushrooms (Boletus, Clitocybe, Inocybe spp.) (p.3712)
Nicotine / tobacco and lobeline (nicotinic agonists) (p.3712)
Opioid poisoning (also causes miosis and physiologic depression) (p.3705)
Cholinesterase activity in plasma and red cells is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning (p.3712)
ECG — may show bradycardia and atrioventricular block (p.3706)
EMG/nerve conduction studies in delayed neuropathy — early repetitive firing of CMAPs and decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation; later, axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (p.3610)
Guillain-Barré syndrome / acute flaccid paralysis — organophosphate, thallium and arsenic poisonings are listed in the GBS differential (p.3620)
Botulism and myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disorders in the acute paralysis differential) (p.3620)
Paralytic shellfish poisoning, ciguatera, type E botulism and tetrodotoxin poisoning — organophosphate poisoning is in their shared differential (ciguatera chapter)

Organophosphate (and carbamate) insecticides, and nerve agents such as sarin, soman, tabun and VX, inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of synaptic acetylcholine at both muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic receptor sites; the resulting overstimulation produces the combined muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS toxidrome. Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' in that they may require metabolic activation, so onset of toxicity can be delayed. Separately, organophosphates bind and inhibit neuropathy target esterase, with axonal degeneration of the gracile fasciculus and corticospinal tracts producing a delayed sensorimotor polyneuropathy. (p.3610, p.3712, p.3704)

Belongs to the depressed physiologic state / cholinergic toxidrome; miosis is common and is most pronounced in opioid and cholinergic poisoning, distinguished from other depressant syndromes by muscarinic and nicotinic signs (p.3705).

Muscarinic features: seizures, excessive secretions (lacrimation, salivation, bronchorrhoea and wheezing, diaphoresis), and increased bowel/bladder activity with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, and incontinence of faeces and urine (p.3712).
Nicotinic features: hypertension, tachycardia, muscle cramps, fasciculations, weakness, and paralysis — note these oppose the muscarinic picture, so vital signs can be mixed (p.3712).
Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712).
Organophosphates and carbamates can produce bradycardia and atrioventricular block on ECG (p.3706).
Organophosphate (and amanita/mushroom) poisoning can present as acute, often systemic-compromising diarrhoea (p.46/Acute Diarrhea chapter).
Organophosphates can cause a delayed organophosphate-induced neuropathy: early generalised weakness from neuromuscular blockade, then an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy ensues (p.3610).

Vital signs may be discordant: muscarinic effects cause bradycardia while nicotinic stimulation can cause hypertension and tachycardia, so a 'normal' or mixed heart rate does not exclude poisoning (p.3712).
Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' requiring metabolic activation, so a patient may be initially well or minimally symptomatic and deteriorate later (p.3704).
Cholinesterase activity is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning — a key confirmatory threshold not to overlook (p.3712).

Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712). Outcome and reversibility of any poisoning depend on the functional reserve of the individual or target organ, influenced by age and preexisting disease (p.3704).
Bronchorrhoea, wheezing and excessive secretions with progression to respiratory failure — the usual cause of death (p.3712)
Nicotinic weakness, fasciculations and paralysis (p.3712)
Seizures (p.3712)
Bradycardia / atrioventricular block (p.3706)

chunks.text: Excess production of catecholamines, usually by a benign neuroendocrine tumour of chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla (80-85%) or in extra-adrenal paraganglion tissue (paraganglioma). The catecholamine surge drives paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating and cardiac arrhythmias, and produces a hyperdynamic catecholaminergic state. Chronic/episodic catecholamine exposure can cause microvascular myocardial ischaemia (microinfarcts similar to those seen with stimulant toxicity) and a catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy; the same mechanism of sudden catecholamine release underlies stress (takotsubo / apical ballooning) cardiomyopathy (hypertension, cardiomyopathy and cardiac-tumour chapters).

chunks.text: PMR sits on the same disease spectrum as giant cell arteritis, an antigen-driven panarteritis of medium- and large-sized vessels with mononuclear infiltrates and frequent giant cell formation. Activated CD4+ T lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells are central; restricted clonal T-cell receptor expansion suggests an antigen residing in the arterial wall. Two CD4 T-cell lineages (IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17) participate in vascular inflammation, with IL-6 signaling driving hepatic acute-phase protein (CRP, and effects on ESR) production. Familial aggregation and HLA-DR4 / HLA-DRB1*04 associations have been reported for the GCA end of the spectrum (p.2945).

Primary Sjogren's syndrome - polyarthralgia and mild synovitis can mimic RA, and ~50% are RF-positive; distinguished by predominant sicca symptoms, ANA positivity and anti-Ro/SSA in about two-thirds (Harrison 22e p.2847).

Spondyloarthropathies (psoriatic arthritis, enteropathy-associated arthritis) - distinguished by sacroiliitis, enthesopathy, and presence of psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease (Harrison 22e p.2847).

Polymyalgia rheumatica in elderly patients - can resemble seronegative RA; PMR centres on neck/shoulder and hip girdle, whereas RA predominantly affects wrists/hands and ankles/feet, especially at onset (Harrison 22e p.2847).

Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema (RS3PE) - features prominent distal-limb pitting edema (unusual in RA) and responds promptly to low-dose prednisone (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Paraneoplastic syndromes - may be confused with early RA (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Virus-related polyarthritis syndromes - can mimic RA and cause transient RF production, but usually resolve within 2-3 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Hepatitis C-related arthropathy - often involves small joints of the hands and is RF-positive in about half of cases, but generally anti-CCP negative (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Subacute bacterial endocarditis and chronic hepatitis B/C - chronic infections that can produce a positive RF and confound interpretation (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Anti-CCP (ACPA) antibodies - high specificity (~95%) for RA; useful diagnostically and prognostically (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Synovial fluid aspiration with cell count and crystal/microbiology analysis - confirms inflammatory arthritis and excludes infection or crystal disease (Harrison 22e p.2847).
MRI - greatest sensitivity for synovitis, effusions and early bone/bone-marrow changes; bone marrow edema predicts subsequent erosions (Harrison 22e p.2848).
Musculoskeletal ultrasound with power Doppler - detects synovitis, increased joint vascularity and erosions, often more than plain films; portable and radiation-free (Harrison 22e p.2848).
ANA and ANCA - may be positive in RA (~30% ANA, occasional p-ANCA), but anti-MPO/anti-PR3 should be negative (Harrison 22e p.2847).
High-resolution chest CT - to detect and characterise interstitial lung disease (UIP vs NSIP patterns) when respiratory symptoms arise (Harrison 22e p.2840).
Chronic tophaceous gout - can mimic severe RA, and tophi may be mistaken for rheumatoid nodules (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Pseudogout (CPPD crystal arthritis) - inflammatory arthritis excluded via synovial fluid crystal analysis (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Osteoarthritis - non-inflammatory; DIP involvement and synovial fluid under 2,000 WBC/uL favour OA over RA (Harrison 22e p.2839, p.2847).

RA is a chronic, systemic, symmetric erosive polyarthritis driven by an interaction of genetic predisposition (e.g., the HLA shared epitope) and environmental triggers such as cigarette smoking. Antigen-presenting cells activate synovial CD4+ T cells (via TCR-MHC class II and CD28-CD80/86 co-stimulation), which differentiate into TH1 and TH17 subsets. These activate B cells that mature into plasma cells producing autoantibodies (RF and anti-CCP/ACPA); immune complexes form within the joint and activate complement, amplifying inflammation. T effector cells stimulate synovial macrophages and fibroblasts to release pro-inflammatory cytokines, with TNF-alpha playing a central role by upregulating endothelial adhesion molecules and driving IL-1, IL-6 and GM-CSF production. TNF-alpha also disrupts the bone balance: it raises DKK-1 (inhibiting Wnt-driven osteoblastic bone formation) and promotes osteoclastogenesis through M-CSF and RANKL signalling, with osteoprotegerin acting as a decoy that limits bone loss. The net result is pannus formation, cartilage and bone erosion, and generalised inflammatory bone loss (Harrison 22e p.2845).

Early-morning joint stiffness lasting more than 1 hour that improves with activity is characteristic; the earliest joints involved are typically the small joints of the hands and feet (Harrison 22e p.2839).
Wrists, MCP and PIP joints are most often affected; isolated DIP involvement usually reflects coexistent osteoarthritis rather than RA itself (Harrison 22e p.2839).

Flexor tendon tenosynovitis is a frequent hallmark, producing reduced range of motion, weakened grip and trigger fingers, and can lead to tendon rupture (most commonly flexor pollicis longus) (Harrison 22e p.2839-2840).
Anti-CCP (ACPA) and RF are useful both diagnostically and as prognostic biomarkers; anti-CCP carries the most value for predicting worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2839, p.2847).

Anti-CCP has sensitivity similar to RF but much higher specificity (approaching 95%), so a positive anti-CCP in early inflammatory arthritis helps distinguish RA from other arthritides; testing both RF and anti-CCP adds incremental yield because some patients are positive for only one (Harrison 22e p.2847).
About three-quarters of RA patients are seropositive (RF and/or ACPA) and one-quarter are seronegative; seronegative RA is a clinical diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2847).
A fever above 38.3C (101F) at any point in the course should raise suspicion of systemic vasculitis or superimposed infection rather than being attributed to RA activity alone (Harrison 22e p.2840).

Approximately 30% of RA patients are ANA-positive and some have p-ANCA, but anti-MPO and anti-PR3 are not expected and their presence points to an ANCA-associated vasculitis instead (Harrison 22e p.2847).

Synovial fluid in RA is inflammatory (typically 5,000-50,000 WBC/uL, neutrophil-predominant) versus under 2,000 WBC/uL in osteoarthritis; aspiration is most useful to confirm inflammation and to exclude infection or crystal arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2847).

The 2010 ACR-EULAR criteria are classification (not diagnostic) criteria intended to identify early patients likely to progress; a positive RF or anti-CCP alone does not establish the diagnosis without supporting clinical features (Harrison 22e p.2847).

A negative RF does not exclude RA - IgM RF is found in only ~75% of patients, and RF also occurs in other connective tissue diseases, chronic infections and 1-5% of healthy people (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Accelerated growth of subcutaneous nodules can occur in up to 10% of patients on long-term methotrexate and should not automatically be read as worsening disease (Harrison 22e p.2840).
Rheumatoid nodules and chronic tophaceous gout tophi can be confused with one another (Harrison 22e p.2840, p.2847).
Periarticular osteopenia, the classic earliest x-ray finding, is difficult to appreciate on plain (especially digitised) films, so early radiographs may appear normal (Harrison 22e p.2848).

Most patients show persistent, waxing-and-waning progressive disease; about 10% (particularly seronegative) remit spontaneously within 6 months, while a minority follow either a relapsing explosive course or an aggressively erosive course (now less common with modern therapy). Early disability is driven mainly by joint inflammation (potentially reversible) and later by cumulative irreversible joint damage. Overall mortality is roughly twice that of the general population, with excess deaths from respiratory illness, cardiovascular disease and infection; median life expectancy is shortened by about 7 years in men and 3 years in women. Worse survival is associated with systemic extraarticular involvement, low functional capacity, low socioeconomic status, low education and chronic prednisone use. Cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death (Harrison 22e p.2848). Seropositivity for RF and especially anti-CCP predicts worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Fever above 38.3C (101F) during the course should prompt evaluation for systemic vasculitis or infection rather than being ascribed to RA activity (Harrison 22e p.2840).

RA patients have the highest incidence of septic (most often S. aureus) arthritis due to chronically inflamed joints, glucocorticoid therapy and breakdown of nodules/vasculitic ulcers; TNF inhibitors add risk of mycobacterial and other infections (Harrison 22e Chap. 124, p.~).
Atlantoaxial (C1-C2) subluxation can cause compressive myelopathy; neurologic signs may evolve slowly with progressive instability (now seen in under 10% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.2840).
New-onset numbness, tingling or focal weakness (mononeuritis multiplex) suggests systemic rheumatoid vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2841).
Two- to fourfold increased risk of lymphoma (most often diffuse large B-cell), greatest with high disease activity or Felty's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2841).

Diagnosis is supported by the 2010 ACR-EULAR classification criteria (for patients with at least one joint of definite clinical synovitis not better explained by another disease), scored 0-10 across four domains - joint involvement (0-5), serology (RF/ACPA, 0-3), acute-phase reactants (CRP/ESR, 0-1), and symptom duration (0-1); a score of 6 or more fulfils requirements for definite RA. Disease activity (the main driver of treatment decisions) is tracked with composite indices: ACR 20/50/70 improvement criteria (mainly for trials) and continuous measures including DAS, SDAI, CDAI and RAPID3 used in practice. Functional disability is measured with the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) (Harrison 22e p.2847-2848).

Salicylate increases sensitivity of the CNS respiratory center and directly stimulates the medullary chemoreceptor, driving hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. It also uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, inhibits Krebs cycle enzymes, and stimulates carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, generating unmeasured endogenous anions (and increased lactate) that produce a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (p.376, p.3714).

Classic course: early nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis and alkaline urine, evolving to a mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; late stages show acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression (p.3714).
Salicylates are the most common cause of drug-induced respiratory alkalosis, acting by direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory chemoreceptor (p.376).
Only part of the elevated anion gap is attributable to salicylate itself; concurrent lactic acid production and other endogenous unmeasured anions also contribute (p.370, p.3714).
Cerebral and pulmonary edema can develop in severe poisoning; non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS) is a recognized complication (p.3705, p.3714).
Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, and seizures can occur in salicylate toxicity (p.3714).
Ketosis can accompany salicylate poisoning and may mimic other causes of ketoacidosis (p.3705).
Salicylate is detected on quantitative serum assay; serum levels guide management and are usually available within an hour (p.3706).

Enteric-coated and sustained-release salicylate preparations cause delayed/slow absorption and can form gastric concretions (bezoars), acting as a 'toxic time-bomb' with continued rising levels (p.3705, p.3752).
Vigorous gastric lavage, if used, should be with isotonic saline, NOT NaHCO3 (p.370).
Only a portion of the anion gap is due to salicylate itself; do not assume the whole gap reflects drug level (p.370).
Acid (acidic) diuresis is never indicated and is potentially harmful (p.3752).
Acetazolamide can cause systemic metabolic acidosis if excreted bicarbonate is not replaced, which markedly reduces salicylate clearance (p.370).
Delayed/slow absorption from enteric-coated, sustained-release, or concretion-forming salicylate means a single early level can underestimate toxicity; repeat levels (p.3705, p.3752).

Stages by clinical/acid-base course: (1) early respiratory alkalosis with alkalemia, alkaluria, nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation; (2) mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; (3) late acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression, cerebral and pulmonary edema in severe cases. Severe-toxicity markers include coma, cerebral edema, seizures, pulmonary edema, renal failure, progressive acid-base disturbance, and salicylate level >7 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) after acute overdose (p.3714).

chunks.text: A delayed, T-cell-mediated (type IVa, cytotoxic) severe cutaneous adverse reaction. A drug or metabolite-altered antigen is presented in association with a risk HLA class I allele by keratinocytes or other antigen-presenting cells; a restricted T-cell receptor on skin-enriched CD8+ T cells recognizes this drug-HLA complex, triggering activation and release of cytolytic mediators (notably granulysin) that cause full-thickness epidermal keratinocyte death and detachment. Proposed antigen-presentation models include hapten/prohapten covalent binding, the pharmacologic-interaction (p-i) noncovalent model, and the altered-peptide-repertoire model (as proven for abacavir-HLA-B*57:01). Carbamazepine SJS/TEN shows a highly restricted V-alpha/V-beta TCR repertoire shared among HLA-B*15:02 patients. A risk HLA allele alone is insufficient; non-MHC factors such as drug metabolism (e.g., CYP2C9*3 slow metabolism with phenytoin) contribute. (Harrison 22e p.417-420)

Painful rash with mucosal erosions and skin detachment after a new drug suggests SJS/TEN, not cellulitis.
Red flags: Skin detachment — manage like a burn; high mortality
[guideline] management
Rosacea (malar rash mimic — but rosacea involves the nasolabial folds, whereas lupus malar rash spares them) (p.2829)
Rheumatoid arthritis, or RA-SLE overlap ('rhupus') (p.2829)
Drug-induced lupus (antihistone antibodies; ~6-12% of lupus cases; rarely renal/CNS; resolves on stopping the drug) (p.2827, 2835)
Other systemic autoimmune diseases sharing ANA subtypes: myositis/dermatomyositis, Sjögren's syndrome, systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue/overlap syndromes (anti-RNP) (p.2832)
Migraine or tension headache (lupus headache can be difficult to distinguish) (p.2829)
Glucocorticoid-induced psychosis (must be excluded before attributing psychosis to neuropsychiatric lupus) (p.2829)
Acute lupus pneumonitis — pulmonary infiltrates can be radiographically indistinguishable from pneumonia (p.2829)
Infectious encephalitis — should be ruled out before attributing acute psychosis/confusional state to CNS lupus (p.2829)
Infection as a cause of cytopenias — SLE cytopenias are multifactorial (disease activity, medication, or infection) (p.2830)
Epstein-Barr virus and other viral infections — may both trigger and mimic flare via interferon induction (p.2828)
ANA by immunofluorescence is the best screening test (positive in ~95%; titer ≥1:80 favors SLE); repeated negatives make SLE unlikely but ~5% are ANA-negative (p.2831-2832)
Quarterly screening of CBC and renal indices in asymptomatic patients, since hematologic and renal flares can be silent (p.2832)
Anti-dsDNA (highly specific, ~40-70% prevalence) and anti-Sm (most specific, ~30%) — the only ANA subtypes in the EULAR/ACR criteria (p.2832)
Anti-Ro/SSA — useful when ANA-negative but clinically suspicious; linked to neonatal lupus, congenital heart block, sicca, photosensitivity, SCLE (p.2831-2832)
Antihistone antibodies — suggest drug-induced lupus (positive in ~75% of DIL) (p.2832, 2835)
Antiphospholipid panel: anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-1 (IgG/IgM/IgA) plus lupus anticoagulant by dilute Russell viper venom time (~50% prevalence) (p.2831-2832)
Random urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCr) or 24-h urine protein with eGFR and serum creatinine; renal biopsy when UPCr >0.5 and/or declining function (p.2830, 2832)
Renal biopsy with ISN/RPS lupus nephritis classification (the only single finding that alone meets EULAR/ACR criteria — class III or IV) (p.2827, 2830)
CK and aldolase with muscle biopsy if inflammatory myopathy suspected (p.2829)
Emerging urinary biomarkers of renal inflammation/fibrosis: urinary IL-16, CD163, type 1 IFN, TGF-beta (p.2832)
Atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome / TTP-like microvascular thrombotic crisis (hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, microvascular thrombosis, schistocytes, low ADAMTS13, high LDH) (p.2831)
Antiphospholipid syndrome thrombotic events presenting as stroke, DVT/PE, Budd-Chiari, or Libman-Sacks embolism (p.2829-2831)
Glucocorticoid-induced complications mimicking active disease (steroid myopathy, hyperglycemia, psychosis, avascular necrosis) (p.2829, 2833)
Macrophage activation syndrome / hemophagocytic syndrome (acute hemophagocytic syndrome listed among severe SLE manifestations) (p.2833, and HLH associated with SLE p. table 67824 region)

SLE arises from overactive innate and adaptive immunity with autoantibodies directed at nuclear components (nucleic acids, nucleosomes, RNA-binding proteins). Impaired clearance of cellular debris — driven by high neutrophil turnover/NETosis and defective complement-mediated phagocytosis — overwhelms macrophages and dendritic cells. Accumulated nucleic acids engage toll-like receptors and nucleic-acid sensors in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, driving type 1 interferon production that primes the immune response. Autoreactive B cells (including expanded age-associated B cells) lose tolerance and, with help from T follicular/T peripheral helper cells, mature into autoantibody-secreting plasma cells, while regulatory T-cell function is defective. Resulting immune complexes deposit in tissues and cause inflammation, repair, and eventual fibrosis after recurrent flares. Strong genetic component (monozygotic twin concordance 24% vs 2% dizygotic; >150 GWAS loci, with the MHC the strongest and nearly half of loci linked to type 1 interferon; monogenic complement-pathway deficiencies — C1q, C1r/s, C2, C4 — cause severe SLE). Environmental triggers include UV light, smoking, crystalline silica, mercury/toxins, sex hormones, EBV, and gut microbiome/permeability changes (p.2827-2829).

Roughly 90% of SLE patients are women, most of childbearing age; prevalence is highest among Black women, then Hispanic, White, and Asian/Pacific Islander women; disease tends to be more severe in non-White patients (p.2827).

Antiphospholipid antibodies/APS coexist in about a third of SLE patients and markedly raise risk of arterial/venous thrombosis, stroke (reported in up to 19%), Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and pregnancy loss (p.2829, 2830, 2831).
Autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical diagnosis, so a positive serology in a symptomatic patient supports attributing nonspecific complaints to SLE (p.2827, 2829).
Most patients have active disease despite therapy or recurrent flares; treatment goals are low disease activity (SLEDAI 0-4) or remission on ≤5 mg/day prednisone equivalent (p.2829, 2832).

A proposed clinical split distinguishes type 1 lupus (classic inflammatory/organ manifestations such as nephritis, arthritis, vasculitis that respond to immunosuppression) from type 2 lupus (fatigue, diffuse pain, brain fog, depression, sleep disturbance that respond poorly to immunosuppression) (p.2827).

Anti-dsDNA titers and C3/C4 levels track disease activity: anti-dsDNA is produced by short-lived plasmablasts that turn over quickly, and complement falls during high activity as it is consumed by immune complexes (p.2832).
Rising anti-dsDNA and falling C3/C4 can serve as warning signs of impending active nephritis even in an asymptomatic patient (p.2830).
Lupus arthritis is typically non-erosive (Jaccoud-like reversible deformity from ligamentous laxity); overlap with rheumatoid arthritis is termed 'rhupus' (p.2829).
Pain out of proportion in a single hip, shoulder, or knee — especially with prior corticosteroid use — should raise concern for avascular necrosis of bone (p.2829).

Accelerated atherosclerosis is a major cause of premature death, notably myocardial infarction and stroke in young patients without traditional risk factors, and is the leading cause of death after ~5 years of disease (p.2829, 2836).

Distinguishing flare from infection is a central challenge: cytopenias and constitutional symptoms can stem from disease activity, medication, OR infection, and acute lupus pneumonitis can look identical to pneumonia on imaging — infection must be excluded before escalating immunosuppression (p.2829-2830).

Classification criteria (2019 EULAR/ACR; 2012 SLICC) were built for trial enrollment, not diagnosis — diagnosis remains an individualized clinical judgment; relying on criteria alone can mislead, and ANA-negative or incomplete-lupus patients are excluded by EULAR/ACR (p.2827).

A positive ANA or even antihistone antibody alone does not confirm SLE — many drugs induce a positive ANA in patients who never develop symptoms, and antihistone antibodies occur in most SLE cases too (p.2835).

Drug-induced lupus can be hard to separate from SLE because skin biopsy and many labs overlap; presence of additional SLE-specific autoantibodies (rarely seen in DIL) and symptom resolution after stopping the drug help distinguish (p.2835).
Acute psychosis/confusion may be glucocorticoid-induced rather than neuropsychiatric lupus — and infectious encephalitis must also be ruled out (p.2829).
Single-joint pain out of proportion may be avascular necrosis (steroid-related), not arthritis flare (p.2829).
Estrogen-containing contraceptives/HRT should be avoided in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies or moderate-severe/active lupus due to thromboembolism risk (p.2836).

Prognosis and survival vary widely by geography, race/ethnicity, and access to care/medications. Renal disease, especially class IV nephritis, carries substantial risk of ESRD and death (~20% within 10 years), and is more severe in non-White patients. Accelerated atherosclerosis is a major cause of premature death and the leading cause after ~5 years of disease, driven by both traditional risk factors and lupus-specific factors (antiphospholipid antibodies, high disease activity, low C3, high glucocorticoid dose, high homocysteine/leptin). Glucocorticoid exposure independently accrues irreversible organ damage (cataracts, osteoporotic fractures, avascular necrosis, diabetes) even at doses as low as 5 mg prednisone equivalent. Class V (membranous) nephritis has a better prognosis than class III/IV. Sustained low disease activity (LLDAS) for 2+ years is associated with significantly less damage. Recent meta-analyses suggest an increased overall cancer risk and cancer-related mortality (p.2830, 2835-2836).
Rapidly declining eGFR, rising proteinuria, or active urinary sediment — class III/IV proliferative lupus nephritis; ~20% of class IV patients die or reach ESRD within 10 years (p.2830)
Crescentic / rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (cellular crescents or fibrinoid necrosis) — poor prognostic features (p.2834)
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage with capillaritis (p.2829)
Mesenteric vasculitis — risk of intestinal perforation, bleeding, and ischemia (p.2830)
Neuropsychiatric flare: seizures, acute psychosis/confusion, transverse myelitis (p.2829)
Atypical HUS/TTP-like crisis: hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, low ADAMTS13, microvascular thrombosis (p.2831)
Severe thrombocytopenia (<20-50 x10^9/L) with bleeding risk; severe hemolytic anemia (p.2830, 2833)
Stroke or arterial/venous thrombosis suggesting APS (p.2829-2830)
Pulmonary arterial hypertension, prior arterial thrombosis, or severe end-organ damage — highest maternal mortality; pregnancy should strongly be reconsidered (p.2836)

Disease activity is graded for treatment using SLEDAI/SLEDAI-2K (low disease activity = SLEDAI 0-4; remission/DORIS = SLEDAI 0). EULAR severity tiers: mild (constitutional symptoms, mild arthritis, rash <=9% BSA, platelets 50-100, SLEDAI <=6); moderate (RA-like arthritis, rash 9-18% BSA, platelets 20-50, serositis, SLEDAI 7-12); severe (major organ-threatening disease e.g. cerebritis, myelitis, pneumonitis, mesenteric vasculitis; platelets <20; TTP-like or acute hemophagocytic syndrome; rash >18% BSA; SLEDAI >12). Lupus nephritis is graded by ISN/RPS renal biopsy classes I-V (class I mesangial deposits; II mesangial proliferative; III focal proliferative; IV diffuse proliferative; V membranous; III/IV +/- V combinations), with class III/IV (and III/IV+V) being proliferative forms warranting aggressive therapy (p.2827, 2830-2831, 2833-2834).

chunks.text: SVC syndrome results from obstruction of the superior vena cava causing a severe reduction in venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Obstruction may be due to external compression, direct tumour invasion, intraluminal thrombosis (often device-related), or fibrosis. Venous congestion produces facial/upper-body swelling, distended neck veins, and development of collateral venous channels over the chest wall. The 'hot quadrate' focal hepatic hotspot on CT reflects portosystemic shunting between the SVC and portal vein. Chronic SVCS can produce 'downhill' oesophageal varices (cephalad-to-caudad flow, opposite to portal-hypertension 'uphill' varices), which may bleed late.
