chunks.text: A panarteritis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically branches of the carotid (especially the temporal artery) but systemically involving the aorta and its branches. Histology shows mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within the vessel wall with frequent giant cell formation, intimal proliferation, and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina; organ damage results from ischemia of involved vessels. It is considered an antigen-driven process: CD4+ T cells enter via the adventitial vasa vasorum, become activated, and drive macrophage differentiation, with restricted clonal T-cell expansion suggesting an arterial-wall antigen. Lesional T cells produce mainly IL-2 and IFN-gamma; both IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17 lineages contribute and may differ in glucocorticoid responsiveness. Associated with HLA-DR4 and HLA-DRB1*04 variants. (Harrison 22e p.2902)

chunks.text: Acute mortality directly from GCA is uncommon; when fatal it is usually due to cerebrovascular events or myocardial infarction. Other causes of thyrotoxicosis besides Graves' disease must be considered (e.g. toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goitre, destructive thyroiditis, ectopic thyroid tissue, factitious thyrotoxicosis); radionuclide scan/uptake or color-flow Doppler ultrasonography helps distinguish hyperthyroidism from destructive thyroiditis (Harrison 22e p.3078).
Suppressed TSH with elevated total and unbound (free) T4 and T3 (Harrison 22e p.3078).

T3 toxicosis (only T3 raised) in 2-5% of patients, more in areas of borderline iodine intake; T4 toxicosis (raised T4, normal T3) is occasionally seen when hyperthyroidism is iodine-induced (Harrison 22e p.3078).
TRAb (TSH receptor antibody) measurement to support a diagnosis of Graves' disease (Harrison 22e p.3078).
Watch for confounding biochemistry: elevated bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, plus microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, may accompany thyrotoxicosis (Harrison 22e p.3078).

Thyroid storm represents a severe, decompensated form of thyroid hormone excess (thyrotoxicosis), typically arising when an acute stressor is superimposed on partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism. Excess circulating thyroid hormone drives a hypermetabolic, hyperadrenergic state; high cardiac output produces a bounding pulse, widened pulse pressure and may precipitate or worsen heart failure or angina, particularly in the elderly or those with pre-existing heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3077, p.3080).
Thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm) is a rare, life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Characteristic features include fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea and jaundice (Harrison 22e p.3080).

Often precipitated by an acute intercurrent illness (e.g. stroke, infection, trauma, diabetic ketoacidosis), by surgery (especially thyroid surgery), or by radioiodine treatment given to a patient whose hyperthyroidism is only partially treated or untreated (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Apathetic thyrotoxicosis: in the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss, and can be mistaken for depression (Harrison 22e p.3076).
Thyrotoxicosis may be complicated by a form of hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, particularly common in Asian males (Harrison 22e p.3076).
Treatment of the thyrotoxic state alone restores sinus rhythm in up to 75% of patients with thyrotoxicosis-associated atrial fibrillation who have no underlying cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.3077).
Radioiodine therapy in a patient with partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism can itself precipitate thyrotoxic crisis (Harrison 22e p.3080).
In the elderly, thyrotoxicosis may be masked (apathetic thyrotoxicosis), delaying recognition (Harrison 22e p.3076).
Mortality remains high (4-17%) even with treatment, usually from cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Fever, delirium, seizures or coma in a thyrotoxic patient indicate thyroid storm (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Death is most often due to cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080).

chunks.text: TTP arises from deficient or antibody-inhibited ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease that cleaves von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWF is secreted by endothelium as ultra-large multimers; when these are not cleaved they persist and drive pathological platelet adhesion and aggregation, producing microvascular thrombi. ADAMTS13 deficiency alone is not sufficient — congenitally ADAMTS13-deficient individuals develop TTP only episodically, implying a second trigger. In HUS the dominant lesion is endothelial injury with deposition of fibrin in capillary/arteriolar walls, predominantly in the kidney; typical (diarrhoea-associated) HUS is driven by Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7, while atypical HUS results from dysregulated activation of the complement alternative pathway with consequent endothelial damage. The shared downstream picture is microvascular platelet/fibrin thrombi causing red-cell fragmentation (MAHA), consumption thrombocytopenia and end-organ ischaemia (Harrison 22e pp.967-968, 800-801).

chunks.text: Plasma exchange transformed TTP outcomes, reducing mortality from roughly 85-100% to about 10-30%. Relapse is common: 25-45% of plasma-exchange-treated patients relapse within 30 days of apparent remission and 12-40% relapse late, with relapse more frequent in those with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency at presentation. In diarrhoea-associated HUS roughly 40% of children need some dialysis but overall mortality is <5%; non-diarrhoeal HUS carries higher mortality (~26%). Untreated atypical HUS had acute-phase mortality up to ~15% with up to 50% progressing to end-stage renal disease, though spontaneous remission occurs and relapse is likely with re-exposure to a trigger. Cancer-/chemotherapy-associated HUS has a high case-fatality rate, with most patients dying within months (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801, 638).

Red flags: Haematological emergency — urgent plasma exchange

Urgent upper GI endoscopy
Crossmatch, coagulation
Vasoactive (terlipressin) + antibiotic prophylaxis
Variceal bleeding (non-infective) — Hepatology / GI
Haematemesis/melaena in a patient with chronic liver disease suggests variceal bleeding.
Red flags: Major haemorrhage — resuscitate; antibiotics reduce mortality in cirrhotic GI bleed
[guideline] management
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) - upper + lower respiratory tract granulomatous vasculitis plus pauci-immune glomerulonephritis; PR3/cANCA in >90% of active disease (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940)
Lymphomatoid granulomatosis - EBV-positive angiocentric B-cell proliferation with lung/skin/CNS/kidney involvement that mimics GPA but is not a true vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2941)

Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) - pauci-immune small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis with frequent glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis but no granulomas; MPO/pANCA in ~75% (Harrison 22e p.2942)
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis / Churg-Strauss (EGPA) - asthma, eosinophilia, extravascular granuloma, vasculitis; ANCA (anti-MPO) in ~48% (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944)

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) - necrotizing vasculitis of small/medium muscular arteries with microaneurysms, sparing lungs and glomeruli; associated with hepatitis B (and C); consider DADA2 in early-onset disease (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945)
Giant cell (temporal) arteritis with polymyalgia rheumatica - medium/large-vessel arteritis in patients over 50 (Harrison 22e p.2945-2946)
Takayasu arteritis - large-vessel arteritis of the aorta and its branches in young women (Harrison 22e p.2946-2947)
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein) - small-vessel immune-complex vasculitis with palpable purpura, arthralgia, GI symptoms, glomerulonephritis; IgA/C3 on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2947-2948)
Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis - strongly associated with hepatitis C virus infection (Harrison 22e p.2936)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture's syndrome) - other cause of pulmonary-renal syndrome to distinguish from ANCA-associated vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2941)
Bacterial (infective) endocarditis - can produce a false-positive pANCA and a vasculitis-like multisystem picture (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and rhinoscleroma - midline destructive infections that mimic GPA upper-airway disease (Harrison 22e p.2941)
Disseminated gonococcal infection (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Pulmonary histoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Coccidioidomycosis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Syphilis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Lyme disease (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Whipple's disease (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Bacterial airway infection in cystic fibrosis - associated with a non-anti-MPO pANCA pattern (Harrison 22e p.2937)
ANCA with antigen specificity - anti-proteinase-3 (cANCA) and anti-myeloperoxidase (pANCA) testing, interpreting in light of pretest probability (Harrison 22e p.2937, p.2941)
Hepatitis B and C serology in all suspected PAN (and in cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis) (Harrison 22e p.2945)
Echocardiography in all newly diagnosed EGPA because cardiac involvement drives mortality (Harrison 22e p.2944)
Serum complement and IgA levels in IgA vasculitis (complement normal; IgA elevated in about half) (Harrison 22e p.2948)

Tissue biopsy of a clinically involved organ for definitive diagnosis; in GPA, lung biopsy has the highest yield (necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis), upper-airway biopsy often shows only inflammation, renal biopsy shows pauci-immune GN (Harrison 22e p.2941)
Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence in IgA vasculitis (leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA and C3 deposition) (Harrison 22e p.2948)
Catheter-directed dye arteriography for PAN (microaneurysms of renal/hepatic/visceral arteries) - MR/CT angiography lack adequate resolution (Harrison 22e p.2945)
Temporal artery biopsy (3-5 cm segment, serial sections, because involvement is patchy/segmental); may remain positive up to ~14 days after starting glucocorticoids (Harrison 22e p.2946)
Temporal +/- axillary artery ultrasonography for the noncompressible 'halo' sign in GCA (Harrison 22e p.2946)
MR/CT angiography (and investigational PET) to assess large-vessel disease in GCA and to image the whole aorta and branches in Takayasu arteritis (Harrison 22e p.2946, p.2947)
Acute-phase reactants - ESR and/or CRP (note IL-6 inhibitors suppress CRP/ESR, removing them as activity markers in treated GCA) (Harrison 22e p.2946)
Complete blood count - anaemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis as inflammatory markers; striking eosinophilia in EGPA (Harrison 22e p.2940, p.2943)
Atheroembolic (cholesterol embolisation) disease - listed as a mimic of vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Migraine (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Fibromuscular dysplasia (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Heritable disorders of connective tissue (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Segmental arterial mediolysis (SAM) (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2937)
IgG4-related disease - cause of aortitis/periaortitis distinguished histologically from Takayasu (IgG4+ plasma cells, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis) (Harrison 22e p.2947)
Antiphospholipid syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Atrial myxoma (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Lymphoma / carcinomatosis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type) - EBV-associated cause of midline destructive disease mimicking GPA; never irradiate true GPA airway lesions (Harrison 22e p.2941)

Drug toxicity - cocaine (cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions can show anti-human-neutrophil-elastase ANCA), levamisole (cocaine adulterant; causes cutaneous infarction, granulocytopenia, vasculitis-mimicking serology), amphetamines, ergot alkaloids, methysergide, arsenic (Harrison 22e p.2937, p.2941)
Sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's) (Harrison 22e p.2937)

Vasculitis is inflammation of and damage to blood vessel walls, usually compromising the lumen and causing ischaemia of supplied tissues; any size, type, or location of vessel may be affected, and disease may be primary/single-organ or secondary to another illness. Most syndromes are at least partly immune-mediated through three broad mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.2936): (1) Immune-complex formation/deposition (e.g., IgA vasculitis, lupus vasculitis, serum sickness, hepatitis-B-associated vasculitis, hepatitis-C cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis) - resembling serum sickness, complexes deposit in vessel walls, activate complement (notably C5a, chemotactic for neutrophils), and neutrophils infiltrate and release enzymes that damage the wall. (2) ANCA production (GPA, MPA, EGPA) - when neutrophils/monocytes are primed by TNF-alpha, IL-1, or alternative-complement activation, PR3 and MPO translocate to the cell membrane where ANCA can engage them, triggering degranulation, reactive oxygen species, endothelial injury, and release of IL-1/IL-8. (3) Pathogenic T-lymphocyte responses and granuloma formation (GCA, Takayasu, GPA, EGPA) - cytokine (IFN-gamma) activated endothelium expresses HLA class II and interacts with CD4+ T cells, with IL-1/TNF-alpha inducing adhesion molecules (ELAM-1, VCAM-1). The 1992/2012 Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature underpins the classification of these syndromes by predominant vessel size (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942).

Suspect vasculitis in any patient with an unexplained multisystem illness; specific clues include palpable purpura, pulmonary infiltrates with microscopic hematuria, chronic sinusitis, mononeuritis multiplex, unexplained ischemic events, and glomerulonephritis with multisystem disease (Harrison 22e p.2937).
Saddle-nose deformity (from nasal septal perforation) and subglottic stenosis (~16% of GPA, may cause severe airway obstruction) are characteristic upper-airway sequelae of GPA (Harrison 22e p.2940).
Mononeuritis multiplex is a recurring vasculitic clue - common in EGPA (up to ~72%) and PAN (~51%), and also seen in GPA and MPA (Harrison 22e p.2940, p.2943, p.2944).

EGPA (Churg-Strauss) requires asthma, peripheral blood eosinophilia (>1000 cells/uL in >80%), and clinical features of vasculitis; eosinophilic tissue infiltration and extravascular granulomas are characteristic (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944).

Cardiac involvement (myocarditis, pericarditis, coronary vasculitis) is the leading cause of death in EGPA, accounting for ~39% of mortality; echocardiography is advised in all newly diagnosed patients (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944).

PAN does NOT involve pulmonary arteries and does NOT cause glomerulonephritis, granuloma, or significant eosinophilia; venule involvement points away from PAN and toward microscopic polyangiitis (Harrison 22e p.2944).

PAN classically causes microaneurysms of small- and medium-sized renal, hepatic, and visceral arteries; catheter-directed dye arteriography (MR/CT lack resolution) can be diagnostic when accessible tissue is unavailable (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945).

Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively in those over 50; jaw/tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, and headache precede the dreaded complication of ischemic optic neuropathy with sudden blindness - therapy should not be delayed for diagnostic testing (Harrison 22e p.2945).
GCA and polymyalgia rheumatica are considered spectrums of one disease - PMR occurs in 40-50% of GCA, and 10-20% of isolated PMR later develop GCA (Harrison 22e p.2945).
Takayasu arteritis should be strongly suspected in a young woman with diminished/absent peripheral pulses, an inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy, or arterial bruits (Harrison 22e p.2946-2947).
Hemoptysis may be the first sign of alveolar haemorrhage in MPA (~12%); upper-airway disease and pulmonary nodules are atypical for MPA and instead suggest GPA (Harrison 22e p.2942).

The first step in suspected vasculitis is to exclude conditions that mimic it - especially infections - particularly before starting empirical immunosuppression in a deteriorating patient (Harrison 22e p.2937).
GPA carries an increased risk of venous thrombotic events (DVT/PE); maintain a heightened awareness even though routine anticoagulation is not recommended (Harrison 22e p.2940).

Definitive diagnosis usually rests on biopsy of clinically involved tissue; 'blind' biopsy of organs with no clinical evidence of involvement has very low yield and should be avoided. Arteriography is used when PAN, Takayasu, or primary CNS vasculitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2937-2938).

ANCA-associated vasculitides (GPA, MPA, EGPA) share small-vessel involvement and ANCA positivity but have distinct clinical phenotypes and should be regarded as separate entities (Harrison 22e p.2937).

cANCA targets proteinase-3 (PR3) - present in >90% of active GPA; pANCA targets myeloperoxidase (MPO) - only anti-MPO antibodies are convincingly linked to vasculitis (MPA, EGPA, GPA, isolated necrotizing crescentic GN) (Harrison 22e p.2937).

A pANCA pattern NOT due to anti-MPO can occur in nonvasculitic conditions: rheumatic/nonrheumatic autoimmune disease, inflammatory bowel disease, certain drugs, and infections including endocarditis and bacterial airway infection in cystic fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2937).

ANCA titres do not reliably track disease activity - GPA can be active despite negative ANCA, titres correlate poorly with activity, and patients in remission may keep high ANCA for years (Harrison 22e p.2937, p.2941).

Predictive value of a positive ANCA in GPA is ~90% with active glomerulonephritis but falls to 30-60% in sinus/lung disease without renal involvement; tissue biopsy is then needed to exclude infection or malignancy that may give a false-positive ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2941).

In GPA the renal lesion is a pauci-immune (no immune-complex deposition) focal segmental glomerulitis that can evolve into rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940).

Treating a rise in ANCA titre as a relapse - only ~43% relapse within 1 year of an ANCA increase, so a rising ANCA alone should not prompt reinstitution or escalation of immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2941).
Missing DADA2 (adenosine deaminase 2 deficiency) in early-onset PAN-like vasculitis, which responds to TNF inhibitors rather than standard PAN therapy (Harrison 22e p.2944).

Relying on ANCA to diagnose vasculitis in sinus/lung disease without renal involvement, where positive predictive value is only 30-60% and biopsy is needed to exclude infection/malignancy with false-positive ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2941).
Performing 'blind' biopsies of clinically uninvolved organs - yield is very low (Harrison 22e p.2937).
Starting immunosuppression before excluding infectious mimics, especially in a rapidly deteriorating patient (Harrison 22e p.2937).
Irradiating upper-airway lesions assuming GPA when the diagnosis is actually NK/T-cell lymphoma - GPA airway lesions should never be irradiated (Harrison 22e p.2941).
Overlooking cocaine/levamisole-induced midline destruction, which can produce vasculitis-mimicking serology (anti-elastase ANCA) and granulocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.2941).
Using CRP/ESR to monitor disease activity or assess infection in GCA patients on IL-6 inhibitors, which suppress these acute-phase reactants (Harrison 22e p.2946).
Attributing every minor ESR/CRP rise during a GCA prednisone taper to a flare - small increases may not reflect arteritis, and can also be caused by infection (Harrison 22e p.2946).
Mislabelling a necrotizing vasculitis with venule involvement as PAN - venule involvement indicates microscopic polyangiitis, not PAN (Harrison 22e p.2944).

Untreated GPA was historically fatal within months; with cyclophosphamide-based therapy >90% improve, ~75% achieve complete remission, and 5-year survival exceeds 80%, but 50-70% of remissions later relapse and many accrue irreversible damage (renal insufficiency, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, saddle-nose deformity, chronic sinus dysfunction) (Harrison 22e p.2941). Treated MPA has a ~74% 5-year survival, with deaths from alveolar haemorrhage or GI/cardiac/renal disease, and relapse in at least ~34% (Harrison 22e p.2942). Untreated EGPA has a ~25% 5-year survival; treated, prognosis is favourable (~72% at 78 months), but myocardial involvement causes ~39% of deaths (Harrison 22e p.2944). Untreated PAN has a poor 5-year survival of 10-20% (deaths from GI and cardiovascular causes); prednisone plus cyclophosphamide markedly improves survival, with relapse in ~10-20% (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945). In GCA acute death is uncommon, but patients face late mortality from aortic aneurysm rupture/dissection (18x more likely to develop thoracic aortic aneurysm than the general population) (Harrison 22e p.2946). Takayasu outcomes vary widely (overall survival >=94% in some North American series; 5-year mortality 0-35% elsewhere), and the disease is usually chronic and relapsing (Harrison 22e p.2947). IgA vasculitis has an excellent prognosis with rare mortality and only 1-5% of children progressing to end-stage renal disease (Harrison 22e p.2948).
Active glomerulonephritis is always classed as severe disease even with normal renal function (Harrison 22e p.2941)
Alveolar/pulmonary haemorrhage - severe manifestation of GPA/MPA; hemoptysis may be the first symptom of alveolar haemorrhage in MPA (Harrison 22e p.2941, p.2942)

Visual symptoms in a patient over 50 with headache - ischemic optic neuropathy in GCA can cause sudden, irreversible blindness; do not delay treatment for diagnostic workup (Harrison 22e p.2945, p.2946)
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine in ANCA-associated vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940, p.2942)
Jaw/tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, or a tender/nodular temporal artery - cranial ischaemic features of GCA (Harrison 22e p.2945)
Inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy, absent pulses, or bruits in a young woman - suggests Takayasu large-vessel involvement (Harrison 22e p.2947)
Bowel infarction/perforation and GI bleeding in PAN - leading causes of death (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945)
Cardiac involvement in EGPA - the chief cause of death (Harrison 22e p.2944)
Signs of deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism in GPA given the increased venous thrombotic risk (Harrison 22e p.2940)

Vasculitides are classified by predominant vessel size per the Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942): LARGE-VESSEL (giant cell/temporal arteritis, Takayasu arteritis); MEDIUM-VESSEL (polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease); SMALL-VESSEL, which splits into ANCA-associated (GPA, MPA, EGPA) and immune-complex (IgA vasculitis/Henoch-Schonlein, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis). The chapter also separates PRIMARY syndromes from SECONDARY vasculitis (associated with probable etiology e.g. drug-induced, hepatitis-B/C-related, cancer-associated; or with systemic disease e.g. lupus, rheumatoid, sarcoid vasculitis), and single-organ vasculitis (cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, cutaneous arteritis, primary CNS vasculitis, isolated aortitis) (Harrison 22e p.2936). For management stratification, ANCA-associated vasculitis is divided into SEVERE (life- or organ-threatening; e.g., alveolar haemorrhage, and active glomerulonephritis is severe even with normal renal function) versus NONSEVERE/limited disease - severity depends on both extent and the specific organ involved (e.g., nodular pulmonary disease without respiratory compromise is nonsevere, whereas alveolar haemorrhage is severe) (Harrison 22e p.2941).
